exp.0:4:
Paul says that, through Jesus Christ, God gave him grace (a favor he did not deserve) and apostleship, that is, the assignment of being sent out as a messenger. His purpose is that people from all nations believe and obey. The obedience that comes from faith can be understood as obedience that springs from faith, or as obedience that consists in believing. Both ideas go together. All of this is done for his name, that is, by the authority of Christ.

Paul presents himself to the believers in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. He has just spoken of Jesus as the Son of God and a descendant of David. Now he explains his mission: to bring this message to all peoples, not only to the Jews. In this way he prepares the Romans for the rest of his letter.

For today: true faith does not stay in words. Today you can ask God to show you one concrete step of obedience to Jesus.
exp.0:5:
Paul tells the believers in Rome that they too belong to the nations among whom God calls people to obey through faith.

Paul writes this letter to the church in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. In the verses before this one, he explains that God gave him the task of calling all the nations to faith. Here he reminds them that they are not outside that plan, but inside it.

For today: your faith is not an accident or an achievement of your own, but a response to a call from Jesus. That gives you identity and purpose. Live today with the assurance that you belong to him and that he invited you first.
exp.0:10:
Paul says he longs to see the Christians in Rome so that he can share with them some spiritual gift and so strengthen them.

Paul is writing this letter to a church he had not yet met in person. Earlier he told them that he prayed for them and asked God for the opportunity to visit them. He does not speak with pride: in the next verse he makes clear that he also wants to be encouraged by their faith. Scholars understand that "spiritual gift" in different ways, and the text does not say exactly what it was.

For today: do not see your Christian life only as receiving. Seek out someone in your church, pray for that person, and share with them a word of encouragement or a teaching from the Bible. God can strengthen both of you.
exp.0:12:
Paul tells the Christians in Rome something he wants them to know: many times he planned to visit them, but something has kept him from coming until now. He wanted to have some fruit among them, meaning to see spiritual results in their lives, just as among the other non-Jewish peoples. "Gentiles" are those who are not Jews.

Paul writes this letter to a church he did not yet know in person. He makes clear that his absence is not a lack of interest. Although he does not say here what held him back, in Romans 15:22 he mentions that his work in other places kept him from coming.

For today: when you cannot be with someone you love, do not let them slip from your mind. Write to them, pray for that person, and look for them as soon as you can. And if your plans are delayed, trust that God is still guiding your path.
exp.0:17:
This verse says that God shows his righteous anger from heaven against all the wickedness and wrongdoing of people. Those people hold back the truth, that is, they suppress it or restrain it, because they prefer to live in what is wrong. Ungodliness means living without reverence for God, and unrighteousness means treating others badly.

Paul speaks here, writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that the gospel saves everyone who believes. Now he explains why all of us need that salvation: humanity has rejected the truth that God made known in creation, as the following verses say. Scholars debate how that anger is expressed, but the text indicates that God is not indifferent to evil.

For today: examine honestly whether there is some truth you are avoiding for the sake of comfort. Ask God for the courage to accept it and to live in line with it.
exp.0:19:
Although we cannot see God, this verse says that his eternal power and divine nature can be recognized when we look at what he has made. The words "clearly seen" mean that these things are plainly noticed and understood. The word "without excuse" means that no one has a reason to say they knew nothing about God.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome. Earlier he spoke of God's anger against those who hold back the truth, that is, who suppress it or reject it because of their wickedness. Here he explains that God has made himself known through creation, and that the problem is not a lack of signs, but that many did not respond with thankfulness or honor.

For today: when you see a sunrise, a tree, or the night sky, pause for a moment and give thanks to God. Let creation lead you to worship the Creator.
exp.0:28:
It says that those who rejected God ended up filled with every kind of wickedness. The list includes unrighteousness (injustice), fornication (sexual immorality), malice (a desire to harm), greed (always wanting more), envy, murder, strife (quarreling), deceit, and malignity (hidden ill will).

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Before speaking of the gospel as salvation for everyone, he shows that humanity needs to be rescued. He explains that when people turn away from God, he gives them over to their own corrupt minds, and this shows in their actions. The list continues in the verses that follow.

Today we can examine our hearts with humility. It is easy to point out the sins of others, but this list includes envy, strife, and deceit, which also touch us. Ask God to cleanse you and change you.
exp.1:4:
A stubborn person, one who does not want to change their attitude or turn back to God, is building up punishment for themselves, the way someone stores up a treasure, but of wrath. Storing up means gathering and keeping. That punishment will be seen on the day of judgment, when God will show that his judgment is completely just.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He had been speaking against those who judge others for their sins while doing the same things themselves. They think they will escape from God. Paul reminds them that God's kindness and patience are not permission to carry on as before, but an invitation to repent.

For today: do not confuse God's patience with indifference. If there is something God is showing you, do not put it off or make excuses for yourself. Tell the truth to him today, ask for forgiveness, and take one concrete step of change. His kindness is guiding you toward that path.
exp.1:11:
This verse says that everyone will be judged by God in a fair way. Those who sinned without knowing the law of Moses (the non-Jews) will also perish, that is, they will be separated from God. And those who sinned while knowing the law (the Jews) will be judged according to that law. To perish means to be lost, to not receive salvation.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that God shows no favoritism. The Jews might have thought that having the law would free them from judgment, and the Gentiles might have thought that without a law they had no guilt. Paul shows that no one escapes: everyone needs the mercy of God.

For today: do not use your knowledge of the Bible, your church, or your family as an excuse to feel secure, and do not think that ignoring God takes away your responsibility. Be humble, recognize your need for Christ, and live out what you already know of the truth.
exp.1:14:
This verse says that the Gentiles, although they did not receive the law of Moses, show that the essential part of the law is written on their hearts. Their conscience confirms this, bearing witness within them. Their thoughts sometimes accuse them when they do wrong, and at other times they defend or excuse them.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who were both Jews and Gentiles. He wants to show that no one can boast before God. The Jews had the law written down, but hearing it is not enough; it must be obeyed. The Gentiles, without that law, also have an inner sense of good and evil. Some understand that Paul speaks of Gentiles in general, and others of Gentiles who believe.

For today: do not ignore your conscience when it troubles you. Bring it to God with humility, asking him to shape it through his Word and to forgive you through Christ.
exp.1:22:
Paul asks a piercing question: does someone who boasts of having God's law dishonor God by disobeying that same law? To boast means to take pride in something or show it off. To break the law means to violate one of its commands. To dishonor God means to bring disrespect upon him through your conduct, failing to honor his name.

Paul writes to the church in Rome. Here he addresses someone who is confident in knowing the law, and many understand this to refer to Jews who felt superior. His point is that having the law or being circumcised is not enough if one's life does not reflect it. Everyone needs the grace of God.

For today: knowing the Bible or speaking well of the faith is not enough. Examine whether there is anything you teach others that you yourself do not practice, and ask God for help to live it out with humility.
exp.1:27:
This verse says that being a true Jew does not depend on what can be seen on the outside. Circumcision, the physical sign on the body, is not the most important thing either.

The speaker is the apostle Paul, writing to the Christians in Rome. He shows them that both Jews and non-Jews need God. Some Jews trusted in their heritage and their rituals, but they did not obey God. Paul tells them that what counts is the heart, as the next verse explains.

For today: let us not confuse faith with outward appearances, such as going to church, using certain language, or belonging to a tradition. Let us ask God to transform our hearts, so that our lives are sincere before Him.
exp.2:14:
They are quick to act, without God, in order to do harm. The verse says their feet are swift to shed blood, which means they rush to hurt or kill. The phrase shows that violence is not something that costs them effort, but something they run toward.

Paul is writing in his letter to the Romans. Here he gathers several passages from the Psalms and Isaiah (such as Isaiah 59:7) to show that everyone, both Jews and non-Jews, is under sin (Romans 3:9-12). He does not say that every person is equally violent, but that sin affects everyone and can lead to these extremes.

For today: violence begins in the heart, with anger, contempt, or harsh words. Today you can ask God to heal your anger and seek peace with someone before the resentment grows. Christ is the one who gives us forgiveness and a new heart.
exp.2:16:
It says that the people described have not known the path of peace. "Have not known" means they have not walked on it or made it their way of life. Peace here is not merely the absence of quarrels, but living in harmony with God and with others.

In his letter to the Romans, Paul brings together several quotations from the Old Testament, mainly from the Psalms and Isaiah (Isaiah 59:7-8), to show that everyone, both Jews and non-Jews, is under sin. The verse before speaks of violence and harm; this one says that no peace comes out of that. His aim is that no one should justify themselves and that everyone needs God.

For today: before judging others, let us recognize that we too need the peace that comes from God. Let us ask him to heal our words, reactions and relationships, so that we may be people who seek peace.
exp.2:17:
This verse says that the people it describes have no respect or reverence for God. "Fear of God" does not mean living in dread, but taking him seriously and honoring him. "Before their eyes" means that God is not in their minds or guiding what they do.

Here the apostle Paul is speaking. In Romans 3:10-18 he joins several quotations from the Psalms and from Isaiah to show that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, is under sin. This verse closes that list and returns to Psalm 36:1. Paul wants to reach his conclusion: no one is saved by keeping the law, but everyone needs the grace of God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, in our everyday decisions, we take God into account. Let us ask him for a heart that respects him and seeks to please him, with humility, knowing that we depend on his mercy.
exp.2:18:
It says that everything Scripture teaches as law is addressed to those who received it, that is, to the Jews. Its purpose is that no one has an excuse, and that everyone is silenced, with nothing to say in their own defense. Thus the whole world comes under accountability before God.

Here the apostle Paul speaks in his letter to the Romans. He has just cited several texts from the Old Testament that show that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, is under sin. With this he prepares the way to explain that salvation does not come from keeping the law, but from the grace of God.

For today: instead of justifying ourselves or comparing ourselves with others, we can humbly recognize that we need God. That honesty draws us closer to his mercy.
exp.2:20:
It says that now God has openly shown his righteousness, that is, his way of declaring people right before him, and that he did this without depending on the law of Moses. The word "but" at the start of the verse introduces this contrast. It also notes that this righteousness is not something new or contrary to Scripture, since the law and the prophets, that is, the Old Testament, already spoke of it.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that no one becomes righteous before God by keeping the law, because the law shows sin but does not remove it. With "but now" he changes the subject: after the bad news, he announces the solution. The following verse clarifies that this righteousness comes through faith in Jesus Christ.

Today we can stop trying to earn God's favor through efforts and merits. If you feel insufficient, trust in Jesus and rest in what God has already done. From there, obey with gratitude, not with fear.
exp.2:23:
God declares people righteous even though they do not deserve it. Being "justified" means that God accepts us and regards us as free from guilt before Him. "Freely" means as a gift, without payment. "Redemption" is release through a payment, like when a slave is bought back. That payment was made in Christ Jesus.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that everyone, both Jews and non-Jews, has sinned and falls short of the glory of God. For this reason, no one can be saved by their own merits. This verse presents the answer: God offers salvation as a gift through Jesus.

Today we can stop trying to earn God's love through effort and guilt. If you have trusted in Christ, you can come near to God with gratitude and peace, knowing that your place before Him is a gift, not a reward.
exp.2:25:
This verse says that God showed his righteousness at the present time, that is, in the era of Christ. In this way it is made clear that God is just and, at the same time, that he is the one who declares righteous everyone who trusts in Jesus. God's declaring someone free from guilt before him is what the verse is describing.

Here the apostle Paul speaks, in his letter to the Christians in Rome. He explains that everyone has sinned and that no one is saved by their own works. God passed over the sins of the past with patience, and on the cross of Christ he showed that he had not ignored them. Paul wants us to see that forgiveness does not make God unjust.

For today: when you feel unworthy, do not try to earn forgiveness through effort. Trust in what Jesus did for you and live with gratitude and peace.
exp.2:26:
It says there is no room left for boasting or for feeling superior before God. "Boasting" means pride or self-importance. "Excluded" means it was shut out. Paul asks by what principle boasting was shut out, and he answers that it was not by the principle of works but by the principle of faith, that is, trusting in what God did in Christ.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome, both Jews and Gentiles. He has just explained that everyone has sinned and that God makes people right with himself through faith in the blood of Jesus. So no one can claim credit of their own, neither the Jews through the law nor the Gentiles through their culture. Right after this he says that God is God of all.

For today: when you feel better than others because of your effort or your service, remember that your place before God is a gift. Be more thankful, compare yourself less, and treat others with humility.
exp.3:1:
Paul says that if Abraham had been declared righteous by his works, he would have reason to feel proud. But before God he has nothing to boast about. To be declared righteous means to be accepted by God. To boast means to show pride in something.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has been explaining that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, needs God's grace. Abraham was the great example for the Jews, so Paul asks what he found. Right away he answers from Scripture: Abraham believed God, and that was credited to him as righteousness.

Today we can remember that we do not win God's favor by our merits. If you feel inadequate today, trust in what God offers. If you feel superior, give thanks, because everything is his gift.
exp.3:5:
Paul says that David also spoke of the happiness of the person to whom God credits righteousness without that person having done works to earn it. The word "blessed" means happy, joyful, favored. "Credits" means that God places to someone's account a righteousness that the person did not earn by their own merits.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and explains that no one is saved by their works. Earlier he spoke of Abraham, and now he cites David, who in Psalm 32 celebrated God's forgiveness. With this he shows that Scripture teaches the same thing throughout its history: God justifies by grace, not by payment.

For today: you do not have to strive to earn God's love. You can come to Him with confidence, thankful for His forgiveness, and obey Him out of gratitude, not out of fear or to win His approval.
exp.3:8:
Paul asks whether this blessedness, the happiness of being forgiven, belongs only to the circumcised, meaning the Jews, or also to the uncircumcised, meaning those who are not Jews. He recalls that, according to Scripture, faith was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness. Being reckoned means that God regarded him as righteous.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, a community of both Jews and non-Jews. He has just quoted King David (Psalm 32) about forgiveness. He will soon show that Abraham was declared righteous before he was circumcised, so the promise is for everyone who believes.

Today, no one needs to belong to a particular group, perform a rite, or have a good record to be forgiven. We can come to God with simple trust, believing in his promise, and also receive with respect those who come from other paths.
exp.3:9:
Paul asks a question and answers it right away. He wants to know when God counted Abraham's faith as righteousness: was it when Abraham was already circumcised, or when he was still uncircumcised? The answer is clear: it was before the circumcision.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who were both Jews and non-Jews. He explains that God declares a person righteous through faith, not through rituals. According to Genesis 15, Abraham believed long before he was circumcised (Genesis 17). So Abraham is an example for everyone who believes.

For today: you do not need to earn God's favor through rites, merits, or a good record. Trust in Jesus just as you are, and let that faith show in the way you live.
exp.3:11:
This verse says that Abraham is the father of the circumcised, but not of all of them simply by that fact alone. He is the father of those who, in addition to being circumcised, walk in the steps of the faith that Abraham had while he was still uncircumcised. The word "steps" is the key: they are the footprints left behind, living the way he lived, trusting God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who were both Jews and non-Jews. He explains that God declared Abraham righteous because of his faith, before he was circumcised. So Abraham is the father of all who believe, and circumcision on its own does not save.

Today, belonging to a church, a believing family, or a tradition is not enough. God looks at the trust of the heart. Ask yourself: am I following in the steps of faith, trusting God even when I do not see the outcome?
exp.3:14:
It says that the law produces wrath, that is, God's righteous anger against sin. The law shows what God requires, and when someone fails to keep it, they stand under judgment. And where there is no law, there is also no violation, which means crossing over a clear command.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that Abraham received God's promise through faith, not by keeping the law. If the inheritance depended on the law, faith would accomplish nothing, because no one keeps it perfectly. That is why the promise comes by grace.

For today: instead of trusting that your efforts make you acceptable before God, humbly acknowledge where you fall short and rest in his grace. That trust also leads you to obey him out of gratitude, not out of fear.
exp.3:15:
The promise of God is received by faith, so that it is a gift of his grace and not a payment for obeying the law. In this way the promise stands firm and secure for all the offspring, that is, the descendants of Abraham. This includes those who have the law (the Jews) and also those who share the faith of Abraham, even though they have not received the law. Abraham is called the father of all who believe.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He has just said that if the inheritance depended on keeping the law, faith would be of no use. He wants to show that Abraham was counted as righteous because he believed, before receiving the law, and that for this reason the promise reaches everyone who trusts in God.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love by your performance. Trust in Christ and rest in his grace; from there, obey with gratitude and not out of fear.
exp.3:16:
Paul quotes the promise God made to Abraham: he would become "father of many nations." That promise holds good before God, the one in whom Abraham believed. Paul describes God as the one who gives life to the dead and who "calls those things which be not as though they were": he speaks of what does not yet exist as if it already existed, because his word is certain to be fulfilled.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that Abraham is the father of all who believe, whether they are Jews or not, because the promise is received through faith and by grace, not by keeping the law. Abraham and Sarah were already very old, and even so he trusted in God.

Today, when something seems impossible or without a way out, we can keep trusting that God keeps what he promises, even when we cannot yet see it. Praying and waiting in faith is a good first step.
exp.3:19:
This verse says that Abraham did not waver or become filled with distrust at what God promised him. On the contrary, he grew strong in his faith and gave glory to God.

Pablo writes to the Christians in Rome to explain that God declares a person righteous through faith, not through their works. He uses Abraham as an example. God had promised him a son, even though he was nearly a hundred years old and Sarah could not have children. His faith did not ignore the difficulty; he saw it and still trusted God.

For today: when your situation seems impossible, you do not have to pretend there is no problem. You can acknowledge it honestly and still rely on what God has said, thanking him in advance for his faithfulness.
exp.3:20:
Paul says that Abraham was completely certain that God would do what he had promised, because God has the power to carry it out. "Fully persuaded" means he had no doubts. "Able" means God has the capacity and the strength to do it.

Here the apostle Paul speaks in his letter to the Romans. He presents Abraham as an example of faith. Although Abraham and Sarah were already very old to have children, he trusted God's promise. Paul wants to show that God counted him as righteous because he believed, not because of his works.

For today: when a promise of God seems impossible, remember who God is and not only how your situation looks. You can pray and trust that he is faithful and capable, and keep going with patience.
exp.3:23:
This verse says that what God did for Abraham was not written for his sake alone, but for us as well. To those of us who believe in God, who raised up Jesus our Lord, the same thing will be credited to us. Being credited means having something placed to someone's account; here, God counts us as righteous.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that Abraham believed God's promise and for that reason was counted as righteous, not because of his works. Now he applies that example to all believers: the same faith unites us with Abraham.

For today: you do not have to earn God's favor through perfect efforts. Trust in Jesus, who died and rose again, and rest in the fact that God receives you through that faith. From there, live with gratitude and obey with joy.
exp.4:0:
This verse says that when someone trusts God and believes in Jesus, God declares them righteous, that is, He treats them as someone with no guilt before Him. For that reason there is no longer hostility toward God, but peace. That peace comes through Jesus Christ, not through our own works. "Justified" is a courtroom word: it means declared righteous.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, in his letter to the Christians in Rome. Before this verse he explained that everyone has failed and that Abraham was accepted because he believed. Now he sums up what that brings: peace with God. He then says that this faith gives us access to grace, hope, and strength, even in trials.

For today: if you feel guilty or far from God, remember that your peace with Him does not depend on your performance, but on Christ. Pray today, thanking Him, and rest in that peace.
exp.4:4:
This verse says that Christian hope does not leave us in shame, meaning it does not disappoint us or end in nothing. The reason is that God has poured out his love into our hearts, like water that fills completely. He does this through the Holy Spirit, whom God has given us as a gift.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome. He had been speaking about how, having been made right with God through faith, we have peace with God. For that reason he can say that even trials bear a fruit: patience, proven character, and hope. Then, in the verses that follow, he shows the greatest proof of that love: Christ died for us while we were weak and did not deserve anything.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, do not look only at the problem. Remember that God loves you and that his Spirit can confirm it to you. Ask him to give you that assurance and rest in it.
exp.4:8:
This verse says that if God has already declared us righteous through the blood of Christ, then much more will he save us from his wrath. "Justified" means declared righteous, forgiven, and accepted before God. "His blood" points to the death of Jesus on the cross. "Saved from wrath" refers to being delivered from God's judgment against sin.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he said that Christ died for us while we were still sinners. Now he reasons this way: if God did the hardest thing when we were enemies, he will surely do the rest now that we are his friends. He wants to give them security and hope.

For today: when you doubt whether God still accepts you, remember that your salvation rests on what Christ has done, not on your performance. Rest in that security and live thankfully, with confidence.
exp.4:9:
Paul says that we were enemies of God, but God reconciled us to himself through the death of Jesus. The word "reconciled" means that the broken relationship was restored. If God did the hardest thing when we were his enemies, how much more will he keep us now that we are his friends. The phrase about being saved by his life refers to the risen Christ, who lives and sustains our salvation.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, explaining that salvation is a gift from God received through faith. In the verses before this one he speaks of God's love, which was shown while we were still sinners. Here he states that this love gives us a firm hope for the future, including salvation from the wrath of God.

For today: if you doubt that God will sustain you because you feel weak or fail, remember that he loved you while you were far away. Rest in his love and speak with him with confidence, knowing that Christ lives for you.
exp.4:12:
This verse says that sin was already in the world before God gave the law to Moses. But it explains that where there is no clear law, sin is not charged to someone's account as a formal wrong. Even so, the next verse shows that death reigned during that time.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that everyone, both before and after Moses, is under sin and death through Adam. In this way he prepares the comparison with Christ, who brings grace and life. Scholars explain in various ways how being charged with sin relates to the death of those who did not have the law.

For today: let us not downplay sin by thinking, "If no one has told me, it does not matter." Let us humbly recognize our need for Jesus and rest in his grace, which is greater than our wrongdoing.
exp.4:14:
This verse says that God's gift is not like the fall of Adam, because it is far greater. Through the sin of one man, Adam, many died. But the grace of God, that is, his favor that we do not deserve, and the gift, abounded much more for many through Jesus Christ. The "gift" here is the free gift, and a "trespass" is a fall into sin or disobedience.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that we are made right with God through faith. Here he compares Adam with Christ, who is described as a pattern of the one to come. Adam brought death; Christ brings life. Paul wants to show that grace far exceeds sin. Scholars debate how far the phrase "the many" should be applied, but the central contrast is clear.

Today, when your failure or your past weighs on you, remember that the grace of Christ is greater. Receive it with humility and live thankfully, sharing with others the forgiveness you have received.
exp.4:18:
This verse compares two men: Adam and Jesus Christ. Through Adam's disobedience, the many were made sinners, that is, placed or declared in the condition of sinners. Through Jesus' obedience, the many will be made righteous, that is, placed in right relationship with God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he explained that everyone needs salvation and that it is received by faith. Here he shows that just as sin entered the world through one man, grace also came through one man. Christians debate how the effect of Adam's sin is passed on, but all agree that Christ is the solution.

For today: you do not have to earn God's acceptance by your own efforts. Rest in the obedience of Christ, and let that grace move you to obey him out of gratitude, not fear.
exp.4:20:
Here is how the verse reads. It says that sin functioned like a king who ruled over humanity and led it toward death. But now grace, that is, God's undeserved favor, is the one that rules. It does this through righteousness, that is, by giving people a right standing before God, and its goal is eternal life. Everything happens through Jesus Christ, who is called Lord.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He is comparing Adam, whose disobedience brought sin and death, with Christ, whose obedience brings righteousness and life. He closes this section by saying that grace has the final word.

For today: if you feel trapped by your failures or your past, remember that you no longer have to live under the rule of sin. Today you can ask Christ for help and trust that his grace is stronger than your weakness.
exp.5:10:
It says that believers should consider themselves dead to sin, but alive to God through Jesus Christ. Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that Christ died to sin once and now lives to God. Paul teaches that whoever trusts in Christ is united with him in his death and resurrection. That is why he asks them to see themselves this way, and from there he moves to practical commands: not to let sin rule over them.

For today: when temptation comes, remember who you are in Christ. Before you act, say in prayer: "Lord, sin is no longer my master; today I want to live for you." Then take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.5:12:
It says that we should not hand over the parts of our body to sin so that they become tools of wickedness. Instead, we should give ourselves to God, as people who have passed from death to life, and use our members as tools for doing what is right.

Here the apostle Paul speaks to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that, through union with Christ, the believer is dead to sin and alive to God. Now he encourages them to live in line with that new reality. Afterward he clarifies that grace is not permission to sin, but the strength that frees us from sin's control.

For today: each day we can ask ourselves how we will use our hands, words, and eyes. This morning, offer them to God in prayer and use them to serve, to speak the truth, or to help someone.
exp.5:19:
It says that when believers lived under the rule of sin, they had no relationship with righteousness. That is, they were free from it: it did not govern them, and they did not pursue it.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He uses the image of slavery, something very familiar in his time, to explain that no one lives without a master. He says he speaks in human terms so that they can understand him better. He reminds them that they once served sin, and now, through the work of Christ, they serve righteousness.

For today: ask yourself whom you are obeying in your daily habits. A freedom without God is often just another form of slavery. Today you can give God one concrete decision, such as your words or your time, and ask him for help to live in righteousness.
exp.5:21:
Paul says that now believers are no longer under the power of sin, but serve God. From that service comes a fruit: sanctification, which means being set apart for God and growing in a clean life that resembles Christ. At the end of this path is eternal life.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He is comparing two ways of life: serving sin, which leaves shame and ends in death, or serving God, which bears good fruit and life. He wants to encourage them to live according to the freedom Christ gave them, without using it as an excuse to sin.

For today: each day we can ask ourselves whom we are serving with our decisions. Ask God for help to leave a habit that harms you and practice one that brings you closer to Him, trusting that His grace sustains you.
exp.5:22:
This verse says that sin works like an employer that pays a wage: what one earns by working for it is death. Eternal life, by contrast, is not earned but received. The gift comes from God and is found in Christ Jesus, whom the text calls our Lord.

The speaker is the apostle Paul, writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he reminded them that living under sin brought shame and ended in death. Now, freed and made servants of God, their path leads to a transformed life and to eternal life. Paul uses the image of two masters to show the contrast. Many understand "death" as separation from God, and others also include physical death.

Today we can stop trying to earn God's favor through effort and receive his gift with gratitude. That gratitude, in turn, encourages us to serve him in the decisions of each day.
exp.6:0:
Paul asks the brothers whether they do not know something they already understand well: the law has authority over a person only as long as that person lives. Paul is speaking to those who know the law, that is, the law of Moses.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He has been explaining that in Christ we are free from the rule of sin. Now he uses the example of marriage, which appears in the following verses: death ends the legal obligation. Scholars discuss some details of the comparison, but the central idea is that death changes our relationship to the law.

Today we can live without fear of condemnation, because in Christ we are no longer under that yoke. That freedom is not an excuse for sin, but an invitation to obey God out of love and gratitude.
exp.6:3:
It says that believers "died" to the law through the body of Christ, that is, through his death on the cross. Now they belong to another: to Jesus, who was raised. The purpose is to bear fruit for God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He uses the example of marriage: the law releases the wife when the husband dies. In the same way, the person united to Christ in his death is freed from the law's dominion. Some explain the image in different ways, but the central idea is that we now live united to the risen Christ.

For today: do not live trying to earn God's favor through effort and fear. Belong to Christ, and let his life in you produce fruit such as love, patience, and kindness.
exp.6:9:
It says that God's commandment was given so that people would live, that is, to guide them toward a good and full life. But Paul found that, in his experience, that same commandment ended up leading him to death.

Paul speaks in the first person about the relationship between the law and sin. Interpreters debate whether he is referring to his childhood, his life before Christ, Israel, or a general human experience. What is clear is his point: the law is not bad, but sin takes advantage of it to show its power, as the next verse says.

Today we can recognize that not even the best rules can change our hearts. We need the grace of Christ, not only our own effort.
exp.6:18:
Paul says that he does not manage to do the good he wants, and that he ends up doing the evil he does not want. It is a struggle between what his heart longs for and what he actually does.

Paul writes in the first person, explaining how God's law shows sin but does not give the strength to overcome it. Many believers think he is speaking of his life before he knew Christ; others understand that he describes the believer's constant struggle. Scholars interpret it in both ways. In the next chapter, he speaks of the freedom that the Spirit gives.

If you feel that you fail even though you want to do what is right, do not lose heart or hide it. Acknowledge your weakness before God with sincerity, ask him for help each day, and rely on his grace, not only on your own effort.
exp.6:24:
Paul gives thanks to God through Jesus Christ, who answers his question about who will deliver him. Then he sums up his struggle: with the mind (his way of thinking and his deepest desire) he serves the law of God, but with the flesh, that is, his weak nature inclined to evil, he follows the law of sin.

Paul speaks in the first person and expresses great distress over the inner struggle between the good he wants and the sin that drags him down. Scholars disagree about whether he is describing his life before he knew Christ, his life as a believer, or a general experience. What is clear is that deliverance comes through Jesus.

Today, when you feel defeated by your own failures, do not stay stuck in guilt. Come before God honestly, give thanks for Jesus, and ask him for help with the next step.
exp.7:3:
What it says: God sent his Son so that what the law required as righteous would be fulfilled in us. This is for those who do not live according to the flesh, that is, guided by their impulses and selfish desires, but according to the Spirit, guided by the Spirit of God. Since the verse reads "the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us," the phrase means that God's just requirement is carried out in those who live this way.

Context: Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that the law could not save because human weakness stood in the way, but Christ condemned sin and set us free. Next, Paul contrasts two ways of living: that of the flesh, which leads to death, and that of the Spirit, which gives life and peace.

For today: We need not struggle only with our own strength. Each morning, ask the Spirit to guide your decisions, words and reactions, and trust that Christ has already given you a new life.
exp.7:5:
It says that the mindset of the flesh, that is, the way a person thinks, what they desire, and where they lean, ends in death. By contrast, the mindset of the Spirit leads to life and peace. Here "flesh" does not mean the physical body, but a life lived apart from God, driven by selfishness and sin. "Spirit" refers to the Holy Spirit who guides the believer.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has been explaining that Christ freed us from condemnation and that the believer now lives led by the Spirit. In this verse he contrasts two paths: what fills each person's mind shows where their life is heading. Some scholars understand "death" as separation from God, and others also see it as the decline of present life. Perhaps it includes both.

Today we can ask ourselves: what do I fill my thoughts with most? Praying, reading the Bible, and asking God for help every day directs the heart toward his peace.
exp.7:9:
It says that if Christ lives in the believer, the body is still subject to death because of sin, but the spirit has life because of righteousness. Some understand "spirit" as the human spirit made alive; others understand it as the Holy Spirit. Both readings are possible.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining the difference between living according to the flesh and living according to the Spirit. He wants to encourage them: although the body suffers and grows old, whoever belongs to Christ already has true life, and the next verse promises that God will also give life to their mortal bodies.

For today: when you feel tired, sick, or weak, remember that your worth and your hope do not depend on your body. Ask God to sustain you today, and trust his promise of resurrection.
exp.7:12:
This verse says there are two paths. If someone lives according to the flesh, that is, letting their desires and sinful nature rule them, they end in death. But if, with the help of the Spirit, they put to death the deeds of the body, they will live. Putting to death here means making sin lose its power over a person. The phrases about dying and living are commonly understood as separation from God versus full life with Him.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that the Spirit who raised Jesus lives in believers. That is why he says we owe nothing to the flesh. He will then show that those led by the Spirit are children of God.

For today: do not fight a bad habit alone. Ask the Spirit to strengthen you, and take concrete steps, such as staying away from what makes you fall and seeking brothers and sisters who can pray with you.
exp.7:21:
Verse 22 says that the whole creation groans and suffers together, like a woman in labor pains, and that it has continued this way until now. The word "creation" here refers to all that God has made, not only to people. The verse says that creation groans together, and "together" means at the same time as one. The labor-pain image is one of suffering that announces something new.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that creation was subjected to corruption and that it will be set free. Some think he speaks of nature as a whole; others, of everything created in general. His point is that the present suffering is not the end, but the prelude to something glorious.

For today: when suffering or a broken world wears you down, do not think that God has forgotten you. You can groan honestly before Him, and at the same time wait with patience, because that pain points toward a promised renewal.
exp.7:27:
It says that those who love God can be sure that everything that happens to them, even what is hard, God is guiding toward something good. Some understand that "all things" includes even suffering, and that this "good" refers above all to being shaped into the likeness of Christ.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of the weakness we feel, of the Spirit who prays for us, and of the sufferings of the present time. He wants to give them comfort: God has a firm purpose, which he then explains in the verses that follow.

Today, when you go through a painful situation, you do not have to pretend that it does not hurt. You can pray honestly and trust that God is still at work, even when you cannot yet see the result.
exp.7:28:
God, who knew his people beforehand, also appointed them in advance to be transformed so that they would resemble Jesus, his Son. In this way Jesus would be the firstborn, that is, the first and most honored, among a large family of brothers and sisters. Christians have understood the phrases about knowing beforehand and appointing in several ways, but all agree that the goal is for us to become like Christ.

Paul is writing to believers in Rome. He has just said that God works all things together for the good of those who love him, even in suffering. Here he explains what that final good is: being shaped into the image of Jesus. It is a promise that gives firmness.

For today: when you go through trials, remember that God can use them to shape your character. Ask him today to help you respond with the patience, humility, and love of Jesus.
exp.7:29:
This verse describes a chain of actions that God takes on behalf of those who belong to him: he predestined them, he called them, he justified them (declared them righteous, forgiven), and he glorified them (he will give them a fullness of glory with Christ). The verse is written in the past tense, as if everything were already accomplished, to show that God is sure in his work.

Paul is writing to the believers in Rome. He has just said that God uses all things for the good of those who love him, even in suffering. Here he gives them a firm reason: their salvation begins and ends in God. Christians understand differently how predestination and human freedom relate to each other, but the emphasis of the text is on assurance.

For today: when you doubt or go through trials, remember that your salvation rests on God's faithfulness, not on your effort. It rests on the fact that he will finish what he began.
exp.7:33:
This verse asks a question: who will be able to condemn those whom God has chosen? The answer is Christ, who died for us, rose again, is at the right hand of God (that is, in the place of honor and authority), and intercedes for us, that is, he pleads on our behalf before the Father.

The apostle Paul is writing to Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God gave up his own Son for us and that he is the one who justifies, that is, who declares the believer righteous. Paul uses questions like those in a courtroom to show that no one has the authority to condemn anyone who is in Christ. Afterward he speaks of the trials that cannot separate us from his love.

When guilt or the mistakes of the past speak loudly to you, remember that Christ has already died for you and today intercedes for you. Pray with confidence, without fear of being rejected.
exp.7:34:
Paul asks who could separate believers from the love of Christ, and he lists hard trials: tribulation (pressure and suffering), distress (a tightness of the soul), persecution, hunger, nakedness (lack of clothing and resources), danger, and the sword. In this older rendering, the sword refers to violence or death.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that God justifies them and that Christ died, rose again, and intercedes for them. That is why no one can accuse or condemn them. Now he applies that security to suffering. He quotes Psalm 44 to show that the pain of God's people is not a sign that God has abandoned them, and he affirms that in all these things they are more than conquerors through Christ.

Today, when you go through a trial, do not take it as proof that God has stopped loving you. Tell him honestly what you feel, and remember that Christ continues to intercede for you.
exp.7:37:
Paul says he is completely certain of something: nothing on the list he names will be able to separate us from God's love. He mentions death and life, angels, rulers, and powers (spiritual forces or authorities, and some think human authorities as well), the present, and what is to come. The sentence finishes in the following verse.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of suffering and persecution, and he quotes Psalm 44 to show that believers go through hard trials. Even so, he affirms that they triumph through Christ, who loved them. His certainty does not come from circumstances but from the love of God.

When fear, illness, loss, or an uncertain future make you doubt, remember that your security does not depend on how strong your faith feels at that moment, but on the steadfast love of God in Christ. Tell him so in prayer, and rest in that today.
exp.8:3:
Paul says that the Israelites received great privileges from God. They were adopted as his people, they saw his glory, they received the covenants, and the law was given to them. The phrase about the giving of the law is an old expression, and the rest of this comment has been removed because it explains a word not found in the verse above. They also received the service of God, that is, the way of worshiping him, and the promises.

Paul, a Jew who followed Christ, writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just expressed his deep sorrow because many of his people have not believed in Jesus. For that reason he lists what God gave them, to show how much his people are worth and how much their situation grieves him.

For today: value the blessings God has given you, but do not take them for granted. Use them to draw close to him, and pray with sincere love for those who do not yet know him.
exp.8:6:
Paul says that being a biological descendant of Abraham does not automatically make someone a true child of God. He cites Genesis 21:12: God said that the promised descendants would be called through Isaac, not through all of Abraham's children, such as Ishmael.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and feels great sorrow because many of his own people have not believed in Christ. Someone might think that God's word has failed. He answers that God has never promised salvation through blood alone, but has always worked through his promise and his calling.

For today: let us not trust our family, church, or tradition as if that could save us. What matters is to respond in faith to God's promise, and to give thanks that his love does not depend on our lineage, but on his grace.
exp.8:9:
This verse adds a second example. Paul says that this happened not only with Sarah and Isaac, but also with Rebecca, who conceived by one man, that is, became pregnant by one man, Isaac. He is referring to the twins Esau and Jacob, children of the same father and the same mother. The word "conceived" means to become pregnant.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and explains that being a descendant of Abraham does not guarantee being a child of the promise. With Isaac, and then with Jacob, he shows that God works according to his purpose and his calling, not according to family origin. Christian interpreters disagree about how to understand election in this passage, but all of them recognize that God acts by grace.

For today: do not trust in your family, your church, or your merits to feel accepted by God. Receive his calling with humility and gratitude, and treat others with the same grace that you have received.
exp.8:11:
It was said to her, Rebekah, the wife of Isaac, that God had told her her two twin sons would have different destinies: the older, Esau, would serve the younger, Jacob. This was contrary to the custom of that time, when the firstborn son held the place of privilege.

Paul speaks to believers in Rome, and quotes Genesis 25:23. He wants to show that God's promises do not depend on physical descent or on merit, but on his calling. He said this before the children were born or had done anything. Christians have understood in various ways how far this election reaches: whether it refers to nations, to individuals, or to both. Paul himself stresses that God is not unjust.

For today: we can rest in the fact that our relationship with God begins with his grace, not with our achievements. This leads us to humility and gratitude, instead of boasting or comparing ourselves with others.
exp.8:15:
This verse says that God's salvation and blessing are not obtained simply because a person wants them, nor through one's own effort. Everything depends on God, who shows mercy, that is, compassion we do not deserve.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just quoted what God said to Moses to answer a question: is God unjust when he chooses some people over others? Paul answers that he is not, because mercy is a gift from God and not a debt. Christians understand in different ways how this relates to human free choice, and among believers there is debate about this.

Today we can live with humility and gratitude, without boasting of our spiritual achievements. We can work hard and desire what is good, but rest in the fact that God sustains us by his mercy.
exp.8:24:
Paul quotes the prophet Hosea to say that God calls "my people" those who were not his people before, and "beloved" her who had not been beloved.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and explains that God's plan includes both Jews and Gentiles. Hosea originally spoke of Israel, which had turned away from God and yet would be restored. Paul applies those words to the Gentiles who are now being called. Some scholars see here an application of the principle, and others see a broader fulfillment; in either case, the theme is the mercy of God.

No one is so far away that God cannot draw them near. If you feel like an outsider or unworthy, remember that God's mercy calls you by your name. And toward others, show that same welcome.
exp.8:28:
It says that Isaiah had already announced something: if the Lord of hosts, God, had not left Israel a seed (that is, a descendant, a small remnant that survived), the people would have been destroyed like Sodom and Gomorrah.

Paul speaks here, quoting Isaiah 1:9. He is explaining why many of his people did not believe in Christ, and yet God's promise has not failed. God has always preserved a faithful remnant by his grace, not because of the people's merits.

For today: if you remain alive in faith, it is not by your own strength, but because God sustains you. Give thanks today for his mercy and trust that he cares for his own, even when they seem few.
exp.8:32:
It says that God placed in Zion, that is, in Jerusalem and among his people, a stone that causes some to stumble and fall. But whoever believes in it will not be put to shame, that is, will not be let down.

Paul is speaking here about Israel. Many sought to please God through their works and not by faith, and that is why they stumbled. Paul joins two passages from the Old Testament (Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16). Almost all Christians understand the stone to be Christ, as Peter also shows in his letter.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we trust in Jesus or in our own merits. We can stop trying to earn God's favor and rest in what Christ has already done. Whoever trusts in him can have peace, even when others see it as something strange.
exp.9:4:
Paul says that Moses described the righteousness that comes from the law this way: whoever does all its commandments will live by them. The point is that the law requires complete obedience in order to reach life.

Paul, in his letter to the Romans, speaks about his own people, Israel. They had zeal for God, but they wanted to gain his approval by their own effort, and they did not accept Christ. Paul contrasts this path with the righteousness that comes through faith, which he presents right after. Some scholars debate exactly how this contrast fits together, but the central point is clear: the law demands, faith receives.

Today it is easy to think that God accepts us because of how well we behave. This verse invites us to stop measuring ourselves by our achievements and to rest in Christ, obeying him out of gratitude, not out of fear or to earn his love.
exp.9:10:
This verse says that anyone who puts their trust in Jesus will not be put to shame. "Put to shame" means to be let down or disappointed, like someone who trusted in something and it failed them. The promise is that faith placed in Christ will never end in shame.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome and quotes the Scripture, probably Isaiah 28:16. He is coming from speaking about believing with the heart and confessing with the mouth. He then says that this promise is for everyone, Jews and Gentiles, with no difference. Paul wants to show that salvation is offered to everyone who believes.

Today, if you sometimes feel fear or hesitation about speaking of your faith, remember this promise. Trusting in Jesus will not leave you disappointed. You can speak of Him simply, knowing that God keeps what He promises.
exp.9:11:
This verse says there is no difference between the Jew and the Greek, that is, between the people of Israel and the other nations. Jesus is the same Lord over all, and he is generous with everyone who calls upon him, that is, who asks him for help and salvation in faith.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, made up of both Jews and non-Jews. He has just explained that salvation is received by believing in the heart and confessing with the mouth. Here he makes clear that this promise is for everyone alike, with no privilege based on origin. He will go on to say that everyone who calls upon the Lord will be saved.

Today, this text invites us not to look down on anyone or to think that someone is too far from God. We can pray and speak about Christ with anyone, knowing that he receives with generosity everyone who seeks him.
exp.9:12:
This verse says that anyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. The word "call" here means to pray to him, to ask him for help and trust him. "Saved" means receiving God's salvation, his forgiveness and life with him.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that there is no difference between Jews and Greeks, because Jesus is Lord of all and is generous to everyone who calls on him. Paul quotes a promise from the prophet Joel to show that salvation is open to all people. He then explains that people need someone to proclaim this good news to them.

Today, if you feel far from God or unworthy, this promise is for you. You can pray simply and put your trust in Jesus. And if you already know him, think of someone you could speak to about him.
exp.9:19:
Paul says that Isaiah spoke with great boldness (the word meaning here is with daring and without holding back). God declares that he was found by people who were not looking for him, and that he revealed himself to those who did not even ask about him.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and explains why many from Israel did not believe in Christ, while people from other nations did believe. He quotes Isaiah 65:1 to show that this had already been announced in the Scriptures. God was not failing: his plan had always included all peoples. The verses that follow show his patience with Israel.

For today: do not give up on any person who seems far from God. He can find them without their seeking him. Pray for them, treat them with love, and share your faith simply, trusting that God is the one who takes the initiative.
exp.9:20:
God says that all day long, that is, constantly and patiently, he stretched out his hands toward Israel. Stretching out the hands is a gesture of invitation and pleading, like someone calling another person to come back. But that people was disobedient (they did not want to obey) and gainsaying (they argued against him and answered back in opposition).

Paul quotes here from Isaiah 65:2. He has just explained that the gospel also reached non-Jews, something Moses and Isaiah had already announced. With this verse, Paul shows that most of Israel did not reject the message for lack of opportunity, but out of resistance. Even so, the image reveals the heart of God: he still keeps his arms open.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are answering God's invitation or arguing with it. Today is a good day to set aside pride, listen to his voice, and draw near to him with simplicity.
exp.10:2:
Paul is quoting the complaint of the prophet Elijah. He tells God that they have killed his prophets, that his altars have been torn down, and that he alone is left, and that now they are seeking his life.

Paul writes in a letter to the Romans and answers this question: Did God abandon Israel? He says no, and he offers himself as an example, since he is an Israelite. He recalls that Elijah (1 Kings 19) felt completely alone, but God answered him that he had kept seven thousand faithful people. In this way, Paul shows that God always preserves a remnant.

For today: when you feel alone in your faith or believe that everything is lost, remember that God sees what you cannot see. Speak with Him honestly, as Elijah did, and seek out other believers who will encourage you.
exp.10:3:
Paul quotes what God answered Elijah. The divine reply is the voice of God. God says he has kept for himself seven thousand men who never bowed the knee before Baal, that is, who did not worship that idol.

Paul speaks of Israel and asks whether God has rejected them. He answers that he has not. He recalls when Elijah, discouraged, thought he was the only faithful one left (1 Kings 19). God showed him that there were many more. Paul says that in his own time there was also a faithful remnant, preserved by God's grace, not by their merits.

When you feel alone in your faith, remember that God knows who belongs to him and always has other faithful people you cannot see. Take heart, remain faithful, and seek fellowship with other believers.
exp.10:5:
It says that salvation and God's favor come by grace, that is, as a gift that cannot be earned. If it depended on works, it would no longer be a gift. Grace and effort to earn something cannot be mixed as if they were the same thing.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just recalled that, in the time of the prophet Elijah, God preserved seven thousand faithful people. In the same way, in his own time, a group of believing Israelites remained, chosen by grace. Paul wants to show that God has not abandoned his people, and that this remnant exists by God's kindness, not by merit.

For today: if you feel tired of trying to be good enough for God, rest in his grace. Obey him out of love and gratitude, not to buy his acceptance.
exp.10:9:
This verse asks that the eyes of certain people be darkened so that they cannot see, and that their back be bent over forever. The phrase about bending the back means that their spine is bowed under a heavy burden, like slavery or constant suffering.

The apostle Paul quotes here Psalm 69:22-23, attributed to David. He speaks of many of his people, Israel, who had not recognized Jesus as the Messiah. But he soon makes clear that their fall is not permanent: in the verses that follow he says that their stumbling opened the door to non-Jews, and that God still has purposes for Israel.

For today: when someone rejects faith, let us not judge them with pride. Better to pray for that person with hope, remembering that God is still at work and that his mercy can reach anyone.
exp.10:12:
Paul now addresses the believers who were not Jews, whom he calls "Gentiles." He reminds them that he is an apostle sent to them, and he says that he magnifies his ministry, meaning that he values it and carries it out with seriousness and joy.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there were both Jewish and non-Jewish believers. He has just explained that the fall of many of his people opened the way for others to receive salvation. Here he clarifies that his work among the Gentiles has a broader purpose: according to the next verse, he hopes it will stir in some Jews the desire to turn back to God.

For today: value the calling God gave you and do it well, but without looking down on anyone. Let your faith and your service be so attractive that others want to know God.
exp.10:14:
This verse says that the rejection of Israel, that is, their turning away from God, brought about the reconciling of the world, because the gospel reached the Gentiles. Then Paul asks what will happen when Israel is accepted again. His answer is that it will be life from the dead, an expression that some understand as a great spiritual renewal and others as the final resurrection.

Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles, speaks to the non-Jewish believers in Rome. He honors his ministry and hopes that his own people will feel holy jealousy and that some will be saved. Right away he uses the picture of the olive tree to show that the Gentiles must not look down on Israel.

Today we can guard against spiritual pride. If God has received us by pure grace, we should pray for those who have turned away and treat them with hope, not contempt.
exp.10:16:
It says that some of the branches of the olive tree were broken off, and that you, being a wild olive tree (an uncultivated, wild olive), were grafted in among them in their place. In this way you came to share in the root and in the rich sap and abundance of the good olive tree.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there were both Jewish believers and believers from the nations. The broken branches represent the Israelites who did not believe; the wild olive represents the believers from the nations. Paul wants to keep the non-Jewish believers from thinking they are superior. Interpreters debate some details of the image, but the emphasis is clear: the blessing comes from the root, which is God's promise to Israel.

For today: remember that your faith is a gift, not something you earned. Treat others with humility and gratitude, and pray for those who do not yet believe.
exp.10:17:
It says we should not boast or look down on the branches, that is, the Jews who were broken off from the olive tree. If someone feels superior, he should remember that it is not he who supports the root, but the root that supports him.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, and he speaks above all to believers who are not Jews. He uses the image of an olive tree: the root represents God's promises to Israel, and the Gentiles were grafted into that tree. Paul wants to prevent pride and contempt toward the Jewish people.

Today we can remember that our faith rests on what God has done, not on our own merit. This leads us to live with humility and to treat with respect those who think differently or do not yet believe.
exp.10:18:
Someone might think: "The branches were cut off so that I could be grafted in in their place." "Grafted in" is an older way of saying joined to a tree that already exists. The wild olive is a tree that grows without cultivation.

The apostle Paul speaks to believers of non-Jewish origin in Rome. He uses the image of an olive tree, which represents God's people. Some branches, Israelites who did not believe, were broken off. Paul anticipates a proud attitude on the part of the non-Jews and corrects it: they do not hold up the root, but the root holds them up.

For today: remember that your place before God is a gift of his grace, not something you earned. When you feel tempted to look down on others, give thanks, be humble, and pray for them with compassion.
exp.10:23:
Paul uses the picture of an olive tree. You, who were not Jewish, were like a branch of a wild olive tree, cut off from its natural tree and grafted into a good olive tree, which goes against what is normal. So if God could do that with you, how much more can He graft the Jews, who are the original branches, back into their own olive tree?

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, many of them of non-Jewish origin. He wants them not to feel superior to Israel, which had largely rejected Christ. He reminds them that they are grafted in by God's kindness, not by their own merit.

For today: let us live with humility and gratitude. Everything we have in God is grace, so let us not despise anyone or give up on any person.
exp.10:25:
Paul says that Israel will be saved.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, both Jews and Gentiles, so that they will not think of themselves as better than the Jews who did not believe in Jesus. He uses the image of the olive tree: the Gentiles are branches grafted in, and the natural branches can be grafted back in. Christians do not agree on what "all Israel" means. Some think of the Jewish people in the future, others of all believers, Jews and Gentiles alike.

Today, do not look down on anyone with pride. If salvation is a gift from God, pray with hope for those who do not yet believe.
exp.10:27:
Regarding the good news of the gospel, the people of Israel appear as "enemies" of God, since most of them did not accept it, and this turned out for your good, you non-Jewish believers. But regarding the choosing, that is, God's selection of them, they remain deeply loved because of their ancestors: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The word "you" in the first part refers to the same people addressed here.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who were a mix of Jews and non-Jews. He explains to them that the rejection by many Israelites is not the end of the story. God opened the door to the nations, but he has not forgotten his promises to Israel. Some understand "enemies" as enemies of God, and others as opponents of the gospel; the text allows both readings.

Today we can treat with humility and love those who do not yet believe, without looking down on them with pride. If God remains faithful to his promises, we too can trust that he will not abandon us.
exp.10:30:
This verse says that the people of Israel, for now, have not believed in Christ. But God uses that situation to show mercy to the non-Jews (the Gentiles, that is, "you"). And the final goal is that Israel also receive that same mercy. "Mercy" means compassionate love that forgives us even though we do not deserve it.

Paul, a Jewish apostle, writes to the church in Rome, made up of Jews and Gentiles. He explains that God has not abandoned Israel, because his promises are not canceled (v. 29). Christians have understood in various ways how and when Israel will receive that mercy, but Paul makes clear that God has a plan of compassion.

For today: no one is beyond the reach of God's mercy. If you have received forgiveness, do not boast; give thanks and pray with hope for those who today seem far from God.
exp.10:33:
This verse asks two questions whose answer is obvious: no one. No one has fully understood the thoughts of God, and no one has been his counsellor, that is, someone who teaches him what to do.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has explained how God acts with Israel and with the nations, and he concludes that his mercy reaches everyone. Faced with something so great, Paul offers no more arguments but worships. He draws on ideas from the Old Testament, such as Isaiah 40:13, to remind us that God is wise beyond what we can measure.

Today, when you do not understand what God allows in your life, you can rest in the fact that he is wise and good. You do not need to have all the answers to trust him and worship him.
exp.11:4:
This verse says that although we are many different people, all who believe in Christ form one single body. Moreover, each one belongs to the others: we need one another and are united among ourselves.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, in his letter to the Christians in Rome. Before this verse, he asks them for humility: that no one think of himself more highly than he ought, because God gave each person a measure of faith. He uses the image of the body, with many parts and different functions. Afterward, he speaks of the different gifts God gives.

For today: do not compare yourself with others or feel useless. Today, look for a concrete way to serve someone in your church or community, and give thanks for the contribution of someone different from you.
exp.11:6:
This verse says that each person should devote themselves faithfully to the gift God has given them. Whoever has the gift of serving others in practical tasks, let them give themselves to serving. Whoever has the gift of teaching, let them give themselves to teaching. The word "teaching" here refers to the teaching of the truth.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that the church is a body with many members, and that each one has different gifts, given by the grace of God. Paul wants to prevent pride and envy, and to encourage everyone to help one another.

For today: do not compare yourself with others. Ask God in prayer how you can serve your church, and do it with steadiness and humility, knowing that your contribution is needed.
exp.11:7:
This verse continues the list of gifts that God gives to his church. It says that whoever has the gift of exhorting, that is, encouraging and advising, should devote himself to it. Whoever gives, that is, shares what he has to help others, should do so with generosity and sincerity, without hidden motives. Whoever leads, that is, directs, should do so with care and diligence. And whoever shows mercy, helping those who suffer, should do so with cheerfulness.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he asked them for humility, and he reminded them that they form one body with many members. Each one has a gift given by the grace of God, and all should use it to serve others. Then the passage goes on to speak of sincere love.

For today: think of one concrete way to serve this week, and do it with a good spirit. Helping with joy, without complaining or seeking applause, relieves the other person and honors God.
exp.11:15:
This verse says that believers should live in harmony and think alike about what matters. Having the same mind means sharing the same feeling and seeking the same good. Those who are proud are the ones who consider themselves superior. Joining with ordinary people, without looking down on them, is what it means to associate with the lowly. And being wise in your own opinion means believing that you are always the one who is right.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, where there were people of different backgrounds, Jews and non-Jews. In this passage he explains how faith is lived out in daily dealings: blessing those who persecute, sharing joys and sorrows, and seeking peace. The humility he asks for here helps keep the community from being divided by pride.

Today we can practice this by truly listening to someone who thinks differently, or by reaching out to someone who usually goes unnoticed, before insisting on being right.
exp.11:16:
It says that we should not return harm for harm. If someone does us wrong, we do not answer with another wrong.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome. In this passage he explains how to live out love in practice: with humility, unity, and compassion. Shortly after, he asks them to seek peace as far as possible and to leave vengeance to God, quoting the Scriptures (Deuteronomy 32:35). This shows that wrong received is not answered with self-righteous justice, but by trusting in God.

Today, when someone offends you, whether in person or on social media, do not repay them in kind. Wait, breathe, pray, and choose a calm and respectful response. In this way your witness speaks well of Christ.
exp.12:1:
This verse says that whoever opposes the authority is, in fact, resisting what God has established, and that such people bring punishment upon themselves.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, who lived under the power of the Roman Empire. He teaches them that the order and justice of rulers serve the good of society. The verses that follow explain that authority should punish evil. This text does not say that every ruler is just; other passages in the Bible show believers who obeyed God rather than unjust orders (Acts 5:29).

Today we can respect the laws and those in authority, pay what is owed, and pray for them, without ceasing to obey God in conscience.
exp.12:4:
It says we should submit to civil authorities for two reasons: to avoid punishment and, above all, out of conscience, that is, from an inner conviction that it is the right thing before God. Submit means living in obedience and respect. The rulers are the authorities, and the sword symbolizes their power to punish.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, a city that was the center of the empire. He explains that God uses the order and justice of the authorities to restrain evil and protect people. The verses that follow apply this to paying taxes. Christians have debated how far this obedience extends when a government commands something unjust or contrary to God, and this passage does not address that case directly.

Today, fulfill your obligations, such as paying taxes and respecting the laws, even when no one is watching, because you do it for God and with a clear conscience.
exp.12:5:
This verse says that Christians pay taxes because the authorities are God's servants, that is, servants whom God allows to maintain order. Taxes are the money people pay to the government. The phrase "attending continually upon this very thing" means they devote themselves to that task: governing, protecting justice, and restraining evil.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, who lived under the empire. He had been speaking about submitting to the authorities, not only out of fear of punishment but out of conscience. Paying taxes was a concrete way of living out that attitude. Some scholars think there were tensions over taxes in Rome, but this is debated.

For today: fulfill your obligations, such as declaring and paying what is owed, with honesty and without resentment. Do it as an act of integrity before God, even when you do not agree with everything the government does.
exp.12:7:
It says we should not owe anyone anything, that is, we must pay what is due. But there is one debt that is never fully paid: loving others. The person near us is "neighbor", and whoever loves is already doing what God asks in his commandments.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He had been talking about paying taxes and giving respect to whom it is due. Now he widens the idea: beyond legal obligations, we all have a debt of love. He then explains that commandments such as not killing or not stealing are summed up in loving your neighbor as yourself.
