For today: before thinking only about keeping rules, ask yourself how you can treat with love the person in front of you. Pay your bills on time and, in addition, do one concrete act of kindness for someone today.
exp.12:10:
Paul says it is already time to wake up from spiritual sleep. Paul explains that the full salvation is now nearer than when we first began to believe. "This" refers to living in love, as he said before.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, and he has just explained that love sums up the law. Now he gives urgency to that call: the time is short and Christ will return. Believers interpret in different ways when that final salvation will happen, but all agree that Paul asks us to live awake and alert, not distracted or spiritually asleep.

Today we can ask ourselves: in what area have I been spiritually drowsy? Perhaps it is a relationship I have neglected, or a habit I keep postponing to change. Choose one concrete thing and act today, asking God to help you love someone through actions.
exp.12:11:
This verse uses the image of night and day. The night is life without God, and the day is the new life that is drawing near with Christ. That is why Paul says we should cast off, or set aside, the works of darkness, meaning bad habits. Instead, we should put on the armor of light, that is, live with clean and steady conduct.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that love fulfills the law, and now he calls them to wake up from spiritual sleep. The salvation that is nearer is complete salvation, which will come when Christ returns. Interpreters debate how to understand that timing, but the call to live with urgency is clear.

Today we can ask ourselves which habit lulls us spiritually to sleep. This week, let us set aside one of them and practice something concrete of light: an act of love, honesty, or service.
exp.12:12:
Paul invites us to live honorably, as people who live in the full light of day. He names behaviors we must leave behind: eating and drinking to excess, sexual immorality, and quarrels and jealousy. Quarrels are fights or disputes, and jealousy is envy.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that the night is nearly over and that the day of salvation is drawing near. For this reason he calls them to put aside the works of darkness and to clothe themselves with Jesus Christ, as the following verse says.

Today we can ask ourselves what hidden or disordered habit keeps us from living in the light. Perhaps it is excess, a harmful relationship, or resentment. Today you can bring it to God in prayer and ask him for strength to begin again.
exp.13:1:
Here the verse says that some people have the freedom of conscience to eat anything, without worrying about rules about food. Another person, whom Paul calls "weak" in the faith, eats only vegetables, that is, herbs and greens. The word "weak" here is not an insult; it speaks of someone whose conscience still feels bound by certain restrictions.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where believers of Jewish background and believers of non-Jewish background lived side by side. There were disagreements about food, and not all the reasons are known for certain; they could have been rules from the law, or avoiding meat offered to idols. Paul does not want these differences to divide the church.

For today: when another believer acts differently from you in secondary matters, do not despise or judge them. Receive them with respect, and remember that you both answer to the same Lord.
exp.13:2:
This verse says that the one who eats everything should not look down on the one who avoids certain foods, and the one who does not eat them should not criticize the one who does. The reason is that God has already received both. To look down on someone is to treat them as if they were worth little, and to judge here means to condemn the other person.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome, where believers of Jewish background and believers of non-Jewish background lived side by side. They had differences about food and special days. Paul is not dealing with the central truths of the gospel, but with matters where people's consciences differ. That is why he asks that the one who is weaker in faith be welcomed without fighting over opinions.

Today, when another believer does something differently from you in a secondary matter, such as the kind of music or certain customs, do not look down on them or condemn them. Remember that God has accepted them too, and treat them with respect.
exp.13:6:
It says that none of us lives only for himself, and no one dies only for himself. Our life and our death have to do with others and, above all, with God.

Here the apostle Paul is speaking to the Christians in Rome. There were disagreements among them about which days to keep and which foods to eat. Paul reminds them that, although they think differently on those matters, each one seeks to honor the Lord. Therefore they must not judge or look down on one another. The verses that follow explain that we belong to Christ, both in life and in death.

For today: before criticizing a brother who thinks differently on secondary matters, ask yourself whether he is trying to honor God. Respond with respect, patience, and love, remembering that both of you belong to the same Lord.
exp.13:8:
Here is what it says: Christ died and came back to life with a clear purpose: to be Lord over everyone, both those who have already died and those who are still living.

Context: Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome, where some were judging one another over differences about food and special days. Just before this verse he says that we belong to the Lord, in life and in death. Here he gives the reason: Christ paid that price and has authority over all. So judging a brother or sister means taking a place that belongs only to Christ.

For today: When you find it hard to accept a fellow believer who thinks differently on secondary matters, remember that he also belongs to Christ. Before you criticize him, pray for him and treat him with respect, leaving the judgment in the Lord's hands.
exp.13:12:
Paul says that we should no longer judge one another. Instead, we should firmly decide not to put a stumbling block or an occasion to fall in our brother's way. A stumbling block is something that makes another person fall; an occasion to fall is a trap that leads him to sin or to lose his faith.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there were believers with different views about foods and special days. Earlier he reminded them that all of us will give account to God, so it is not our place to be judges of others. Then he explains that, although the food itself is not wrong, it can harm someone whose conscience has doubts.

For today: before criticizing someone for a questionable practice, ask yourself how you can care for his faith. Sometimes love means giving up something that seems permissible to you, so as not to wound a brother.
exp.13:13:
Paul says that he is convinced, trusting in the Lord Jesus, that no food is unclean in itself. But if someone believes that something is unclean, then for that person it is unclean.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome, where there was tension between believers from a Jewish background, who kept the rules about food, and believers from a non-Jewish background, who ate everything. Paul does not order them to fight over this. He asks them not to judge one another and not to cause a brother to stumble, because each one will give an account to God.

Today, there are matters where sincere Christians think differently, and these are not sins in themselves. Before using your freedom, ask yourself whether it will help or wound a brother's conscience. Love first, and avoid arguing over secondary matters.
exp.13:14:
It says that if your brother is hurt or saddened by what you eat, you are no longer acting in love. And it asks you not to ruin, because of your food, someone for whom Christ died. Paul writes to the believers in Rome, where there were disagreements about food. Some believed certain foods were unclean; others, with a freer conscience, ate everything. Paul says that nothing is unclean in itself, but he asks the strong not to despise or cause to stumble those whose conscience is more sensitive.

Today, before you use your freedom in matters the Bible neither commands nor forbids, think about how it will affect the person near you. Love sometimes means giving way, without imposing your opinion or mocking another's conscience.
exp.13:16:
This verse says that the kingdom of God, that is, the way God rules and lives among his people, does not depend on what one eats or drinks. What marks it is righteousness (living in an upright way), peace, and the joy that the Holy Spirit gives.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there were believers with different views about certain foods. Some felt free to eat anything and others did not. Paul asks that those who feel strong not wound or cause to stumble those whose conscience is more sensitive. He reminds them that Christ died for them.

Today, do not make your tastes or customs a reason to quarrel with other believers. Before arguing, ask yourself whether your attitude promotes peace and helps build up your brother or sister. Try to care for others with love.
exp.13:22:
Romans 14:23 says that whoever doubts whether something is right and does it anyway is condemned, because he did not act from faith, that is, from a conviction held before God. Whoever has doubts in his conscience is the one described here. Being condemned means being found guilty. Anything done against one's own conviction, without trust in God, is sin.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where some believed certain foods or days were forbidden and others felt free. He asks them not to despise or judge one another. Here he teaches that each person should act according to his conscience before God, without causing others to stumble. The word "faith" here is understood mainly as a conviction of conscience, though some read it more broadly.

Today: before doing something questionable, pray and ask yourself whether you can do it with peace before God. And do not pressure others to act against their conscience.
exp.14:0:
This verse says that Christians whose faith is more mature and secure should patiently carry the weaknesses of those who are less firm. The word "bear" means to endure or help carry a burden. The "weak" are those who are weak in faith or in conscience. And "not to please ourselves" means not living only to seek what we enjoy or what suits us.

Paul writes to the believers in Rome. In the previous chapter he speaks of disagreements over foods and special days. Some had a more sensitive conscience and others a freer one. Paul includes himself among the strong and asks them not to despise others, but to support them, following the example of Christ.

For today: if you have more clarity or experience in the faith, do not mock someone who still doubts or struggles. Be patient, listen, help, and avoid doing anything that would make them stumble, even when you have the freedom to act.
exp.14:1:
It says that each of us should try to please our neighbor, that is, the people who are near us. But not to flatter them or to look good, but for their good and for their edification, that is, to help them grow and be strengthened in faith.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were differences among believers about foods and special days. He asks that the stronger in faith be patient with the weaker and not think only of themselves. Right away he gives Christ as the example, who did not seek his own.

Today, before you give an opinion or act, you can ask yourself how to help that person grow. For example, being patient with a brother or sister who is just beginning in the faith, encouraging them kindly instead of criticizing them.
exp.14:3:
Paul says that whatever was written in earlier times, meaning the Scriptures of the Old Testament, was written down to teach us. Its purpose is that, through steady endurance and through the encouragement the Scriptures give, we might have hope.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome, where there were tensions between believers from different backgrounds. He has just quoted a psalm about Christ, who endured insults without seeking his own pleasure. Paul shows that those ancient words had a purpose for the church of his own time. Then he prays that God would give them unity.

For today: read the Bible regularly, not only to be informed, but to ask God for strength in difficulties. And when it is hard for you to get along with someone, remember how Christ bore with others, and ask him for patience.
exp.14:7:
Paul says that Christ Jesus became a servant of the circumcision, that is, a servant to the Jewish people (the circumcised). He did this for the truth of God, meaning God's faithfulness to his word, in order to confirm the promises God made to the fathers, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where Jews and non-Jews had tensions. He asks them to accept one another as Christ accepted them. He reminds them that Jesus first served Israel, fulfilling what had been promised, and that this also opens the way for the Gentiles to glorify God for his mercy, as the following verse says.

For today: if Christ became a servant for others, we can patiently accept those who are different from us in culture or customs, and seek unity so that God may be glorified.
exp.14:10:
Paul quotes an invitation for all the nations that are not Jewish to praise the Lord. "Gentiles" means the peoples who do not belong to Israel. The word "all" shows that no one is left out of this invitation.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, where Jewish and non-Jewish believers were experiencing tension. Here he quotes the Old Testament, which appears to be Psalm 117:1, to show that God always wanted the nations to praise him. It is the third quotation in a row with that same purpose: to encourage them to accept one another and to worship together.

For today: praise belongs to no one and has no boundaries. This week, look for a way to praise God alongside someone very different from you, from another culture, age, or church, and welcome that person as God welcomes them.
exp.14:11:
This verse says that Isaiah announced that a descendant of Jesse, the father of King David, would come. That descendant will rise to rule over the Gentiles, that is, the nations that were not Jewish, and they will place their hope in him.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews, who had tensions between them. He quotes the Old Testament (Isaiah 11:10) to show that God always planned to include all peoples. Many understand that this descendant of Jesse is Jesus.

Today we can remember that hope in Christ is for everyone, regardless of origin or culture. This week, approach someone different from you with respect and kindness, and pray that Christ may be their hope too.
exp.14:13:
Paul tells the Christians in Rome that he is sure they are full of goodness and knowledge. For that reason they are able to admonish one another, that is, to advise and correct one another with kindness.

Paul writes this letter to a church he had not yet met in person. After giving several instructions, he softens his tone and acknowledges the good that is among them. In the verses that follow he explains that he was direct in some parts because God entrusted him with serving the Gentiles, that is, the non-Jewish peoples.

For today: when you have to correct someone, begin by recognizing the good that God has already done in that person. A word spoken with respect and trust is received better, and it helps us grow together in faith.
exp.14:14:
Paul tells the brothers in Rome that he has written to them in this letter with considerable frankness on some points. He did it to remind them of things they already knew. He explains that he can speak this way because of the grace, or favor, that God has given him.

Paul is the one writing. He has just praised the Christians in Rome, saying they are full of goodness and knowledge. Even so, he does not want them to think he is correcting them out of pride. He makes clear that his authority comes from the calling God gave him as a servant of Jesus Christ to the Gentiles, that is, the non-Jews.

We can correct or encourage others, but with humility, without pride, and with respect. Before speaking, it is good to acknowledge the good that is in the other person. In this way the truth is spoken with firmness, but also with love and grace.
exp.14:17:
Paul says that he would not dare to speak of anything that Christ has not accomplished through him. He is referring to what Christ achieved in bringing the non-Jewish nations (the "Gentiles") to obey God, both by his words and by his deeds.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that he is a minister of Christ to the Gentiles and that he can boast about what God has done. Here he makes clear that he does not take pride in his own merits, but in the work of Christ through his ministry. The verses that follow mention miracles and the power of the Spirit.

For today: when God uses your life to bless others, give the credit to Christ and not to yourself. Serve with humility, with words and with deeds, and trust that it is He who gives the fruit.
exp.14:18:
Paul says that the gospel advanced through mighty signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God. Because of this, from Jerusalem and its surroundings all the way to Illyricum, he fully preached the gospel of Christ, that is, he proclaimed it completely in that region.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and wants them to know him before he visits them. He does not boast about himself, but about what Christ has done through him. Illyricum was northwest of Greece. We do not know for certain whether he reached it or only its borders.

For today: do your work for God with effort, but depend on the Spirit. When something good comes of it, do not keep the glory for yourself; give it to Christ, who truly gives the fruit.
exp.14:22:
Here Paul says that he no longer has any room left in these regions, meaning that he had already proclaimed the gospel throughout that area of the eastern Mediterranean. In addition, for many years he had longed to visit the believers in Rome.

Paul probably wrote this letter from Corinth. Earlier he had explained that his aim was to preach where Christ was not yet known. That kept him from going to Rome many times. Now he feels that his work in those lands has reached its conclusion, and he thinks of Spain, passing through Rome. Scholars are not certain whether he actually went to Spain.

For today: let us learn from Paul to have clear goals and to wait with patience. God may delay our plans while he uses us somewhere else, and that waiting is also part of his purpose.
exp.14:30:
Paul asks the Romans to pray that God will deliver him from the unbelievers in Judea, that is, from those who did not believe and opposed him. He also asks that the gift he is bringing to Jerusalem will be well received. The "saints" are the believers.

Paul writes from Corinth, near the end of his third journey, before going to Jerusalem. He is carrying financial help that the churches of Macedonia and Achaia gathered for the poor believers there. He knows he is in danger, and he is also concerned that some Jewish believers may distrust him and not welcome the offering from non-Jewish churches. That is why he asks for prayer.

For today: do not face the hard things alone. Ask others to pray for you, and pray for them. Also, pray that your service will be done with humility and become a blessing.
exp.14:31:
Paul says that he hopes to come to the brothers and sisters in Rome with joy, if God permits it, and to be refreshed together with them.

Paul writes at the end of his letter to the Romans. Before going to Rome, he will bring a gift to the poor believers in Jerusalem, and he knows there is danger there. That is why he asks them for prayer. Note that he speaks of God's will: he does not take his arrival for granted, but his plans depend on God. How his journey went, the Bible tells later in Acts.

For today: make your plans with hope, but commit them to God in prayer. And seek the company of other believers, for God uses his people to give us encouragement and rest.
exp.15:7:
Paul sends greetings to Amplias and calls him "my beloved in the Lord." Paul does not only name him; he expresses real affection for him, and he makes clear that this affection rests on the faith they share in Christ.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. At the end he sends greetings to many people by name. We know nothing more about Amplias; the Bible does not tell his story. It was a common name in that time, and yet Paul remembers him with warmth.

For today: set aside time to express appreciation to someone in your church or your close circle, even if that person is little known. A sincere message or phone call can encourage them greatly, because in Christ no brother or sister goes unnoticed.
exp.15:9:
Paul asks that Apelles be greeted, saying he was "approved in Christ." This means his faith had been tested and had come through approved, like gold that withstands the fire. He also says to greet "them which are of Aristobulus' household," that is, those in his house, who could have been relatives or servants.

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. At the end he names many brothers and sisters to show closeness and honor. We do not know more about Apelles, nor whether Aristobulus was a believer; some think only part of his household was, but this cannot be stated with certainty.

Today we can imitate Paul: recognize by name and with affection those who have remained faithful through trials. A word of gratitude to someone who has served with steadiness can greatly encourage their faith.
exp.15:10:
Paul sends greetings to Herodion, whom he calls his kinsman, meaning a relative or a fellow Jew (the word can mean both). He also greets those of Narcissus's household, but only those who are in the Lord, that is, the believers in that household.

Paul is writing this letter to the Christians in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. At the end he names many people to show them affection and to strengthen the unity of the church. Who Narcissus was exactly is not known for certain; some think he may have been a well-known person in Rome, but this is only a guess. The household included family members and servants.

Today we can follow Paul's example: remember others by name, value believers who go unnoticed, and express appreciation to them through a greeting, a message, or a prayer.
exp.15:14:
Paul asks that a group of people be greeted: Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas. He also sends greetings to all the believers who are with them. The word "greet" in this verse is the instruction to pass on greetings from him. "Saints" refers to the Christians, the people set apart for God.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, and at the end he names many people. These were probably groups that met in homes. The Bible says nothing more about exactly who they were; some think Philologus and Julia were a married couple or relatives, but that is not certain.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to those whom almost no one remembers. We can follow Paul's example by encouraging others by name: today, write to or greet someone in your church and thank God for their faith.
exp.15:15:
Paul asks that Christians greet one another with a holy kiss. It was a greeting of affection and respect between brothers and sisters. He then adds that all the churches of Christ send their greetings.

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Rome and, at the end, greets many people by name. With that greeting he wants to unite the church and show that it is not alone, but part of a larger family. Afterward he warns about those who divide the community.

Today we can care for unity through simple gestures: greeting one another warmly, shaking hands or giving a hug, and reaching out to anyone who feels lonely in the church. Greetings vary from culture to culture, but sincere love remains the same.
exp.15:19:
It says that the God who gives peace will soon crush Satan under the feet of the believers in Rome. "Crush" means to destroy or grind down, and "soon" means quickly. Then Paul wishes them the grace, or undeserved favor, of Jesus Christ to be with them.

Paul writes to the church in Rome. He has just warned them against people who cause divisions and deceive the simple with smooth words. He asks them to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil. His promise recalls Genesis 3:15. Scholars discuss when and how it is fulfilled: whether in the history of the church, or fully at the end.

Today, facing deception and division, we are not alone. We can stand firm in the truth, pursue peace, and trust that God holds the final victory, relying on his grace each day.
exp.15:23:
The verse is a blessing: Paul wishes that the grace of Jesus Christ, that is, his undeserved favor and kindness, be with all the believers in Rome.

Paul dictates this letter, and Tertius, his secretary, writes it down and adds his own greetings. Paul is probably in Corinth, surrounded by companions and friends such as Gaius and Erastus, who send greetings to the brothers and sisters in Rome. Many scholars note that this verse is missing from some ancient manuscripts, where a similar blessing appears in verse 20, and the letter ends with the praise in the verses that follow. For that reason the textual tradition shows some variation.

For today: before you say goodbye to someone, truly bless them. A short prayer or a word of encouragement reminds them that they live by God's grace and not by their own merits.
exp.7:22:
This verse says that not only creation suffers and groans, but we too, as believers. We have the "firstfruits of the Spirit," that is, the first taste, the first sample of what God will give in full. Even so, we groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption as sons, which means the full showing that we are children of God, and for the redemption of our bodies: that our bodies be transformed and freed from suffering and death.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has been speaking of how the whole creation suffers because of the effect of sin and waits to be set free. He wants to encourage believers: their present pain is not the end, and God has already given them the Spirit as a guarantee of what is coming.

For today: if you feel weariness, sickness, or sadness, do not pretend that everything is fine. Groan honestly before God, but with hope, remembering that the Spirit in you is the promise that the best is still to come.
exp.0:7:
Paul begins by saying that the first thing he does is give thanks to God, whom he calls "my God," through Jesus Christ. He gives thanks for all of you in Rome, because your faith is being proclaimed all over the world, that is, throughout the whole known world of that time. The words "first" and "because" point to what matters most to him and why he is thankful.

Paul writes to them from afar, since he had not yet personally met this church. Before speaking of teaching or asking for anything, he greets them with sincere gratitude. In this way he shows affection and builds a bond with them. The verses that follow say that he prays for them and wishes to visit them.

Today we can imitate him: before criticizing or asking, let us take the time to thank God for other believers. And when we see faith in someone, let us tell them, because that encourages them.
exp.0:29:
This verse continues a list of behaviors that Paul describes in people who have turned away from God. Those who slander others and damage their reputations are slanderers, and those who speak with contempt and insolence toward others show a spirit of disrespect. "God-haters" can be understood as people who hate God or as people whom God views with displeasure; it is interpreted both ways. The arrogant believe themselves superior to everyone else, and the boastful constantly promote themselves, while those who invent new forms of evil seek fresh ways to do harm, and those who disobey their parents refuse the authority God has placed in their lives.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that all of humanity needs the gospel, because when God is rejected, life becomes disordered. This list prepares the ground for saying that all of us need the grace of God.

Today we can examine our words: do we speak badly of someone or tear down their reputation? This week, let us ask God for help to bless rather than criticize, and to honor our parents with respect and gratitude.
exp.10:7:
It says that God gave many of Israel a "spirit of stupor," a dullness of heart that left them unable to perceive what God was doing. They had eyes and ears, but they could not see or hear the truth. And this continued "to this very day," that is, until the time of Paul.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and explains why many of his people did not receive Christ, while a group chosen by grace did. To support this, he cites the Scriptures, with echoes of Deuteronomy 29:4 and Isaiah 29:10. He does not say that the door was shut forever; later he shows hope for Israel.

Today, ask God for a sensitive heart. Before reading the Bible, pray: "Lord, open my eyes and my ears." And listen with humility, without trusting in your own merits.
exp.7:6:
This verse says that thinking and living according to the flesh means being hostile to God. The "mindset" is the way of thinking, what a person wants and pursues. The "flesh" here does not mean the body, but our human nature living apart from God. Its mindset does not submit to God's law, and it is not able to do so.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has been explaining that whoever lives according to the flesh ends in death, while whoever lives according to the Spirit finds life and peace. Then he encourages believers: God's Spirit lives in them, so they are no longer controlled by the flesh.

Today we can ask ourselves what fills our minds most each day. A practical idea is to begin the morning by asking the Spirit to guide our thoughts, and not to rely only on our own willpower.
exp.13:7:
It says that our whole life belongs to the Lord. If we are alive, we live for him; if we die, we also die for him. In the end, whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.

The Greek word "ó" is simply "or", and "morimos" means "we die" in the sense that we reach the end of life.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were disagreements among brothers and sisters about secondary matters, such as keeping certain days or eating certain foods. He reminds them that each person, with a sincere conscience, can act for the Lord. For that reason they must not judge or look down on one another.

For today: before you criticize another believer over a secondary difference, remember that he too belongs to Christ. Ask yourself whether your own life, in the big things and in the small, is being lived for the Lord.
exp.8:13:
Paul asks a question that some would have been asking: if God chooses Jacob and not Esau, is God unjust? He answers firmly: "Certainly not!" That is, "by no means." The words "hated" and "loved" are understood in several ways; many believe they express choice and preference, not human hatred.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He has just explained that God's promises depend on his calling and not on physical descent. He anticipates an objection and answers it with the example of Moses: God acts by mercy, and no one can claim from him as if he owed them something.

Today, this invites us to trust God even when we do not understand all his ways. We can rest in the knowledge that his mercy does not depend on our merits, and respond with humility and gratitude.
exp.1:8:
It says there will be trouble and distress for every human being who does evil. The wording describes this trouble as a heavy weight that presses on a person's whole life. This applies first to the Jew, and then to the Greek, meaning the non-Jewish person. The word "first" indicates that the Jews, who had received the law, were the first to be judged, but not the only ones.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, in his letter to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that God judges with justice and without favoritism. The Jews could not feel safe simply because they were Jewish. The following verse sums it up: God does not show partiality, that is, He does not treat anyone with preference.

For today: let us not trust in our religion, family, or reputation as if they would protect us. Let us ask God to examine our heart and help us do good with humility.
exp.1:6:
It says that God will give eternal life to those who keep on doing good without growing weary and who seek glory, honor, and immortality. "Perseverance in doing good" means steady faithfulness, staying firm and not giving up.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. In this passage he explains that God judges everyone fairly, Jews and Gentiles alike, according to their deeds. Earlier he speaks of those who harden their hearts and refuse to turn back; here he shows the other path. Those who seek God steadily receive eternal life. Other passages in Romans make clear that salvation is by grace through faith, and that good works show that faith. Some scholars understand this in different ways, but the emphasis here is that God looks at the heart and the life.

For today: do not lose heart when doing good is costly. Choose one steady act of kindness, such as helping someone, forgiving, or being honest, and ask God for strength to keep going.
exp.10:29:
What it says: Paul reminds the non-Jewish believers that they once disobeyed God. Now, however, they have received his mercy, that is, his compassionate love that forgives. He says this came "through their disobedience," meaning the people of Israel.

Context: Paul writes to the church in Rome, made up of Jews and non-Jews. Some of the non-Jewish believers felt superior to Israel. Paul shows them that the disobedience of many Jews opened the door for the other peoples. But God has not abandoned Israel, and his plan continues. How exactly these events fit together, scholars explain in several different ways.

For today: If you have faith today, remember that it is a gift of God's mercy, not something you earned. That frees us from pride and leads us to pray with love for those who do not yet believe.
exp.0:3:
He says that Jesus was declared Son of God with power. This happened through his resurrection from the dead. "Declared" means that it was shown publicly who he was; it does not mean he began to be the Son. The phrase "through the Spirit of holiness" probably refers to the Holy Spirit or to the holy nature of Christ; it has been understood in both ways. "Power" means strength.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. At the start of the letter, he presents the gospel. He says that Jesus is a descendant of David, as the prophets promised, and also the Son of God. Paul wants them to know in whom they believe and whom he serves as an apostle.

For today: the resurrection of Jesus is the firm sign that he is who he said he was. When you doubt or feel weak, trust that he is still alive and has power. You can pray today: "Lord Jesus, you are my Lord; guide me."
exp.9:5:
This verse says that the righteousness that comes through faith speaks as if it were a person. It warns us not to say in our heart, "Who will ascend into heaven?" as if we had to go up there to bring Christ down to earth.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that Moses taught that whoever does the law will live by it, and that Christ is the end, or the goal, of the law. Now he quotes and adapts words from Deuteronomy 30, where it was said that the commandment was not far away. Paul shows that salvation is already near, because Christ has already come. Scholars explain in several ways how Paul uses that text.

Today, if you doubt that God accepts you, you do not need to do something extraordinary to reach Him. Trust in what Christ has already done, and speak with Him simply and in faith.
exp.2:12:
This verse says that the words of sinners can be deadly and deceitful. "Open graves" are uncovered tombs, from which come a foul smell and death. "Their tongues practice deceit" means they use the tongue to mislead. "Venom of vipers" refers to poisonous snakes; the poison hidden on the lips speaks of evil disguised as kind words.

Paul, the author of the letter, is speaking to believers in Rome. Here he gathers several quotations from the Old Testament, especially from the Psalms (Psalm 5:9 and 140:3), to show that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, needs God. His point is not that every person is equally bad, but that sin reaches all of humanity, including the way we speak.

For today: before you speak, ask yourself whether your words give life or wound. Ask God to cleanse your mouth and your heart, and seek to speak the truth with love.
exp.11:0:
Paul asks the believers to offer their whole selves to God, as a living offering. The word "urge" is a request made with affection, not a command. "Offer" means to give something up to God. "Spiritual service of worship" can be understood as worship that is thoughtful and rooted in the heart, and readers have understood it in several ways.

Paul is writing to the church in Rome. For eleven chapters he explained what God has done through Christ: forgiveness, righteousness, and salvation by grace. Now he says "therefore": since God has been so merciful, the natural response is to live for Him. Obedience springs from gratitude, not from fear.

For today: think about your decisions this week, such as your work, your rest, your words, and your time. Offer them to God in prayer each morning, telling Him that you want to live thankful for His mercy.
exp.6:5:
This verse says that believers are no longer under the rule of the law, as a prisoner would be under the control of a jailer. "Held" means being bound or kept under its authority. The phrase about the old way of the written code describes an obedience that is cold and mechanical, based only on written rules. The phrase about the new way of the Spirit describes a new life, guided by the Holy Spirit.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He uses the example of marriage: death ends a bond. Thus, through Christ, the law no longer dominates or condemns us. Paul does not say that the law is evil; he makes clear that it is not, but rather that it revealed sin without being able to free us from it.

For today: do not serve God out of fear or by keeping a checklist. Ask the Spirit to renew your heart, and obey out of love and gratitude to Christ, who gave you new life.
exp.15:21:
Tertius says that he was the one who wrote down the letter, and from there he sends his own greeting to the Christians in Rome. He does this "in the Lord," that is, as a brother in the faith. The phrase "who wrote down this letter" is the wording your verse uses, so the verse follows it.

Paul was dictating this letter, and Tertius was the secretary who was writing it down. This was a common practice in that time. For a moment, Tertius sets down the work of writing to speak in his own voice. We know nothing more about him; some consider him a Christian from Corinth, but that is a reasonable assumption, not a certain fact.

God values quiet service. Tertius did not preach or found churches, but his work helped this message reach us. Any task done with love "in the Lord" has value, even though almost no one notices it.
exp.8:30:
Paul says that the people of Israel pursued a law of righteousness, a way of becoming right before God, but they did not obtain it. The phrases "pursued" and "has not attained it" are like running a race: they chased after the goal, but they never reached it. The Gentiles, by contrast, who were not seeking it, received it.

The apostle Paul is writing in his letter to the Romans. He grieves over his own people and explains why many Israelites did not accept Christ. According to the following verse, the problem was that they sought righteousness through effort and works, and not through faith.

For today: we can work very hard at being good and still miss the way if we trust in our own achievements. Rest in Christ, and let your obedience be the fruit of your trust in Him, not an attempt to earn God's favor.
exp.7:11:
This verse says that believers have an obligation, but it is not one owed to the flesh. "Obligation" means that we must do something. "Flesh" here is not just the body, but the old way of living, ruled by selfishness and sin. That is why we are not bound to live according to it. The sentence is left open, but the next verse completes it: our obligation is to the Spirit.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God's Spirit lives in them and that the same power that raised Jesus gives them life. That is why he begins with "therefore": if we have already received this life, we have a new responsibility.

Today, when an old habit or temptation calls to you strongly, remember that you owe it nothing. Ask the Spirit to help you choose what pleases God, and take one concrete step today in that direction.
exp.9:15:
Romans 10:16 says that not everyone who hears the good news about Jesus welcomes it. Paul quotes Isaiah, who lamented that few had believed his message. The word "message" in the verse you are reading means what was heard or preached, and "welcomed" here includes believing and responding in trust.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome and has his own people, Israel, in mind. He has just explained that faith comes by hearing the message, and that God sends messengers. Even so, many did not respond. By quoting Isaiah (53:1), he shows that this rejection did not take God by surprise.

For today: share the gospel with love and do not be discouraged if some do not respond. Your part is to proclaim it sincerely; believing is a response that only God can awaken in each person's heart.
exp.1:24:
It says that circumcision does have value, but only if the person observes the law. If someone breaks the law, their circumcision has become as though they were never circumcised. The verse notes that the verse says circumcision "has value," and that a person who breaks the law is one who violates it.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome, and at this point he is speaking to a Jew who takes pride in having the law. Paul does not look down on circumcision, which was the sign of the covenant. What he corrects is the idea that an outward sign is enough, even when a person's life contradicts what they claim to believe.

Today we can think about our own outward signs: attending church, owning a Bible, or calling ourselves Christians. All of that is good, but it does not replace a life that obeys God. Let us ask him that our conduct match what we profess.
exp.12:2:
Paul says that rulers, whom he calls "the one in authority," are usually not a terror to someone who does good, but to someone who does bad. If you want to live without fear of authority, do what is right, and you will have its approval. The word "approval" here means recognition or commendation.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, a city where the Roman Empire ruled. Earlier he has said that all authority exists under God's permission. Here he describes what government should do: promote order and restrain wrongdoing. It is a general description; Paul does not say that every ruler is just, and Christians understand this passage in different ways.

For today: try to live honestly in everyday life, such as paying what you owe and keeping just laws. In this way your good conduct speaks for you.
exp.3:0:
Here Paul asks a question: what did Abraham, whom he calls "our forefather according to the flesh," discover? That phrase refers to Abraham being the physical ancestor of the Jewish people. The word "discovered" in the verse above means something like "obtained" or "gained."

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He has just explained that God declares people righteous through faith, not through the law. Now he uses Abraham, who is highly respected by the Jews, as an example. The verses that follow show his answer: Abraham was not declared righteous because of his works, but because he believed God.

For today: you do not need to earn God's favor through good behavior or a good record. Trust what God promised in Christ, and from there live thankfully and obey with joy.
exp.3:13:
It says that if God's inheritance were gained by living under the law, then faith would be useless and the promise would be worthless. Those who live by the law are the people who trust in keeping Moses' rules. The heir is the one who receives what was promised. The word "useless" means empty, without purpose, and "worthless" means it has lost its value.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who were both Jews and non-Jews. He shows them that Abraham received the promise before he was circumcised and before the law existed. For that reason the promise came through faith, not through works, and so it can reach all who trust in God.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love with your effort. Trust his promise, rest in his grace, and obey him out of gratitude, not out of fear of losing your place.
exp.8:14:
For Paul, this verse says that God spoke to Moses and told him that He will have mercy on whoever He chooses, and He will have compassion on whoever He chooses. The repeated phrase "on whom I have mercy" and "on whom I have compassion" stresses that the choice is free and belongs to God.

Paul is the one writing, and he quotes what God said to Moses in Exodus 33:19. Earlier, Paul spoke about Jacob and Esau and asked whether God is unjust. He answers that He is not, because salvation was never something anyone deserved. Christians have understood in various ways how this relates to human freedom, but they all agree that God is merciful.

Today, this verse invites us to humility and gratitude. If you have received God's forgiveness, it was not because of your merits. That helps us treat others with the same mercy we have received.
exp.11:13:
Explanation:
This explains that we should wish and ask for good for those who harm us because of our faith. "Bless" means to speak well of someone and ask God to favor them. The verse says "bless" twice, once as the main command and once as a repeated word, and it adds "do not curse": do not wish for or ask for harm against them. "Persecute" refers to those who treat us with hostility.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. After explaining what God has done for them in Christ, he shows them how to live that faith in practice. Earlier he speaks of hope, patience in suffering, prayer, and hospitality. Then he speaks of sharing joys and sorrows, and of living with humility. This verse joins both parts: love must reach even our enemies.

Today: if someone speaks badly of you or treats you with contempt, pray for that person by name and, if you can, answer with a kind word instead of revenge.
exp.5:9:
He says that when Christ died, he died to sin "once," meaning one time and for all time. His death is not repeated. And the life he now has, he lives for God. The expression "died to sin" does not mean that Jesus sinned, but that he faced the power of sin and death and completed that work entirely.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that, through faith, whoever is united with Christ shares in his death and his resurrection. He sets Christ forward as both model and foundation: if he is no longer under the power of death, those who are in him must not live under the rule of sin either.

Today we can remember that sin no longer has the final word over us. When you find yourself trapped in a bad habit, pray and decide to live that day for God, trusting in Christ's strength and not your own.
exp.4:2:
Paul says that believers not only rejoice in the hope of God's glory, but also rejoice in their sufferings. To rejoice here means to take pleasure in something with confidence. "Suffering" means pain or hardship, and "perseverance" means steady endurance, the strength to keep going forward.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome and explaining what God does through faith. He has already said that we are made right with God and that we have peace with Him. Now he shows that suffering is not a sign of being abandoned, because God uses it to shape character and strengthen hope, a hope that does not disappoint because His love fills our hearts.

When you go through a difficulty, don't ask only "Why is this happening to me?" but also "What is God forming in me?" Ask Him for help to stay firm, without hiding your pain.
exp.0:13:
Paul says that he has an obligation to all people: to Greeks and non-Greeks, and to the wise and the foolish. The word "non-Greeks" here does not mean savages, but people who did not speak Greek or share Greek culture. To be "obligated" means to owe something and to be bound to pay it back.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He explains that he has wanted to visit them many times, but has been prevented from doing so. His obligation is not because he received anything from them, but because God entrusted him with announcing the gospel to everyone. For this reason he feels bound to share it with people of every culture and every level of understanding.

Today we can remember that the gospel is not only for those we like or who are similar to us. Let us ask God for an opportunity this week to treat someone very different from us with respect and to share his hope with them.
exp.11:19:
Paul says that if someone who treats you as an enemy is hungry or thirsty, you should give him food and drink. "Burning coals" is a picture: by doing good, you place something like fire on that person. "Heap" means you keep piling them up little by little.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and quotes Proverbs 25:21-22. He asks them not to take revenge but to leave judgment to God. The "coals" are understood in several ways: that the person feels shame and repents, or that it is a judgment of God. The next verse, "Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good," supports the first idea.

Today, if someone has offended you, look for a simple way to help him: a kind message, a meal, a favor. Do it not to humiliate him, but to overcome evil with good and leave the rest in God's hands.
exp.14:21:
This verse says that Paul had often wanted to visit the Christians in Rome, but something kept getting in the way. "Hindered" means held back or stopped. "That is why" points back to what he has just said: his work of preaching where Christ was not yet known.

Paul writes this letter to the Romans. He explains that his mission to proclaim the gospel in new places kept him busy in other regions. That is why he had not been able to reach Rome, where there were already believers. Now he plans to go through Rome on his way to Spain. The letter does not detail every obstacle, so it is not wise to invent them.

For today: when your plans are delayed, do not become discouraged right away. God may have you occupied with something important. Remain faithful where you are and keep alive the desire to serve and encourage others.
exp.4:6:
It is very rare for anyone to die for a righteous man, that is, someone upright and faithful to the law. Though someone might possibly dare to die for a good person, someone generous and beloved.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that God's love is certain. First he speaks of how uncommon human sacrifice is, and then, in verse 8, he emphasizes that Christ died for people who were neither righteous nor good. Some scholars debate the exact difference between "righteous" and "good," but the central idea is clear.

For today: when you doubt that God loves you, remember that Christ died for you before you deserved it. Rest in that love and treat others with the same grace.
exp.7:10:
It says that the same Spirit of God who raised Jesus lives in believers. Therefore, God, who raised Christ Jesus from the dead, will also give life to our mortal bodies, that is, bodies subject to death. The word "give life" here describes God restoring life to what is mortal. To "live in" someone means to dwell within them and remain with them.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he explained that, although the body suffers the consequences of sin and will die, the Spirit gives spiritual life. Here he adds a hope: the life God gives does not end in the inner person, but will also reach the body. Many understand this to refer to the future resurrection; some think it also includes strength to live now.

For today: when you feel weak, tired, or afraid of death, remember that the Spirit of God lives in you. Ask him to give you strength to obey today, and trust in the promise of life that God will fulfill.
exp.14:6:
Paul tells us to accept one another, just as Christ accepted us. The Greek word behind this means to receive or welcome someone warmly. The goal of this welcome is to bring glory to God.

Paul is writing to the church in Rome, where Jewish believers and non-Jewish believers lived side by side and had different views on customs and foods. He asks them to come together in unity. The verses that follow show that Christ served both Jews and non-Jews, so that all people might glorify God.

Today, think of someone in your church or family who sees things differently than you do or who is hard for you to get along with. Instead of pulling away, welcome them with patience and respect, remembering that Christ accepted you with all your shortcomings.
exp.5:20:
Paul asks a question so that believers will think about it: what real benefit did they get from the life they lived before? Today they feel ashamed of those things, and the outcome of that path is death. "Fruit" here means the result or gain that came from those choices. "Ashamed" means they feel embarrassed to remember them.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He explains that, by believing in Christ, they stopped being slaves to sin and now serve God. He uses the image of slavery, and he says he does so because of the weakness of your flesh, that is, so that they can understand it better. He invites them to compare their past life with the new one.

For today: when something from the past tempts you to go back, remember where it led and what it left behind. Then ask God for strength to live in his grace, where true life is found.
exp.7:30:
Paul asks, "What then shall we say in response to these things?" and answers with another question: if God is for us, who can be against us? He does not say there will be no opposition, but that no one can defeat the one whom God supports.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained God's plan: to know, call, justify, and glorify his people. After saying all of that, he concludes there is no reason for fear. Right away he reminds them that God gave his own Son for us, proof that he is on our side.

When you feel threatened, judged, or alone, remember that God has already shown his love in Christ. Pray with that confidence and take the next step without fear.
exp.3:7:
It says that the person is truly happy, blessed in the full sense, whose sin the Lord will never count against them. The word "blessed" here means very happy and favored. The word "man" refers to a person, and "count against" means to record something to someone's account.

Paul is explaining that God declares people righteous through faith and not because of their works. To support this, he quotes King David, who in Psalm 32 speaks of the joy of being forgiven. Paul uses David and Abraham to show that this applies to Jews and non-Jews alike.

For today: when you feel the weight of your failures, do not try to earn forgiveness through effort. Come before God with sincerity, trust in what Christ has done, and rest in his forgiveness.
exp.3:12:
Paul says that God promised Abraham and his offspring that they would inherit the world, but not because Abraham kept the law. That promise came through the righteousness that comes by faith, meaning that Abraham believed God and God counted him as righteous.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that both Jews and non-Jews are accepted by God through faith. Abraham lived long before the law of Moses existed, so his example proves that the promise did not depend on it. Scholars understand in various ways what "heir of the world" means, but Paul connects it with the blessing for all nations.

Today we can stop trying to earn God's favor through effort or merit. Trust in His promise, and live grateful and obedient out of that trust.
exp.8:10:
Before Jacob and Esau were born, and before either of them had done anything good or bad, God had already set out his plan. That plan rests on God's choosing, not on what people do, but on his call. The phrase about God's choice means "according to his choosing," and the idea of his plan standing means it would remain firm.

Paul is speaking to believers in Rome, many of them Jews and Gentiles together. He is explaining why not all of Abraham's descendants received the promise. He uses Jacob and Esau as examples: God acts through his choosing and his promise, not through human merit. Christians interpret in different ways how this relates to election and human freedom.

For today: you do not need to earn God's love through your performance. Rest in his grace, thank him for calling you, and respond with a life of trust and humble obedience.
exp.0:26:
Romans 1:27 says that the men gave up natural relations with women and burned with strong desire for one another. It describes men committing indecent acts with other men and receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error. Here "burned" points to intense, disordered longing, "indecent acts" refers to conduct so shameful that it is embarrassing to describe, and "due penalty" refers to the outcome or consequence that followed from their error.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome to show that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, needs the gospel. In this passage he describes how humanity turned away from God, worshiping created things instead of the Creator, and how God gave them over to the consequences of their rebellion. Scholars debate some details of this text, but the central point is that Paul speaks of a humanity that exchanged the truth for a lie.

This passage reminds us that all of us need the grace of God, for the next chapter warns against judging others. Let us examine our own hearts with humility and draw near to God with confidence.
exp.8:19:
Here the verse says that a human being has no right to argue with God or to bring charges against him. It uses the image of a clay pot that asks the one who shaped it, "Why did You make me like this?" The verse's question, "Who are you, O man, to talk back to God?", points to arguing back or disputing with words.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of God's mercy and of his freedom to act. Imagine someone objects, "If God decides, how can he still blame us?" Paul answers by reminding them that God is the Creator and we are his creatures. Some read this passage mainly as personal election, others as God's plan for nations; Christians have understood it in several different ways.

When you do not understand what God allows, do not accuse him. Bring your questions to him with humility and trust, remembering that he is wise and good.
exp.11:5:
Paul says that each believer has different gifts, and that these gifts come from God's grace, not from our merit. He begins with the gift of prophecy, which is speaking on God's behalf to encourage, correct, or guide. It must be used "in proportion to his faith." That phrase can be understood in two ways: according to the faith that God gives to each person, or according to the Christian faith already received. Both ideas call for humility.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just compared them to a body: many members, each with its own function, but all united in Christ. He wants them not to think themselves superior or to despise one another, but to serve together.

For today: think about what God has given you, whether teaching, helping, encouraging, or giving, and use it with humility in your church, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.2:4:
Here Paul raises an objection: if our wrongdoing highlights the righteousness of God, would it be unjust of God to inflict his wrath on us?

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that the unfaithfulness of some does not cancel God's faithfulness. He imagines an opponent who answers him with this objection, and Paul rejects it at once: "God forbid." God does judge the world, and for that reason he cannot be unjust.

For today: do not use God's grace as an excuse to sin. That God can bring something good out of our failures does not make the failure good. Rather, acknowledge your wrong with humility and trust that God is just and merciful.
exp.9:6:
This verse says that no one needs to go down into the abyss, that is, into the place of the dead, to bring Christ back up. The word "abyss" here means the depth where the dead go. "Will descend" means "will go down," and "bring up" means "bring back up from." Paul shows how absurd it would be to think that we would have to do something like that.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and speaks about the people of Israel. He draws on words from Deuteronomy 30:12-14, where Moses says that the word of God is near. Paul applies this to Christ: he has already come and has already risen. Salvation is not earned through impossible efforts, because God has already accomplished it.

Today you can rest from the idea that you must earn God's favor. Christ has already done the work. Trust in him and tell him sincerely that Jesus is your Lord.
exp.6:16:
Paul says that when he does the wrong he does not want to do, it is not really his deepest desire that is acting, but the sin that lives inside him. "Does" means "does," and "living in" means "living in" or "staying in." He is not looking for excuses: he is describing an inner struggle.

Paul speaks in the first person about his fight with sin, and scholars debate whether he is describing his life before he knew Christ or his struggle as a believer. His central point is that God's law is good, because it shows him what is wrong. The problem is not the law, but the sin that lives in weak human nature.

When you fall into something you do not want to do, do not sink into despair. Acknowledge your failure honestly, take responsibility for it, and turn to God, asking for his help and forgiveness. He sustains you in the struggle.
exp.8:2:
Paul says that he himself would wish to be "cut off from Christ," that is, separated from Him and under condemnation, if that could bring his brothers to salvation. "My own flesh and blood" refers to his people, the Israelites, with whom he shares family ties. The words "I could wish" express a longing that he knows cannot be fulfilled.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken with great confidence about the love of God in chapter 8. Now he confesses his deep sorrow because many of his people have not believed in Jesus. He declares that he is telling the truth, and then he recalls the privileges that Israel received from God.

For today: truly loving those who do not know Christ means feeling sorrow for them, praying earnestly, and humbly seeking the opportunity to speak to them about Jesus, beginning with our own family.
exp.5:17:
It says that believers have already been set free from the power of sin and now belong to righteousness, that is, to living as God wants. "Set free" means "released from bondage," and "slaves" refers to those who serve a master completely.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He explains that no one lives without a master: either you serve sin, which leads to death, or you serve obedience, which leads to righteousness. He wants them to understand that their life has changed by the grace of God and that this affects how they live each day. He uses the image of slavery because it was something they understood well.

For today: when temptation comes, remember that sin is no longer your master. Ask God for help and choose one concrete act of righteousness, such as telling the truth or forgiving.
exp.6:19:
What the passage says: Paul explains that when he does what he does not want to do, it is no longer simply he who is doing it, but the sin living in him that does it. The word "living" means "dwelling" or "remaining." "Do" means "carry out" or "perform."

Context: Paul speaks in the first person about the struggle between the desire to obey God's law and the weakness of the flesh. Scholars debate whether he is describing his life before knowing Christ, his life as a believer, or a general experience, and Christians have understood it in different ways. What is clear is that he wants to show that the law reveals sin but does not give the strength to overcome it.

For today: When you fail, do not use this as an excuse, but do not sink into despair either. Acknowledge your weakness honestly, confess your failure to God, and ask him for help every day, for Paul soon points to Christ as the way out.
exp.1:18:
Here Paul describes what a Jew who trusted in the law believed about himself: that he was a guide for the blind, that is, for those who do not know God, and a light for those who live in darkness, that is, in spiritual ignorance. The phrase "if you are convinced" means that you are sure of it.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. In this passage he speaks to someone who boasts of knowing God's law but does not live by it. He is not mocking the law, which is good, but showing that knowing is not enough. The verses that follow make this clear: whoever teaches others must also obey.

For today: before correcting or advising someone, ask yourself honestly whether you practice that same thing. Let your life support your words, and teach with humility, remembering that you too need the grace of God.
exp.9:2:
Paul says that many of his people did not understand how God declares a person righteous. They wanted to stand before God with a righteousness achieved by their own efforts, and so they did not accept the way God himself offers. "Ignorant" means not knowing or not understanding; "submitted" means yielding or accepting with humility.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and speaks with grief for Israel, his own people. He acknowledges that they had genuine zeal for God, but a zeal without right understanding. They believed that keeping the law gave them a righteousness of their own, and they did not see that Christ is the fulfillment and goal of that law, as the next verse says.

For today: it is easy to trust in our good works or in our religiousness to feel accepted by God. We can ask him to teach us to rest in the righteousness he gives through Christ, and to obey him out of gratitude, not out of pride.
exp.7:4:
This verse says there are two ways of living, and that what fills our minds shows which one we follow. "Living according to the flesh" means being guided by the desires and thoughts of human nature apart from God. To "set your mind on" something means giving your attention and interest to it. Those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God sent his Son to deal with sin, because the law could not change the heart. Now he shows the difference between the one who follows his own nature and the one who follows the Spirit. The verses that follow say the first leads to death and the second to life and peace.

For today: think about what you spend most of your thoughts on during the day. Set aside a few minutes to read the Bible or pray, and ask the Spirit to guide your thoughts.
exp.14:28:
Paul tells the Christians in Rome that he is confident of something: when he finally visits them, he will come to them full of the blessing of Christ. The phrase "I will come in the fullness" means that he will arrive with rich spiritual gifts.

Paul writes this letter from the end of his work in the East. Before he goes on to Rome and then to Spain, he must take a gift from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to the poor of Jerusalem. He knows the road has dangers, but he trusts that God will be with him. Scholars debate whether he had in mind a blessing to give, a blessing to receive, or both.

For today: when you serve others, do not focus on what you lack. Go with confidence that Christ has given you something good to share.
exp.6:12:
Paul asks whether the law, which is good, was the thing that brought him death. He answers firmly: certainly not. It was sin that used the good commandment to produce death, and so sin was shown for what it truly is: something terrible. The phrase that Paul uses here, "utterly sinful," means extremely sinful, wicked to a great degree.

Paul speaks in the first person, and scholars debate whether he is describing his life before he knew Christ, his life as a believer, or a general human experience. Either way, he is defending God's law against the idea that it is evil. The law does not create sin; it exposes sin and shows how serious it is.

For today: when God's Word confronts you and makes you uncomfortable, do not see it as an enemy. It is like a light that reveals what is wrong so that you will seek the grace of Christ and receive healing.
exp.9:1:
Paul says that the Israelites are sincere and passionate about God. "Zeal" means enthusiasm, intense eagerness. But that eagerness is "not on the basis of knowledge": it is not grounded in correct understanding, in grasping well what God really asks for. They have passion, but they lack clarity.

Paul, a Jew himself, writes to the believers in Rome. He feels deep sorrow for his people and prays for their salvation. He recognizes that his fellow countrymen seek God with effort, but the following verses explain the problem: they wanted to establish their own righteousness and did not accept the righteousness that God gives through Christ.

Today we can be very devoted in religious matters and still be mistaken. It is wise to combine enthusiasm with the study of the Bible and with the humility to be corrected, remembering that we are accepted by the grace of God in Christ, not by our own effort.
exp.3:10:
He says that Abraham received circumcision as a sign and a seal. In other words, it was a mark that confirmed something already in place: the faith through which he was made right with God while he was still uncircumcised. In this way Abraham became the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that God would also credit righteousness to them. "Credited as righteousness" means that God regards them as righteous before him.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He wants to show that no one is saved by rituals or by keeping the law, but by faith. He uses Abraham, so respected by the Jews, as proof: God accepted him because he believed, before any ritual.

For today: do not trust in your rituals, your family history, or your good works to be right with God. Trust in him as Abraham did, and let your practices express that faith, not replace it.
exp.1:28:
He says that being a true Jew does not depend on what shows on the outside, but on what is within. The circumcision that really matters is the one of the heart, done by the Spirit, and not the one that only follows a written code. The "written code" refers to the law as a mere outward rule. And "praise" means approval or recognition: the one who lives this way does not seek the applause of people, but the approval that comes from God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, among them Jews and non-Jews. He shows them that boasting of having the law or the sign of circumcision is not enough if life does not go with it. His point is that everyone needs God, and that He looks at the heart.

For today: before seeking for others to notice your faith, ask yourself what is really in your heart. Ask God for sincerity, and today do one act of kindness or obedience that no one else knows about.
exp.13:21:
This verse says that the convictions you hold about what is right for you should stay between you and God, without being forced on others or put on display. Blessed is the one who does not feel guilty about what he chooses to do. "Does not condemn himself" means that his conscience does not accuse him, and "approves" means that he endorses what he is doing.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where believers had different consciences about foods and special days. Some ate everything; others, perhaps because of their Jewish background or to avoid meat offered to idols, held back. Paul asks that the strong care for the weak and not cause them to stumble.

For today: in matters where the Bible leaves room for freedom, live with a clear conscience before God, without flaunting your freedom or judging the believer who thinks differently. Before acting, ask yourself: can I do this with faith and without doubts? Does this help my brother?
exp.4:3:
Patience, as the ability to endure with steadiness, produces proof, meaning a tested character, like metal that comes out of the fire clean and strong. And that tested character produces hope.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that we are made right with God by faith, not by works. Now he shows that difficulties are not a sign that God has abandoned us. On the contrary, God uses them to form our character, and hope does not end in shame because God has already shown his love to us in Christ.

For today: when you go through a difficult situation, don't only ask "why me?" Also ask "what is God forming in me?" Endure with confidence in him, and your hope will grow.
exp.15:22:
Paul sends greetings from three people who were with him. Gaius is his host, the one who lodged him in his home, and he also opened his house to the whole church. Erastus is the city treasurer, an official in charge of public money. Quartus is simply called our brother.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, probably from Corinth, and these greetings come near the end. Some scholars think this Gaius is the same man Paul baptized in Corinth, though this is not certain.

This list shows that the church is a varied family: a generous host, a public official, a brother with no known office. All of them matter. Today we can imitate Gaius by offering our home or our time to welcome others, without expecting recognition.
exp.0:30:
This verse follows a list of behaviors that show what life looks like when a person turns away from God. "Senseless" describes people who lack moral sense and good judgment. "Faithless" describes those who do not keep their word or their commitments. "Heartless" means they lack the normal love expected within the family. "Merciless" describes people who feel no compassion for someone who suffers.

Here the apostle Paul speaks, in his letter to the Christians in Rome. He describes how humanity, by rejecting God, ends up damaging its relationships and its own conscience. This is the beginning of an argument: all of us need the gospel, since no one saves himself.

For today: review your close relationships. Is there someone you have not forgiven, or someone you have treated harshly? Ask God for a compassionate heart, and take one concrete step toward reconciliation today.
exp.10:19:
Paul says that is correct: the Jewish branches were broken off because of unbelief, and you, as a Gentile, stand by faith. So you must not be arrogant, but be afraid, with a reverent awe before God. Being arrogant means being filled with pride, and the word "afraid" here speaks of humility and seriousness, not of terror.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there were believers of both Gentile and Jewish origin. He uses the image of an olive tree: Israel is the original branches, and the Gentiles are branches grafted in. He wants to keep the Gentiles from looking down with contempt on the Jews who did not believe.

For today: our faith is a gift, not something we earned. When you see someone far from God, do not think you are better; give thanks, stay humble, and keep trusting in Christ each day.
exp.4:19:
This verse says that the law of Moses "came in," meaning it arrived later, so that the trespass would increase, that is, so that it would become more visible and evident. "But" marks a contrast, and "increased all the more" means that grace went far beyond sin, was much greater than the sin.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and compares Adam with Christ. Through Adam sin and death entered; through Christ come forgiveness and life. Interpreters explain in various ways how the law makes the trespass increase: by showing it clearly, by stirring up rebellion, or both. Paul concludes that grace reigns to eternal life.

If today your failures or your past weigh on you, remember that no guilt is greater than the grace of God. Acknowledge your sin honestly, without hiding it, and come to Jesus trusting in his forgiveness. Then live thankfully, not to earn his love, but because you have already received it.
exp.2:8:
It says that neither the Jews nor the other peoples have an advantage before God. Paul asks, "Are we any better?" and answers plainly, "Not at all." The phrase "under sin" means that he had already shown that all people are under the power and guilt of sin. "Greeks" here refers to people who are not Jewish.

The apostle Paul is speaking, writing to the Christians in Rome. He had just defended that God is just, even when some criticized him or twisted his words. Now he sums up what he explained in the earlier chapters: Jews and non-Jews alike need the mercy of God. Next he will cite the Scriptures to support this.

For today: do not compare yourself with others to feel more acceptable before God. Recognize with humility your need for Him, and treat with compassion those who also struggle with their failings.
exp.13:0:
He says we should welcome with kindness the one whose faith is weak, that is, someone whose faith is still fragile or who has doubts. To accept someone means to take them in and give them a warm welcome. He adds that we should do this without passing judgment on their opinions, meaning without criticizing or condemning their uncertain thoughts.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome. In that church there were believers who thought differently about what to eat and which days to observe. The verses that follow show that some ate everything and others only vegetables. Paul asks that no one despise or judge the other in these secondary matters. Scholars debate the exact details of the conflict, but the counsel is clear.
