Today, if someone in your church is new or unsure in their faith, approach them with patience and kindness. Listen, respond with tenderness, and do not correct them over every small difference.
exp.14:9:
This verse says that the Gentiles, meaning the peoples who are not Jews, are invited to rejoice together with the people of God, Israel. "Rejoice" is a gentle command: "let them rejoice." The phrase "with His people" shows that there are not two separate groups, but one and the same celebration.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where Jews and non-Jews had tensions. To show that the inclusion of the Gentiles was always part of God's plan, he quotes the Scriptures. This line comes from Deuteronomy 32:43, and scholars debate a little about the exact text that Paul follows, but his point is clear: the Gentiles also celebrate what God does.

Today, God calls us to rejoice with people who are different from us, of another culture or background. Try today to welcome someone different in your church and to celebrate with that person what God is doing.
exp.10:10:
Paul asks whether the people of Israel stumbled so badly that they would fall beyond recovery. He answers emphatically: "Certainly not!" Instead, because of their trespass, salvation has come to the Gentiles, that is, to those who are not Jews. The purpose was to make Israel jealous, a longing to return to God as they saw the blessings others were receiving.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, many of whom were Gentiles. He has just quoted David speaking of a hardening. Now he makes clear that this hardening is not the end of Israel. He wants the Gentiles not to think themselves superior and to see God's plan with hope.

For today: do not look down with pride on someone who is far from God right now. God can use even our failures to open paths of grace. Pray for that person and live in such a way that it awakens in them a hunger for God.
exp.10:8:
David says that the table of certain people, meaning whatever gives them comfort and security, should become a trap for them. In the verse, "snare" and "trap" are devices for catching animals, "stumbling block" is something that makes a person fall, and "retribution" means a repayment or deserved punishment.

Paul quotes Psalm 69:22 to explain why many in Israel did not recognize Jesus, while a chosen remnant did. Some understand this as a judgment from God, but Paul makes clear right away that their fall is not final: God uses their stumbling to bring salvation to the Gentiles and to awaken Israel.

For today: what seems safe to us, such as our customs, achievements, or religious habits, can become a trap if it shuts us off from Christ. Let us ask God for a humble and attentive heart, one that listens to his voice today.
exp.0:0:
Paul introduces himself with three descriptions. He is a "servant" of Christ Jesus, that is, someone who belongs to his Lord and lives to obey him. He was "called to be an apostle," meaning sent out with a special mission. And he was "set apart for the gospel of God," chosen to proclaim the good news from God.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. At the start, he explains who he is and with what authority he speaks to them. He says that his message is not his own invention but the gospel of God, which had already been promised in the Scriptures.

For today: before speaking of what you do, remember to whom you belong. Your worth and your purpose come from God's calling, not only from your achievements. Ask him to show you where he wants you to serve him today, in your home, your work, or your community.
exp.8:22:
This verse says that God wanted to make known the greatness and richness of his glory. He did this through "vessels of his mercy," meaning people who receive his compassion. God prepared them in advance for glory.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that God acts with freedom and patience. He uses the image of the potter. In the following verse he makes clear that these vessels include both Jews and non-Jews. Christians have debated for centuries how God's decision and the human response relate here, and there are several interpretations.

For today: if your faith depends on God's mercy and not on your own merits, you can live with humility and gratitude. Today, give thanks for one concrete sign of his compassion, and show that same compassion to someone who needs it.
exp.12:3:
This verse says that civil authority is God's servant, placed there for your good. If you do what is good, you have no reason to fear it. But if you do what is wrong, you should be afraid, because it does not carry the sword for nothing: the sword stands for its power to punish. An agent of retribution means that it carries out justice against the one who does wrong.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, a city with a great deal of political power. He wants them to live in order and not let their faith be confused with rebellion. Some scholars point out that Paul is describing the ideal role of authority, and that the Bible also shows cases where obeying God comes first (Acts 5:29).

Today we can respect the laws, pay our taxes, and be good citizens as part of our witness, praying for those who govern, without ceasing to obey God in what matters most.
exp.2:13:
It says that people's mouths are full of cursing, which means speaking badly about others, swearing, or insulting them. It also speaks of bitterness, which is a way of speaking full of resentment, anger, and harshness. The words reflect what is in the heart.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome. Here he gathers several passages from the Old Testament, especially Psalm 10:7, to show that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, is under sin and needs God. He is not speaking of one particular person, but of the human condition apart from God's grace. Scholars debate how much of this picture describes each individual, but the central point is our need for forgiveness.

Today we can examine how we speak, at home, at work, and online. Before we respond in anger, let us ask God to heal our hearts and help us speak with kindness and truth.
exp.1:2:
Paul asks a direct question: if you pass judgment on others for their wrongdoing while doing the same things yourself, do you really think you will escape God's judgment? The word "judge" is the key idea here, and "the same things" refers to the sins Paul described in the previous chapter.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just shown that sin is serious throughout the whole world, and now he speaks to the person who feels morally superior. Many believe he is thinking mainly of some Jews, but his warning applies to anyone. The verses that follow explain that God's patience aims to lead us to repentance.

Today, before pointing out someone else's fault, it is good to examine our own heart. If we acknowledge our mistakes with humility, we will be able to treat others with more compassion and turn to God to ask for forgiveness.
exp.2:24:
He says that God publicly presented Jesus as an "atoning sacrifice," meaning the means by which the penalty for sin is paid and we are brought back into a right relationship with God. This comes through faith in his blood, which points to his death as a sacrifice. In this way God shows that he is righteous, since in his forbearance he had passed over the sins people committed before, without punishing them in full.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, has sinned and needs to be made right with God as a free gift. Here he explains how God can forgive without ceasing to be just: Christ took the punishment. He then concludes that no one can boast about their own works.

For today: when guilt weighs on you or you feel unworthy, remember that your forgiveness does not depend on your effort, but on what Christ has already done. Trust in him and live with gratitude, not with pride.
exp.6:13:
We know that the law is spiritual, meaning it comes from God and reflects his character. By contrast, Paul says that he himself is "unspiritual," that is, weak and limited by his human nature, and "sold as a slave to sin," bound and dominated by sin like a slave who has been sold.

Paul is speaking here and explaining that the law is not to blame. The law is good; the problem is the sin that is in the human being. Scholars debate whether Paul is speaking here of his life before he knew Christ or of his struggle as a believer. Both views have defenders.

For today: be honest with God about your struggles. Do not blame what is good for your failures; acknowledge your weakness and seek the help of Christ, who gives freedom.
exp.6:22:
Paul says that inside him there are two forces in conflict. One is the desire to obey God, which lives in his mind. The other is a "law," meaning a power or principle that is at work in his body and pulls him toward sin. "In my body" refers to his physical life. "Holding me captive" means being kept prisoner, controlled by something stronger than oneself.

Paul writes to believers in Rome and speaks in the first person about the struggle with sin. Scholars disagree: some believe he describes his life before he knew Christ, others that he describes the struggle of every believer. What follows, "I thank God through Jesus Christ," shows that rescue comes from Christ and not from one's own effort.

If you feel that you want to do good and sometimes fail, you are not alone. Recognize your weakness honestly and turn to Jesus, asking for his help every day.
exp.9:8:
This verse says that if you openly declare with your words that Jesus is Lord, and truly believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. The verse uses the word "confess" and the word "believe," and these mean the same as "declare" and "trust." To be raised from the dead means that God brought him back to life. To be saved means to be rescued and forgiven by God.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he explained that salvation is not earned through human effort, whether by going up to heaven or down into the depths, because God has already brought it near in Christ. The message of faith that Paul preaches is close at hand, in the mouth and in the heart. The verses that follow say that inner faith and spoken confession go together.

For today: if you trust in Jesus, do not hide your faith. Today you can tell God, or someone close to you, simply: "Jesus is Lord, and I believe that God raised him from the dead."
exp.8:29:
What then will we say? Paul asks what conclusion we should draw from all this. He answers that the Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, have obtained it, a righteousness that is by faith. "Pursuing righteousness" means striving to be accepted before God; the phrase "a righteousness that is by faith" explains what kind of righteousness is meant. "Gentiles" are those who were not part of the people of Israel.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where Jewish believers and non-Jewish believers lived side by side. He has been speaking about the faithfulness of God and about how not all of Israel responded to his promise, although a remnant always remained. Now he shows something surprising: people outside the law received righteousness by trusting in Christ, while many who sought it through works stumbled.

For today: we do not need to earn God's favor through effort or a good record. Trust in Christ, receive his forgiveness, and let that gratitude move your obedience.
exp.1:20:
He says that whoever teaches others must also teach themselves. Paul asks pointedly: if you teach that one should not steal, do you steal? The Greek word for "steal" in the original text means to take what belongs to someone else, which is the same act as stealing in the verse you read.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Here he speaks to a Jew who trusted in knowing God's law and saw himself as a guide to others. Paul does not deny that the law is good, but he shows that knowing it is not enough. It must be lived. With this he prepares his teaching that all of us, Jews and non-Jews alike, need the grace of God.

For today: before you correct or advise someone, examine your own life. Ask God to show you the areas where you still do not live what you say you believe, and take one concrete step of change today.
exp.12:6:
This verse asks us to give each person what we owe them. "Taxes" are the payments made to the government on income, property, or goods. "Revenue" refers to other government income, such as duties and fees. "Respect" is serious regard toward those who hold authority, and "honor" is respectful treatment toward those who deserve it.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who lived under a powerful government. Earlier he explained that the authorities play a role in keeping order, and that obeying them is also a matter of conscience. Here he sums this up with concrete examples. Then he adds that the debt that never ends is love for one's neighbor.

For today: be honest in your duties, such as paying your taxes on time and showing respect to those who hold authority, even when you do not agree with them. Do it as part of your witness and your love for others.
exp.14:29:
Paul asks the brothers and sisters in Rome, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to join him in his struggle by praying to God for him. The word "urge" carries the sense of earnest appeal, and the request is rooted in the bond that Christ and the Spirit create among believers.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. He is about to bring a gift to the poor believers in Jerusalem, and afterward he hopes to visit Rome and continue on to Spain. In the verses that follow, he asks for prayer that he would be rescued from those in Judea who opposed him and that his service would be well received.

For today: do not be embarrassed to ask for prayer. Paul, though an apostle, leaned on others. Today you can choose a trusted person, tell them a specific need, and ask them to pray for you. And pray for them too.
exp.2:21:
This verse says that God gives us his righteousness, meaning he accepts us as righteous before him, and that this comes through faith in Jesus Christ. It is for all who believe, no matter who they are. The phrase "there is no distinction" means that no one has an advantage before God.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he explained that no one becomes righteous by keeping the law; the law only shows us our sin. Now he presents the good news: God offers another way, already announced in the law and the prophets. Jews and non-Jews alike need the same thing: all have sinned, and all are forgiven freely by his grace.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love or compare yourself with others. Trust in Jesus and rest in his forgiveness. And treat others with humility, because we all receive the same grace.
exp.10:13:
Paul says that he values his ministry because he hopes that his own people, when they see the blessings the non-Jewish people are receiving, will feel jealous, that is, a longing for what those others have. In this way some of them might be saved. "My own people" means his fellow countrymen, the Jews. To stir up jealousy in them is to awaken a good desire in them to return to God.

Paul, an apostle sent to the Gentiles, writes to believers in Rome. Although most of Israel had rejected Jesus, he does not give them up for lost. He speaks to the Gentiles so that they will not feel superior, and he reminds them that God still loves Israel. Paul does his work in the hope that some will be saved.

For today: live your faith in a way that is so attractive and humble that others feel a desire to know God. And never give up on any person; pray for those who are still far away.
exp.15:4:
Paul asks that the church that meets at their house be greeted. Then he greets Epenetus, whom he calls "my beloved." He says that Epenetus was the first convert to Christ in the province of Asia.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. At the end he names many people to show closeness and gratitude. At that time there were no Christian church buildings as there are today; believers gathered in homes.

God uses ordinary homes to build his church, and he values each person, even someone few remember. We can open our homes to pray or to share the Word, and encourage by name those who serve quietly.
exp.15:24:
This verse opens a closing song of praise. It says that God is able to strengthen and make firm those who believe. He does this through the gospel Paul preaches, which is the message about Jesus Christ. The phrase "to make firm" in the verse above is the sense of the word translated "strengthen." "Mystery" refers to a plan of God that was concealed for ages past and has now been revealed.

Paul is ending his letter to the Christians in Rome, probably written from Corinth, as the closing note indicates. After sending greetings, he closes with praise to God. He sums up his letter: the gospel is the good news that God has revealed, and it is God who sustains his people, not human effort.

For today: when you feel weak or unsure in your faith, do not rely only on your own strength. Return to the message of Jesus Christ, read it, think it over, and ask God to strengthen you. He is able to uphold you.
exp.4:5:
This verse says that Christ died for the ungodly, that is, for those who lived without God. He did this while we were still powerless, unable to save ourselves. "At just the right time" means at the moment God had chosen.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of the hope that does not disappoint, because the love of God fills the heart through the Holy Spirit. Now he shows the foundation of that hope: Christ died for us before we could do anything to deserve it. The verses that follow reinforce this: God showed his love when we were sinners.

For today: you do not need to fix your life first in order to draw near to God. If you feel weak or unworthy, come to him just as you are, trusting that his love reached you before you could respond.
exp.7:38:
It says that nothing that exists can separate us from God's love. "Height" and "depth" speak of the extremes, above and below, and so they cover the whole universe. "Anything else in all creation" means anything that has been created. That love is not far away: it is given to us in Christ Jesus, that is, through him and joined to him.

The apostle Paul speaks in his letter to the Christians in Rome. He has just mentioned suffering, persecution and danger. With this list, which comes from the verses before, he wants to give the believers assurance: no hardship or power, seen or unseen, can cancel the love that God showed in Christ.

Today, when you feel alone, guilty or very weak, remember that your worth does not depend on your mood. Say it in prayer: "Lord, your love sustains me today."
exp.14:19:
Paul says he worked eagerly and with determination to preach the gospel in places where Christ was not yet known. He did not want to build on someone else's foundation, that is, to build on groundwork another person had already laid.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just described how God worked through him, from Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum. In this way he explains his calling as an apostle to the Gentiles, and that is why at times he could not visit them. He quotes Isaiah to show that those who have never heard will understand.

Today we might ask ourselves who has never heard about Jesus: a neighbor, a coworker, or a person in a distant village. We can pray for that person and share the gospel with them in love and simplicity, without belittling the work of others.
exp.15:5:
Paul sends greetings to a woman named Mary. "Greet" means to pass on his greetings or to say hello to her on his behalf. Paul says she "has worked very hard for you," meaning she labored and wore herself out serving. The phrase "for you" shows that her service benefited the Christians in Rome.

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Rome. In chapter 16 he greets many people by name, both men and women, and recognizes their work. We do not know more about this Mary; the text does not say exactly what she did. We only see that Paul valued her and kept her in mind.

God sees and remembers quiet work. Today we can follow Paul's example by thanking those who serve in the church without drawing attention to themselves. A sincere word of gratitude can encourage someone who is tired.
exp.0:24:
They exchanged the truth about God for a lie. Instead of worshiping the Creator, they gave their honor and service to created things. The verse's word for "exchanged" means changed or traded, "created things" are the things that were made, and "the Creator" is the one who made them. At the end, Paul breaks into praise: the Creator is worthy of praise forever.

Here the apostle Paul speaks, in his letter to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that humanity needs the gospel, because people have turned away from God even though they could have known him through creation. The verses before and after describe the consequences of that turning away: God "gave them up," that is, let them follow their own desires.

Today we can ask ourselves what good things, such as money, work or fame, we have placed in the place of God. Let us give Him first place and enjoy everything else with gratitude.
exp.10:11:
Paul says that Israel's failure brought blessing to the whole world. "Trespass" and "failure" describe their stumbling, their refusal to accept Christ and the spiritual loss that followed. "Fullness" means completeness, the idea that Israel would one day be made whole again. If their stumbling opened the way for the Gentiles to receive spiritual riches, how much greater will the blessing be when they are restored!

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, especially the Gentiles. He is a Jew, and it grieves him that many of his people have rejected Jesus. Even so, he teaches that God has not cast them off. Some understand this fullness as a great future turning of Israel to Christ; others see it as a process already underway. Christians debate this.

Today, we can trust that God can bring good even out of failure. And instead of looking down with pride on those who do not believe, let us pray for them with love and hope.
exp.8:0:
Paul says that what he is about to say is entirely true. He affirms it "in Christ," that is, as someone who lives united with Him. He says he is not lying, and adds that his conscience, confirmed in the Holy Spirit, backs up his sincerity. His conscience stands beside him as a witness.

Here the apostle Paul speaks in his letter to the Romans. After celebrating God's love at the end of chapter 8, he begins a new theme: his deep sorrow for his fellow Israelites. The verses that follow say he suffers greatly for them. Paul stresses that he is not exaggerating, because he wants to be believed.

For today: when you speak about something that hurts you, do it with sincerity and without manipulation. Ask the Holy Spirit to shape your conscience, so that your words and your love for others are genuine.
exp.2:29:
Paul says that there is only one God, and because of that, there is only one way for anyone to be declared right before Him: faith. The words "circumcised" and "uncircumcised" refer to Jews and to those who are not Jews. To be "justified" means that God declares a person righteous, free of guilt before Him.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome, who came from both Jewish and non-Jewish backgrounds. Some believed that Jews had a special advantage in being saved through the law. Paul answers with a basic truth: if there is one God, He is the God of all, and He deals with everyone on the same terms. He then makes clear that this does not overturn the law but upholds it.

Today, no matter your background, your church, your culture or your past, no one has an advantage before God. Trust in Christ, and treat other believers as equals, neither feeling superior nor inferior.
exp.5:13:
It says that sin will not be the master of believers. The original word here means it will not rule or dominate over you the way a lord rules over his servants. The reason is that believers no longer live under the law, which only showed what is wrong, but under grace, the undeserved favor of God that brings forgiveness and the strength to change.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just urged them not to let sin reign or give their bodies to it, but to give themselves to God. This verse is a promise that encourages them. Right away he makes clear that grace is not permission to sin, since whoever you give yourself to is the one you serve.

For today: when you feel trapped by a bad habit, do not give up thinking you cannot change. Ask God for help, each day surrender your decisions to him, and live confident that his grace sustains you.
exp.2:5:
Paul responds firmly: "Certainly not!" Someone once argued that if our wickedness makes God's righteousness stand out, then God would be unjust to punish. Paul answers that if that were true, God could not judge the world, and the Bible teaches that he will.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome and imagines the objections of someone who wants to excuse sin. He has already said that the Jews received God's words, but that this does not free them from judgment. Here he defends the fact that God is just and will judge everyone with truth. He himself makes clear that he is speaking "as a man," that is, using a human argument.

For today: do not use God's grace as an excuse to sin. Trust that God is just, and live with humility, knowing that he will judge with truth.
exp.13:10:
This verse says that God himself promises, with an oath ("as surely as I live"), that every knee will bow before him and every tongue will openly acknowledge him. The phrase "as surely as I live" is a solemn oath by God's own life, and "every tongue will confess to God" means acknowledging and praising God.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome who were arguing with one another about foods and special days. He quotes the Old Testament (it appears to be taken from Isaiah 45:23) to remind them that the only Judge is God. In context, the judgment seat is Christ's, and all of us will give an account, not to other believers, but to him.

For today: when you feel the urge to criticize or look down on another believer over secondary differences, remember that you and he will both give account to the same Lord. Better to pray for that person, treat them with respect, and take care that your way of living does not make them stumble.
exp.8:31:
Why not? Because their pursuit was not by faith, but as if it were by works. They tried to gain righteousness through their own efforts instead of trusting God.

The phrase "pursuit" means that they chased after it with effort. "They stumbled over the stumbling stone" means that they fell after colliding with something in their path. That stumbling stone is the obstacle that made them fall.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and feels deep sorrow for his people, Israel. He explains that many Jews worked very hard, but refused to trust God through Christ. That is why the stone spoken of by the prophets, which most interpreters understand to be Christ, became their stumbling block.

For today: it is not enough to strive to be good. Rest in the grace of Jesus, trust in Him, and stop trying to earn God's favor by your own merits.
exp.5:2:
Paul asks whether believers do not know that, having been baptized into Christ Jesus, they were baptized into his death. The word "know" in his question carries the same sense as "know" in the rest of the verse: he means that baptism joins a person with Christ, even in his death. Some understand this as a real spiritual union, and others as a picture of that union; Christians explain it in different ways.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God's grace is abundant, and now he answers an objection: if grace grows where sin is, may we go on sinning? He answers no, because whoever belongs to Christ has already died to sin.

For today: when you feel the temptation to excuse a bad habit by saying that God will forgive you, remember that in Christ you have a new life. Ask God for help to live according to what you already are in him.
exp.0:8:
Paul says that God himself is his witness, meaning that God knows that what he affirms is true. He explains that he serves God "with my spirit," that is, with his whole heart and not only outwardly, in preaching the gospel of his Son. And he assures them that he remembers the believers in Rome constantly, bringing them up in his prayers again and again.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, a church he did not yet know in person. He has just thanked God because their faith was being talked about everywhere. By calling God as his witness, he wants to show that his affection for them is sincere, and so he prepares the ground for asking them to receive him soon.

Today we can imitate Paul by praying steadily for specific people, even those we do not know well. Try writing down a few names today and praying for them regularly.
exp.1:25:
This verse says that if a person who is not circumcised keeps what the law requires, God will regard that person as though they were circumcised. The phrase "requirements of the law" means the commandments and what the law asks of a person. An "uncircumcised" person is one who lacks the physical sign of the Jewish covenant.

The apostle Paul is speaking to Jews who relied on having circumcision and the law, but did not live by them. He wants to show that the outward sign is not enough if the heart and conduct do not obey God. Gentiles who obey put to shame those who merely boast of their religion.

For today: do not trust in labels, baptisms, customs, or church attendance as if they were enough. Ask yourself honestly whether your life reflects obedience and love for God, and ask him to change your heart.
exp.4:15:
Paul says that God's gift does not work the same way as Adam's sin. One sin brought judgment and condemnation. But the gift came after many trespasses, and it ended in justification, that is, in God declaring righteous the one who believes. "Gift" means a free present, and "trespass" is a wrong or a violation of God's law.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome and comparing Adam with Christ. Adam is a pattern or model of Christ, because one man affected many. Paul wants to show that the work of Jesus is far more powerful than the damage caused by sin.

For today: if you carry guilt for your accumulated mistakes, remember that God's grace is not used up by the number of your failures. Confess your sin honestly and rest in Christ, who offers you forgiveness as a gift, not as a payment.
exp.10:1:
Paul affirms that God has not rejected his people, Israel, whom he chose and knew beforehand. Then he asks whether they do not know what the Scripture says about Elijah. "Rejected" means turned away from or set aside. "Foreknew" speaks of a relationship chosen in advance. "Appealed" describes how Elijah brought his complaint to God about Israel.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, made up of Jews and non-Jews. He asks whether God abandoned Israel, because many Jews had not believed in Jesus. He himself is proof that this is not so: he is an Israelite and a believer. He recalls the time of Elijah, when the prophet felt alone and thought everyone had turned away (1 Kings 19). God showed him that he still had a faithful remnant.

For today: when you feel alone in your faith or see everything falling apart, remember that God is faithful to his promises and keeps working, even where you cannot see it.
exp.0:1:
It says that the gospel of God is not a new idea. God "promised beforehand" this good news through his prophets, and that promise was written in the Holy Scriptures, that is, what we today call the Old Testament. The word "beforehand" shows that God announced it long ago.

Paul introduces himself to the Christians of Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. He makes clear that the message he preaches does not contradict the faith of Israel, but fulfills it. This was important because that church included believers of Jewish background and believers of non-Jewish background. The following verse explains that this promise concerns Jesus, the Son of God.

For today: read the Old Testament too. You will see how God was preparing the way for Jesus, and that will strengthen your confidence that God keeps what he promises.
exp.11:9:
It says we should love fellow believers the way family members love one another, with sincere devotion. "Brotherly love" means that kind of family affection. "Outdoing one another in honor" means taking the first step in showing respect and value to the other person, without waiting for them to do it first.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, who is writing to the Christians in Rome. After explaining God's grace, he now teaches them how to live together in community. Just before this, he speaks of gifts and of a love without pretense; this verse shows how that love looks in everyday life.

For today: this week, look for a chance to be the first to acknowledge or thank someone in your church or family. A message, a sincere compliment, or a gesture of respect can make that genuine love visible.
exp.9:0:
Paul says that what he wants most from his heart, and what he asks of God in prayer for Israel, is their salvation. The word "salvation" here means being saved, not good physical health. "Desire" means a deep longing of the will.

The apostle Paul is speaking to the Christians in Rome. In the previous chapter he has just explained his sorrow over his fellow Jews, most of whom had not recognized Jesus as the Messiah. Although they make great efforts to please God, the verses that follow say they lack correct knowledge. For this reason Paul does not judge them coldly, but prays for them with affection.

For today: let us think of someone who does not yet know Jesus, even someone who makes us uncomfortable or who rejects us. Instead of arguing or criticizing, we can pray every day for that person with a loving heart, and look for a kind opportunity to share our faith.
exp.13:4:
Paul says that some believers regard certain days as more important than others, while someone else considers every day alike. He then tells each person that they should be fully convinced in their own mind, that is, settled in their mind and heart about what they do before God.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there were believers from different backgrounds who disagreed about foods and special days. It is not known with certainty which days were meant, although many think they were Jewish festivals or fasts. He asks for respect in matters that are not essential, because each one acts for the Lord.

Today we can be patient with brothers and sisters who practice their faith in a different way on secondary matters. Before criticizing, ask yourself: is this person doing it to honor the Lord? Seek your own conviction in prayer, and treat with love the one who thinks differently.
exp.4:16:
Because of one man's trespass, death ruled over everyone through that one man, Adam. But what Christ offers is far greater. Those who receive God's abundant grace and the gift of being made righteous will reign in life through the one man, Jesus Christ.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and compares Adam with Christ. His purpose is to show that God's grace is more powerful than sin and death. Some understand this "reigning in life" as a reality already present, and others as a future hope; it probably includes both.

Today you can stop trying to earn God's love. Receive his forgiveness each day as a gift, and live with the confidence that sin and guilt no longer hold power over you.
exp.5:3:
Being baptized means we are joined to Christ in his death, as if we had been buried with him. But the story does not end in the grave: just as the Father raised Christ from the dead through his glory, we too can live each day in a new life. The verse says we are to walk in newness of life, meaning we are to live out our days this way.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that God gives grace abundantly, and someone might think, "Then let us keep on sinning." Paul answers, "By no means." Whoever belongs to Christ has already died to sin, so they cannot keep living in it as before. Some understand baptism here as the act of water, and others as spiritual union with Christ; many see both.

For today: if you belong to Christ, your past does not rule over you. Today, choose one old habit that harms you and ask God for strength to replace it with a new action that honors him.
exp.12:0:
Everyone must submit to the governing authorities. "Governing authorities" means those who hold power and rule over us. Paul states that there is no authority except that which comes from God, and that the authorities that exist have been appointed by God.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, the capital of the empire. They lived under a powerful and at times unjust government. Paul wants them to live in an orderly way and to make sure their faith is not mistaken for rebellion. The verses that follow describe the authorities as those who restrain evil. Scholars debate how far this obedience extends when an authority orders something contrary to God.

Today we can respect the laws, pay our taxes, and treat authorities with honor. If a serious conflict arises with our conscience, we pray and act with humility and respect.
exp.11:8:
What it says: Paul says that love must be sincere, with no masks or pretense. Someone who truly loves is free of hypocrisy. Such a person detests what is evil and clings firmly to what is good. The image of clinging suggests holding on tightly and staying close to what is good.

Context: Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of the gifts God gives to each person, such as serving, teaching, encouraging, and giving. Now he shows that all these gifts must be exercised with genuine love. Then he gives concrete examples: affection among brothers and sisters, mutual respect, diligence, and service to the Lord.

For today: This week, check whether any of your displays of affection are merely courtesy or appearance. Do an act of kindness without seeking recognition, and honestly step away from something bad that attracts you.
exp.9:7:
Paul asks, "What does it say?" and answers that the word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart. That word is the message of faith that he and the other apostles were proclaiming. The phrase "the word of faith we are proclaiming" refers to the gospel message being announced.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome and quotes Deuteronomy 30:11-14. He explains that righteousness by faith does not require impossible feats, such as going up to heaven or down into the deep to find Christ. God has already come near to us in Jesus, and the message is within reach of everyone, both Jews and Gentiles.

Today, you do not need to accomplish anything extraordinary to draw near to God. His message is already close to you. You can open your Bible, believe it sincerely, and speak to him today in prayer, using simple words.
exp.15:16:
Paul asks the brothers to watch out for those who create divisions and obstacles, that is, to stay alert to them. An obstacle here means something that makes others stumble and fall away from the faith. These people act against the teaching the believers had already received. That is why Paul tells them to turn away from such people.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome near the end of his letter, after sending greetings. Before saying goodbye, he warns them about those who harm the unity of the church with teachings that go against the gospel. The verses that follow say that such people serve their own appetites and deceive others with smooth and flattering words. Scholars do not agree on exactly who they were.

Today, knowing the Bible well helps us recognize teachings that divide people or lead them away from Christ. With humility and prayer, we can turn away from those who insist on such teachings, while still loving everyone.
exp.5:6:
This verse says that the one who has died is freed from the debt and the power of sin. The word "freed" here means being released from sin's claim. The verse's own wording, "anyone who has died," points to the same idea: a person who has died is no longer under sin's claim.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that when we are joined to Christ, our old way of living was crucified with him. Some were thinking that, since God forgives, they could go on sinning. Paul answers that the one who is united with Christ in his death no longer has to live as a slave to sin. Interpreters explain in different ways how this is lived out in practice, but they all agree that it is real freedom.

For today: when an old temptation comes, remember that you are no longer its slave. Say to God, "Your power has set me free," and take one concrete step to say no.
exp.8:12:
God says, as it is written in the Bible, that he loved Jacob but Esau he hated. The word "hated" sounds very harsh. In biblical language it can mean "loved less" or "did not choose," as seen in Luke 14:26.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews, and explains why many from Israel did not accept Jesus. He quotes Malachi 1:2-3 and Genesis 25:23. His point is that God chose Jacob before the twins were born, without depending on their works. Christians understand in different ways how this choosing relates to human freedom, but Paul stresses that God acts with mercy.

Today we can receive salvation with humility, without boasting of our own merits. If God called us by his grace, let us live thankfully and treat others with that same mercy.
exp.11:3:
Just as each of us has one body with many parts, and each part has a different job, so it is with us. "Members" are the parts of the body, like the hand or the foot. "Function" means the work or role a part performs.

Paul is writing to the believers in Rome. He has just asked them not to live like the world and not to think they are better than others. He uses the image of the body to explain that the church forms one unity, yet each person has a different role. The verses that follow speak of the gifts God gives to each one.

For today: do not compare yourself with others or feel lesser for not having someone else's gift. Ask yourself how you can serve in your church or family, and do it with humility, also valuing what others contribute.
exp.3:17:
Abraham believed when, humanly speaking, there was no longer any reason to hope. The phrase "against all hope" means that, although everything seemed impossible, he kept trusting God. In this way he became "the father of many nations," that is, of many peoples. His "offspring" means his descendants, and "So shall your offspring be" points to the promise that his descendants would be countless, like the stars (Genesis 15:5).

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that God accepts people by faith and not by keeping the law. Abraham is his example, because he believed God's promise before the law was given. For this reason he is the spiritual father of all who believe, whether they are Jews or not Jews.

For today: when your situation seems closed, do not trust in what you see, but in what God has promised. Pray, keep going with patience, and remember that God is faithful, even when you cannot see how.
exp.15:26:
Paul closes his letter with a note of praise: all the glory belongs to the only wise God, and it is given to him through Jesus Christ, forever. "Amen" means "so be it."

The closing note in this translation does not mention where the letter was written or who carried it, so this explanation does not comment on those details.

Paul speaks at the end of his longest and deepest letter, where he explains the gospel: salvation through faith in Christ for both Jews and non-Jews. Today we can end our days, our prayers, and our accomplishments by giving the glory to God and not to ourselves. Before going to sleep, try to thank him for one specific thing and say to him: "To you be the glory."
exp.15:12:
Paul sends greetings to Rufus and to his mother. He calls Rufus "chosen in the Lord," meaning a believer who is valued and outstanding in the faith. He also says that the woman has been a mother to him as well.

Paul ends his letter to the Romans with a long list of greetings to people he knew. Some think this Rufus is the same man mentioned in Mark 15:21, the son of Simon of Cyrene, but that is not certain. We also do not know when that woman cared for Paul as a mother; it may have been a gesture of affection and gratitude.

Today we can value those who have cared for us in the faith, even if they are not blood relatives. A phone call, a message, or a word of thanks to someone who has served us with love can encourage them greatly.
exp.14:16:
Paul says he has reason to exult, but only "in Christ Jesus," that is, because of what Christ has done, and in his service to God, that is, in his spiritual work. To exult means to rejoice in something and speak about it with confidence. The phrase "in my service to God" means "in the work I do for God."

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God made him a servant of Christ to the Gentiles, that is, to non-Jews. His boasting is not about himself: he quickly makes clear that he speaks only of what Christ accomplished through him, by word, deeds, and the power of the Spirit.

We can rejoice in what God does through our service, but without showing off. When something goes well in your work, your family, or your church, thank Christ first and recognize that everything comes from his grace.
exp.11:10:
It says not to let your zeal subside, to keep your spiritual fervor, and to serve the Lord in everything you do. Here "zeal" means earnestness or eagerness about things. "Spiritual fervor" speaks of an inner passion for God, and some believe it refers to the Holy Spirit, others to our own spirit.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. After explaining what God has done for them in Christ, he shows them how to live together in community. Before this he speaks of sincere love and mutual honor; afterward, of hope, prayer and hospitality. This sentence joins love with daily service.

For today: do your work, your household chores or your help in the church with zeal, and offer it to God as service. Begin each morning in prayer: "Lord, I do this for you."
exp.10:6:
Paul says that Israel, as a people, was seeking righteousness before God, but did not obtain it. Instead, "the elect," the group of Israelites whom God chose by grace, did obtain it. The rest were hardened, meaning their hearts closed and they could not recognize Christ. Some understand that God hardened them, and others that God confirmed the hardness they already had.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He asks whether God has abandoned Israel. He answers that he has not: there always remains a faithful remnant, saved by grace and not by works. He then cites the Scriptures to show that this hardening had been seen before.

For today: we cannot earn God's favor through religious effort. Receive his grace with humility, and ask him to keep your heart responsive to his voice.
exp.9:14:
Romans 10:15 says that no one can announce God's message unless they have been sent. Paul quotes Isaiah 52:7: the feet of those who bring good news are "beautiful" because they bring peace with God. Paul's quotation uses "good news" in the same sense that Isaiah's words do.

Paul writes to the church in Rome. He explains that salvation is within reach of both Jews and non-Jews, but to believe, people must hear, and to hear, someone must bring the message. It is a chain: sending, preaching, hearing, believing, calling on the Lord. He then notes that not everyone obeys, as happened in Isaiah's time.

For today: we can be part of that chain. Pray for those who bring the gospel, support them in concrete ways, and, wherever God places you, share simply what Christ has done for you.
exp.0:23:
Because they had rejected God, He gave them over to what their hearts desired. Their impurity was a kind of moral uncleanness. Their desires were strong and disordered. They dishonored their own bodies with one another. The "foolish" people mentioned in the previous verse were those who lacked wisdom.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that all human beings need the gospel. Here he describes how people exchanged the worship of the Creator for idols. To "give over" does not mean that God causes evil, but that He allows people to suffer the consequences of their own path.

For today: when you feel your heart drifting away from God, do not ignore it. Bring it to prayer and return to Him soon, before evil desires carry you further away. God forgives those who repent.
exp.11:11:
Be joyful in hope, patient in affliction, persistent in prayer. This verse brings together three attitudes of the believer: being joyful because of the hope they have in God, being patient when hardship comes, and not giving up on prayer. The word "patient" here means someone who keeps going without giving in. "Affliction" means suffering or difficulty. "Persistent" means someone who keeps praying again and again.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. In this part of the chapter he describes how faith is lived out in everyday life, after having explained what God has done for them. His words sit between the call to serve the Lord with enthusiasm and the call to help those in need and bless those who persecute them. It was a church facing pressure, and Paul encourages them to hold on in this way.

For today: when you go through a difficult time, do not stop praying. Set aside a few minutes each day to speak with God, and remember one of his promises that gives you hope.
exp.7:18:
It says that the creation waits with eager expectation, as if straining forward, for the day when it will be revealed who the children of God truly are. "Creation" here refers to everything that has been made, and "revelation" means that something hidden is brought into full view.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of present suffering and the future glory of those who are children and heirs with Christ. Now he widens the view: creation also suffers because of the fall and waits to be set free. Some understand "creation" as all of nature; others take it in a more limited way, but the general sense is creation waiting for its restoration.

For today: when you suffer or grow tired of a broken world, remember that your pain is not the end. Wait with patience and hope, and care with respect for what God created.
exp.1:17:
He says that this person knows what God wants and is able to tell what is better, because they have been taught the law. The phrase "approve of what is superior" can also be understood as "test the things that differ" or "distinguish what matters"; scholars translate it in both ways.

Paul is speaking to Jews who boasted of their knowledge of the law. He recognizes their real privileges, but he is setting up a point: having the law and knowing it is not enough if it is not lived out. Paul wants to show that all of us, Jews and non-Jews alike, need Jesus Christ.

Today: knowing the Bible is a gift, but it is not the same as obeying it. Ask yourself this week: "What is one thing I already know about God that I am still not practicing?" And take that step with humility.
exp.8:21:
He says that God wanted to show his anger against sin and make his power known, yet still bore with great patience those who are headed toward destruction, described as the vessels of his wrath. Patience is the word for the gentleness and forbearance God showed. The word rendered as known simply means known to all.

The phrase about those prepared for destruction is understood in different ways: some see that God prepared them, while others see that they prepared themselves by rejecting him.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He uses the image of the potter to show that God is free and just in his decisions. He asks, "What if...?", to show that God does not act in haste but with patience, and that his mercy also reaches the Gentiles.

For today: when you see that God is slow to judge evil, remember that his patience is an opportunity for us to repent. Make use of it with humility and trust in him.
exp.3:3:
The verse says that when someone works, their wages are not credited to them as a gift but as an obligation. In other words, pay is something the employer owes the worker. Paul is pointing out that this is how earning works, and it is exactly why salvation cannot be earned.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He explains that no one is declared righteous before God because of their efforts. He uses Abraham as an example: God credited him as righteous because he believed. With the image of wages, Paul shows that if salvation were earned through works, God would owe it to us. But it is received through faith, as a gift.

For today: do not try to win God's love through your good behavior. Do good as a grateful response to his gift, not as a payment so that God will accept you. Rest in his grace.
exp.6:1:
The verse says that a married woman is bound by law to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is released from the law of marriage. The ideas here are simple: the first is being tied to someone, and the second is having a commitment she must keep.

Paul writes to believers in Rome, speaking to those who know the law. He uses marriage as a simple example: the law applies as long as the person lives. Then he explains that believers have died to the law through Christ, in order to belong to the One who was raised from the dead. It is a comparison; some scholars discuss each detail of it, but the central idea is clear.

For today: do not spend your life trying to win God's love by your own efforts. Belong to Christ with gratitude, and let his life in you bear fruit in love and sincere obedience.
exp.14:25:
This verse tells us that the churches of Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to take up a contribution for the poor among the believers in Jerusalem. The word "contribution" here means a gift of money collected from the community. The phrase "were pleased" means they judged it good to do so, of their own free will.

Paul writes to the Romans and explains his plans: he is going to Jerusalem to bring this help, and after that he hopes to visit them on his way to Spain. Later he says that the believers of non-Jewish background felt they owed a debt to those in Jerusalem, from whom they had received the spiritual blessings of the gospel.

For today: Christian generosity springs from gratitude and willingness, not from obligation. Think of someone in your community who is in need, and give something concrete, with joy.
exp.8:16:
Paul quotes what God said to Pharaoh in Exodus 9:16. The phrase "I raised you up" means that God placed Pharaoh in his position of power, or kept him standing. The purpose was to display God's power in him, so that God's name would be proclaimed in all the earth.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and explains that salvation depends on God's mercy, not on human effort. He uses Pharaoh as an example, since God acted in Pharaoh's story to make his name known.

Interpreters debate how God's decision and Pharaoh's own hardness relate to each other; the Bible says that Pharaoh hardened his heart and also that God hardened him.

Today we can rest in the knowledge that God governs history, even when evil seems to win. It is also a call to humility: we cannot boast about what we have received, because everything comes from his mercy. Let us respond with gratitude and with hearts ready to listen to him.
exp.12:9:
Love does no wrong to its neighbor. For that reason, love is what completes the law. The word "love" in this verse is the ordinary word we use here, "neighbor" means any person near us, and "fulfillment" means the completion of the law, that is, what brings the law to its goal.

The speaker is the apostle Paul, writing to Christians in Rome. Earlier he asked them to live in peace and to respect the authorities. Here he sums up the commandments about how to treat others with one idea: love your neighbor as yourself. Afterward he encourages them to wake up and live as people of the light, because the final salvation is nearer.

Before you answer in anger, speak badly of someone, or take advantage of another person, ask yourself: "Does this do good or harm to that person?" Let love guide your decision.
exp.2:2:
Paul asks a question: if some did not have faith, does their lack of faith cancel out God's faithfulness? The word "nullify" means to make something have no value or no effect. The question expects a negative answer, and Paul gives it right away: "By no means."

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome and answering objections that a Jew might raise. He has just said that the people of Israel were entrusted with the word of God. Now he imagines this doubt: if many did not have faith, did God fail in his promise? Paul argues that God is faithful, even when people are not.

For today: the faith of others, or even our own when it wavers, does not change who God is. If you see someone drifting away or failing, do not conclude that God's word has lost its power. Rest in the fact that God is true and keeps what he has said.
exp.7:35:
Those who follow Christ, the verse says, live constantly exposed to death. "For Your sake" means for God's sake. "We face death all day long" means we live with the danger of death continually. "Sheep to be slaughtered" are sheep destined to be sacrificed: they are seen as people without defense or worth.

Paul quotes Psalm 44:22, where God's people suffered even though they remained faithful. He uses it right after naming sufferings such as persecution, hunger, and the sword. With this he shows that pain is not a sign that God has abandoned us. The believers of his time did suffer persecution, and he knew it from his own experience.

For today: when you go through mockery, loss, or trials because of your faith, do not conclude that God has stopped loving you. Pray sincerely and remember that Christ intercedes for you and that his love remains firm.
exp.0:31:
It says that people, although they know that God considers certain conduct worthy of death, not only continue to practice it, but also approve of those who do it. The word "knowing" means that they know or recognize it. The phrase "those who do such things" refers to those who practice such conduct. "Also approve of those who practice them" means that they agree with, support, or applaud them. The phrase "worthy of death" speaks of separation from God and his judgment, not only of physical death.

The apostle Paul speaks in his letter to the Christians in Rome. In this chapter he describes how humanity, by rejecting God, sinks into sin. With the preceding list of wrongs, he shows that all of us need the gospel. Later he will say that God offers forgiveness through faith in Jesus Christ.

For today: let us watch not only what we do, but also what we applaud, share, or find amusing. Let us ask God for humility to recognize our sin and to turn to his mercy.
exp.14:27:
Paul says that, once he has finished his service of delivering the collection gathered for the poor Christians in Jerusalem, he will visit the believers in Rome on his way to Spain. "Having safely delivered this bounty" means carrying the gift to its recipients as he intended. The "bounty" is the result of the love and generosity of the churches.

Paul writes this letter to the Romans from Corinth, as is commonly understood. He tells them of his plans to travel to Rome and then on to Spain. First he must bring the aid from Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem. The Bible does not clearly say whether Paul actually reached Spain, so this cannot be stated with certainty.

For today: first fulfill the commitments you have already made, even when you have great plans ahead. And if you have received something good from others, look for ways to bless them too with what you have.
exp.1:5:
He says that God, in his judgment, will repay each person according to what they have done. The word "repay" means to give back a fair response, and "deeds" refers to the way a person lives, not only to isolated acts. No one is left out of this judgment.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. In this passage he speaks to the one who judges others and thinks he will escape God's judgment. He reminds them that God's kindness and patience are not permission to carry on as before, but an invitation to repent. The verses that follow show that our deeds reveal where the heart is heading. Christians understand this passage together with the rest of the letter, where Paul teaches that salvation is by grace through faith.

Today you can see God's patience as an opportunity, not an excuse. Ask yourself: "Does my way of living show that I have truly turned to Him?" Come to God with humility and sincerity.
exp.4:17:
This verse compares two men: Adam and Jesus Christ. Through the one trespass of Adam, condemnation reached all of humanity. In the same way, through one act of righteousness by Christ, justification and life are given to all people. To be justified means to be declared righteous before God.

Paul is writing to believers in Rome. He wants to show that just as one man opened the door to sin and death, another, Christ, opened the door to forgiveness and life. Christians understand "all men" in different ways: some see that the offer is for everyone, and others see that it applies to those who believe. The verses that follow speak of "the many."

For today: you do not have to earn forgiveness by your own efforts. Receive it with confidence and gratitude, and share it with others.
exp.5:0:
Paul asks a question: if God gives more grace the more we sin, should we keep on sinning so that his grace may increase? The word "continue" in the verse means to keep going, to stay in something. And "increase" means to grow or multiply. Paul answers at once with an emphatic "Certainly not!" That is, absolutely not!

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. In the previous chapter he said that where sin increased, grace increased all the more. Someone might misread that as permission to sin. Paul cuts off that idea at its root, explaining that whoever belongs to Christ has died to sin.

For today: God's grace is not an excuse to live as we please, but a power that transforms us. If you have a habit today that you know displeases God, do not say "God will forgive me anyway"; instead, ask him for help to leave it, grateful for his forgiveness.
exp.1:15:
This verse says that there will be a day when God will judge people's secrets through Christ Jesus. These are the hidden things, the thoughts, motives and secrets that no one else sees. That judgment will be carried out through Jesus Christ. Paul adds "as proclaimed by my gospel," meaning this judgment matches the message he preaches.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he spoke about the Gentiles, who, without the law of Moses, show in their conscience that they know what is good and evil. This verse closes that thought: God judges with justice, including what is inward. Next, Paul will turn to the Jews who trust that they have the law.

For today: it is not enough to look good before people. God looks at the heart. You can pray sincerely and ask him to examine your intentions, and trust that Christ, who will judge, also offers forgiveness.
exp.6:15:
Paul says that when he does something he does not want to do, that very action shows he agrees with God's law. If it bothers him that he does wrong, it is because he recognizes that the law is good. The word "admit" in the verse means "agree" or "recognize" that the law is good.

Paul is explaining that God's law is not the one to blame for sin. He describes an inner struggle between what he wants and what he ends up doing. Christians have understood this passage in two ways: some think it speaks of his life before he knew Christ, and others see it as the struggle of the believer. In both cases, the law is good and the problem lies with sin.

For today: when you feel sorry for having failed, do not become completely discouraged. That pain can show that you love what is good. Bring it honestly to God and ask him for help to change.
exp.0:25:
Because they had rejected God, he left them to their own choices, given over to dishonorable passions. Dishonorable passions are desires that bring shame on the person who has them. The word "exchanged" here means they traded one thing for another. Paul notes that some women traded natural relations for unnatural ones, going against the order of creation as he understands it.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He is showing that all humanity needs the gospel. His argument is that those who exchanged the truth of God for idolatry ended up distorting their own lives as well. The phrase "gave them over" indicates that God allows them to suffer the consequences of their own decisions. Scholars discuss how this passage should be applied, but almost all agree that its purpose is to show that all of us sin.

For today: before pointing out the sins of others, let us examine what we put in God's place, and remember that all of us need his grace.
exp.3:22:
This verse says that what Scripture records about Abraham was not written for his sake alone. The words "it was credited to him" are the key phrase, and they mean that God counted Abraham's faith to him as righteousness. The verse prepares the idea that this is also for others, as the next verse shows.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and explains that God declares people righteous by faith, not by works. He uses Abraham as an example, because Abraham trusted God's promise even when it seemed impossible. Paul wants to show that this ancient story has a present purpose for those who believe in Jesus.

For today: read the stories of the Bible not only as accounts of the past, but as messages for you. Just as Abraham trusted God, you can trust what God has done in Christ. Today, tell God simply that you rest in Jesus, not in your own merits.
exp.1:3:
Some people, the verse says, disregard God's kindness without realizing it. "Kindness" here means gentle goodness, and "tolerance" and "patience" mean that God holds back for a long time before punishing. To "disregard" something is to treat it lightly. The verse states that this kindness aims to lead us to repentance, that is, to turn around and change direction.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he spoke about those who judge others for their sins while doing the same things themselves. Here he asks them whether they think God's silence or delay means there will be no accounting. Then he warns that a hard heart that refuses to repent piles up judgment. Some believe he is addressing a moralistic Jew, but the text does not say this clearly at this point.

For today: when God gives you another chance, do not take it as permission to carry on as before. Ask yourself honestly what you need to correct, and take one concrete step today, such as asking forgiveness or letting go of a bad habit.
exp.9:13:
Paul asks a chain of connected questions. How can someone call on the One they have not believed in? How can someone believe in the One they have not heard of? And how can someone hear without someone to preach? Each step depends on the one before it. The phrase "call on" means calling on God to ask for his help, and "preach" means announcing the message of the gospel.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that God saves everyone who calls on him, whether Jew or Greek. Now he explains that this salvation comes through people who announce the message. In this way he argues that the gospel must be carried to everyone.

For today: faith often comes when someone shares what God has done in their life. Think of a person close to you, and this week look for a simple and kind way to speak to them about Jesus, or to pray for the one who does.
exp.0:11:
Paul explains what he said before. He wants to visit the Christians in Rome, not only to give them a spiritual gift, but also so that he and they can encourage one another. "Each other" means that both sides give and receive. The shared faith is the faith they have in common: theirs and his.

Paul writes this letter to a church he had not yet met in person. He has just said he wants to strengthen them, and now he corrects himself with humility: he too needs encouragement. In this way he shows that the apostle and the believers help one another.

For today: no one is so mature that they do not need the encouragement of others. When you gather with brothers and sisters in the faith, go ready to give encouragement, but also to receive it. Today, encourage someone with a sincere word, and let others encourage you too.
exp.7:8:
Paul tells the believers in Rome that they are controlled not by the flesh, meaning their old nature that opposes God, but by the Spirit. This is true if the Spirit of God lives in them. And whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.

Paul writes this letter to the church in Rome. Earlier he contrasted two ways of living: one centered on oneself and far from God, and another guided by the Spirit. Here he encourages the believers: their identity no longer depends on their own efforts, but on Christ dwelling in them through his Spirit.

For today: instead of living afraid of not being good enough, ask the Spirit to guide you each day. Your life with God rests on the fact that he lives in you, not on your own perfection.
exp.5:5:
This verse says that our old self, meaning what we were before following Christ, was crucified together with Jesus. Because of this, the body of sin is rendered powerless, and we no longer have to be slaves to sin.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He had been explaining that God's grace is no excuse for continuing to sin. He uses baptism as an image: just as Christ died and rose again, the believer leaves behind the old life and walks in a new life. Some understand the body of sin as our nature dominated by sin, and others as the physical body used for evil.

For today: when old habits come back, remember that you are no longer their slave. Ask God for help and act according to your new identity in Christ.
exp.13:15:
Romans 14:16 says that we should not allow what we consider good to be spoken of as evil. "Good" here means something we have or practice that is right in our own eyes. The verse does not name exactly what that good is, and interpreters understand it in different ways. It may refer to Christian freedom, to faith, or to salvation.

The apostle Paul is writing to Christians in Rome, where some believed certain foods were unclean and others did not. Paul tells them that those who are strong in faith have the freedom to eat, but that they should not use that freedom in a way that wounds a fellow believer. If the disagreement leads to quarrels or causes someone to stumble, even a good freedom can come to look bad to others.

For today: before using your freedom in matters that are optional, ask whether it helps or hurts the people around you. Sometimes love means setting aside something you are allowed to do, so that the witness of Christ is seen as good and full of peace.
exp.1:0:
It says that no one has an excuse before God if they judge others. "Have no excuse" means that a person cannot defend or justify themselves. Paul states that when you pass judgment on another person for a sin, you condemn yourself, because you do the same thing.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, in his letter to the Christians in Rome. In the previous chapter he described the sin of the pagans. Here he addresses the person who feels superior and points a finger at others. Many think he refers mainly to some Jews, although his words apply to anyone. His purpose is to show that all of us need the grace of God.

Before criticizing someone, examine your own heart honestly. Acknowledge your failures, and treat others with humility and compassion, remembering that you too depend on God's forgiveness.
exp.14:12:
This verse is a prayer from Paul. He asks that God, who is the source of hope, fill believers with joy and peace as they trust in him. The result is that their hope will grow and overflow, and this happens by the power of the Holy Spirit. Here "power" is the meaning of the word that the verse renders as "power."

Paul writes to the church in Rome, made up of both Jewish and non-Jewish believers. He has just quoted the Scriptures to show that God always intended to include the Gentiles, that is, the peoples who were not Jewish. With this prayer he closes his teaching about living in unity and accepting one another, and hope in Christ is what unites them.

When you feel anxious or discouraged, pray with this verse. Ask God for joy and peace, and trust that he can give you hope through his Spirit.
exp.8:20:
The potter, the verse says, has the right to take the same clay and make from it one vessel for special occasions and another for common use. The point is not that one vessel is bad in itself, but that it serves a less distinguished purpose.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He speaks of God's freedom to show mercy, and he answers the person who objects that this would be unfair. He uses the image of the potter, drawn from the Old Testament (as in Jeremiah 18). Christians have understood in various ways how this relates to God's choosing and human responsibility. But the text emphasizes that God is God, and we are not the ones who judge him.

For today: when you don't understand something of God's ways, pray with humility and trust. He is wise and good, and your place in his hands is not neglect, but care.
exp.11:14:
This verse asks us to share in the feelings of others. To rejoice means to be glad, and those who rejoice are the people who have something to celebrate. So we are glad with the one who is celebrating, and we weep with the one who is suffering. It means sharing the heart of the other person, without indifference.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, in his letter to the Christians in Rome. In this chapter he explains how to live their faith day by day. Earlier he speaks of helping those in need, of being hospitable, and of blessing those who persecute. Afterward he stresses unity, humility, and not repaying evil with evil. This verse brings all of that together: to love is to draw near.

Today you can apply it this way: when someone tells you good news, be truly glad for them, without envy. And when someone is suffering, do not rush to give advice; stay with them, listen to them, and weep with them.
exp.6:8:
Paul says there was a time when he lived "apart from the law," that is, without feeling the weight of the commandment. But when the commandment came to his conscience, sin sprang to life like something asleep that suddenly wakes, and he died, that is, he felt condemned and cut off from God. The word "desire" here means a disordered craving that pulls against what is right.

Paul speaks in the first person and argues that God's law is good, not bad. He explains that the law shows what sin is and stirs it into view in us. Scholars debate who this "I" refers to: Paul himself, Israel, or every person. Even so, the central point is clear.

For today: do not use God's law to feel righteous, but as a mirror that shows your need. When you see your weakness, do not despair; come to Christ, who gives forgiveness and new life.
exp.13:20:
It is better to avoid eating meat, drinking wine, or doing anything that may cause your brother to stumble. "Stumble" means that something leads him to sin or to doubt. Being hurt in his conscience and having his faith grow more fragile are the harms Paul has in view.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there were believers with different convictions about certain foods. Some felt free to eat anything; others, with a more sensitive conscience, did not. Paul does not say that meat or wine is wrong, since he has already affirmed that all things are clean. He asks that love and peace weigh more than their freedom.

Today, before you use your freedom in something debatable, think about who is watching you. If something of yours may confuse or wound another believer's faith, love may lead you to set it aside for a time.
exp.1:16:
Here Paul addresses someone who calls themselves a Jew, that is, who belongs to the people of Israel. That person relies on the law and takes pride in their relationship with God. Relying on the law means leaning on it with confidence, and it is the sense of security that comes from holding a name or identity with honor.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, will give account to God. Now he speaks to the one who feels secure simply because they have the law. Many understand that this begins a warning: knowing the law is not enough if it is not lived out.

For today: having a Bible, going to church, or calling yourself a Christian is a privilege, but it does not replace an obedient life. Ask yourself honestly whether your faith shows in your actions.
exp.10:21:
Look closely at two sides of God: his kindness and his severity. He was severe toward the branches that fell, that is, toward those who did not believe. Toward you he is kind, but on one condition: that you continue in that kindness, that is, that you keep trusting him. Otherwise, you too will be cut off, like a branch removed from the tree.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, most of whom were not Jewish. He uses the image of an olive tree: Israel is the natural branches, and believers from other nations are branches grafted in. Paul wants to prevent them from thinking they are superior to the Jews. Interpreters debate what it means to be "cut off": whether it is losing salvation or a serious warning about genuine faith.

Today, live with gratitude and humility. If you have anything good with God, it is because of his grace, not because of your own merit. Keep trusting him every day.
exp.11:17:
This verse says we should do everything we can to live at peace with everyone. "If it is possible" recognizes that this does not depend on one person alone, and "on your part" means "as far as it depends on you."

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there was tension and opposition. Earlier he asked for humility and not to repay evil with evil. Then he teaches not to take revenge, but to leave justice to God, and to do good even to the enemy. About the "burning coals," some see an invitation for kindness to awaken shame and repentance; others see it as judgment. It is interpreted in several ways.

Today: if you have a conflict with someone, take the first step. Greet them, ask forgiveness if you were wrong, or respond calmly, without demanding that the other person change.
exp.8:27:
