This verse says that the Lord will carry out his sentence on the earth thoroughly and decisively. The phrase "carry out" means that he brings his purpose through to completion, and "thoroughly and decisively" means that he does it fully and without delay. It is a quotation from Isaiah 10:22-23, and translators understand it in several ways, but the central idea is that God acts with determination.

Paul is speaking here about Israel. Although the people were very numerous, only a remnant would be saved. Paul quotes Isaiah to show that this does not mean God has failed. He keeps his word and follows his own plan of grace, which includes the Gentiles as well.

For today: do not take for granted that God will be slow to fulfill what he has said. Live with confidence and with humility, for salvation is a gift of his grace and not a right we inherit.
exp.0:9:
Paul says that when he prays, he asks God that, at last, if it is his will, the way may be opened for him to come to Rome. "In my prayers at all times" means he brings this request before God constantly. "Succeed in coming to you" means that the road is open and the journey goes through. The other phrases in the source are simply the same idea in other words, "to you" and "to you all."

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. He tells them that he remembers them always in his prayers and that he desires to see them so that they may encourage one another in the faith. He notes that he does not impose his own plan but leaves it in the hands of God's will. How that journey came about is another matter that the book of Acts narrates later.

For today: when you have a good desire, such as visiting someone or starting a project, bring it to God honestly and patiently. Ask that his will be done, trust his timing, and keep praying for the people you love.
exp.9:17:
Paul asks a question: "Did they not hear?" And he answers that they did. "Their voice" and "their words" refer to those who proclaim the message. He says their voice has gone out into all the earth, to the ends of the world, that is, to the farthest limits of the known world.

Paul quotes Psalm 19:4 to show that God's message has reached very far. He has just said that faith comes by hearing. Someone might object that Israel did not believe because they did not hear. Paul answers that they did hear. Some think the psalm is applied here to creation and others to the spread of the gospel; the text allows for both.

Today we can remember that God wants everyone to hear his word. We can speak of Christ simply to those around us, trusting that God makes faith grow.
exp.2:27:
It says that a person is declared righteous before God by trusting in Jesus, not by keeping the commandments of the law. "Justified" means declared innocent and accepted by God. "We maintain" means that Paul states this as a firm conclusion drawn from what he has already explained. "Works of the law" refers to efforts to earn God's favor by obeying the law of Moses.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He has just shown that everyone has sinned and that God offers salvation through Christ. For that reason there is no room for boasting: no one is saved on the basis of their own merit. And since God is one, he justifies both Jews and non-Jews by faith.

For today: rest in God's grace and not in your performance. Obey out of gratitude, not to earn his love. And treat others with humility, for we all receive the same thing.
exp.6:2:
It says that a married woman, while her husband is alive, is called an adulteress if she joins herself to another man. But if the husband dies, she is free from that law and is not an adulteress if she marries again. The verse of the phrase "is called an adulteress" is that she will be regarded as one.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, who know the law. He uses marriage as an example: just as death ends the wife's obligation to her husband, death with Christ ends our obligation to the law. Some interpreters debate the details of the comparison, but the central point is clear.

For today: if you belong to Christ, you do not live to earn God's favor through rules, but to bear fruit out of love for Him. Today, instead of asking yourself "what must I do?", ask Him: "how can I please you with gratitude?"
exp.14:4:
Paul prays that God, who gives endurance and encouragement, would grant believers harmony with one another, following the example of Christ Jesus. "Harmony" means living together with a shared mind and purpose. "Grant you" is a request: this unity is a gift from God.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there were believers from both Jewish and non-Jewish backgrounds who differed in customs and judged one another. Before this verse, he reminds them that Christ endured scorn out of love for others, and that the Scriptures encourage us to hope. Afterward, Paul says that this unity leads to glorifying God with one voice.

For today: if you have tension with a brother or sister in the faith, pray for that person and ask God for endurance. Then take a concrete step, such as listening or forgiving, without waiting for them to agree with you on everything.
exp.9:18:
Paul asks, "Did not Israel understand?" and answers with a quotation from Moses. God said he would make Israel jealous through "those who are not a nation," that is, through people who were not his chosen people. The verse says he would make them angry through "a nation without understanding," and it describes that anger as strong displeasure. To make someone jealous means to stir up envy in them.

Paul, the apostle, explains why many of his own people did not believe in Christ. It was not for lack of warning: Israel had heard the message and had the Scriptures. He quotes Deuteronomy 32:21 to show that God had already announced that his message would also reach other nations.

Today, we must not think of ourselves as owners of God's grace or look down on anyone. God calls those whom no one expects. Furthermore, we can live our faith with such humility and joy that others feel a desire to know him.
exp.0:27:
These people did not see fit to acknowledge God. Since they rejected him, God gave them up to a depraved mind, one that is corrupted and unable to judge well, and so they did what ought not to be done, things that are harmful and wrong.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He is showing that all of humanity needs the gospel. Before and after this verse he lists harmful behaviors as the result of turning away from God. That God "gave them up" is usually understood to mean that God allowed them to follow their own path.

For today: do not neglect God in your daily life. Set aside time to pray and read the Bible, and ask him to help you think clearly. If you have drifted away, remember that the same gospel Paul proclaims offers forgiveness and a fresh start.
exp.7:17:
Paul says he is convinced of something: our present sufferings cannot be compared with the glory that will be revealed in us. "I consider" means "I am sure." "Suffering" means enduring pain, and "the glory that will be revealed" is the glory that is coming.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that we are children and heirs of God, and that whoever suffers with Christ will also be glorified with him. Then he speaks of all creation eagerly waiting for that day. His point is that present pain is real, but it is not the end of the story.

Today, when you go through an illness, a loss, or an injustice, you do not have to pretend it does not hurt. You can bring your pain to God and remember that he promises something greater. That hope does not remove sadness at once, but it helps you keep going with peace and patience.
exp.15:0:
Paul introduces a woman named Phoebe and commends her to the Christians in Rome. He calls her "our sister" and describes her as a servant of the church in Cenchrea. The verse uses the word "commend," which means to recommend her to them. The Greek word translated "servant" here means someone who serves or helps. Some believe it referred to an official role in the church; others think it describes her service in general.

Paul writes this letter from Corinth, and Cenchrea was the nearby port. Most likely Phoebe carried the letter to Rome. That is why Paul asks that she be well received and helped in whatever she needs, since she has helped many people, including him.

Today we can notice those who serve quietly in our church and thank them. We can also welcome with affection and help the brothers and sisters who arrive from another place.
exp.7:7:
Those controlled by the flesh cannot please God. "Flesh" here does not mean the physical body, but a way of living controlled by the sinful nature, without God. "Then" shows that this is a conclusion drawn from what came before.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has been explaining that a mind set on the flesh leads to death and is hostility toward God, because it does not submit to his law. Right after this, he assures them that they are not controlled by the flesh but by the Spirit, if the Spirit of God lives in them. It is a comfort, not a condemnation.

Today we can remember that pleasing God does not depend on our effort to be good, but on living united with Christ through his Spirit. Ask him every day to guide your thoughts and decisions.
exp.5:7:
This explanation says that if we have been united with Christ in his death, we trust that we will also share in his life. "We believe" means we affirm it with faith, not that we merely hold an opinion. "Died with Christ" does not refer to physical death, but to the fact that, through faith, our old way of living under sin was joined to the cross of Jesus.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that God's grace is no excuse for continuing to sin. Earlier he spoke of baptism as a sign of this union with Christ. Now he affirms that dying with Christ leads to a new life, like that of Jesus risen, who no longer dies. Many understand that this life begins today and is completed in the final resurrection.

When sin tempts you, remember who you are in Christ. You no longer have to obey it. Ask God for strength and choose today one concrete action that reflects your new life.
exp.1:9:
God promises glory, honor, and peace to everyone who does good. This applies first to the Jew, and then to the Greek, meaning the non-Jewish peoples. The phrase "anyone who" refers to every person without exception. The words "does good" describe a life lived by doing what is good and right.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he spoke of God's judgment on the one who does evil, and here he shows the other side: God also rewards good. He insists that Jews and non-Jews are treated with the same justice, as the following verse confirms: "there is no partiality with God." Some understand that this passage speaks of the fruit of a true faith, not of earning salvation by works.

For today: do not compare yourself to others or judge them by their background or their position. Do good with simplicity, knowing that God looks at the heart and treats everyone with justice.
exp.10:28:
It says that God does not take back what he gives or whom he calls. The "gifts" are the blessings or favors God bestows, and the "calling" is his summons. The word "irrevocable" means that God does not withdraw or cancel them.

Paul writes to believers in Rome, most of whom were not Jewish. He is speaking about Israel, which for the most part had not accepted Christ. Paul wants the believers not to feel superior, and he reminds them that God remains faithful to his promises to the people he chose. Christians have received mercy, and that same mercy remains open to Israel.

For today: if God is faithful even when people fail, we can trust that his calling on our lives does not depend on our performance. And we should treat others with humility, without boasting, because we have all received everything through mercy.
exp.11:2:
Paul tells everyone not to think of themselves as more important than they really are. Instead, each person should think of themselves with sound judgment, which means balance and self-control, according to the measure of faith God has given them. Some understand this phrase to mean faith itself, while others understand it to mean the gifts and abilities that God distributes.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just urged them to offer themselves to God and to renew their minds. Now he applies this to life in the community. He says that he speaks by the grace given to him, meaning the authority God gave him as an apostle. Right after this, he compares the church to a body with many parts.

Today, before you compare yourself with others or boast about your talents, remember that everything you have is a gift from God. Value yourself with humility and honesty, and serve others with what you have received.
exp.2:9:
This verse says that no one is righteous before God by their own efforts. "Righteous" means someone who stands in perfect uprightness before Him. The words "There is no one righteous, not even one" allow no exceptions. "As it is written" shows that Paul is quoting the Scriptures, especially passages from the Psalms (such as Psalm 14 and Psalm 53).

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that both Jews and non-Jews are under sin, that is, under its power and guilt. He wants no one to boast of being better than others, so that he can show afterward that salvation comes through faith in Christ and not through our own merits.

For today: instead of comparing ourselves with others to feel good about ourselves, we can humbly recognize our need for God. This frees us from pride and condemnation, and leads us to thank Him for His grace and to treat others with compassion.
exp.7:14:
They say that those who belong to Christ did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns them to fear. They received the Spirit of adoption to sonship, the Spirit by whom we cry out, "Abba! Father!"

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that those who are led by the Spirit of God are his children. The verses that follow say that the Spirit confirms this identity and that the children are also heirs with Christ. Paul contrasts living in fear, like a slave, with living secure, like a beloved child.

For today: when you feel afraid of not being enough before God, pray to him, "Father." Speak to him with confidence, without pretending or hiding, remembering that his love does not depend on your achievements, but on the fact that you are his child.
exp.0:16:
This verse says that in the gospel the righteousness of God is shown, or made visible. That righteousness comes by faith, and faith is the way from beginning to end. "Reveals" matches the verse's wording. The phrase "from start to finish" is understood in several ways: from one stage of trust to a deeper trust, or from God's faithfulness to ours. Paul quotes Habakkuk 2:4: the righteous will live by faith.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that he is not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God to save everyone who believes, Jew or Greek. Here he explains why: in the gospel God shows how he makes us right with himself.

For today: you do not have to earn God's favor by your good behavior. Trust in Christ every day, even in your doubts and failures, and let that trust shape the way you live.
exp.7:24:
If we hope for what we do not yet see, we wait for it patiently. The word "but" here simply connects this thought to what came before, and the patience described means waiting steadily, holding on without giving up. Christian hope looks toward something God has promised that has not yet come to pass.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that all creation groans, and that we ourselves groan while we wait for the adoption, that is, the full redemption of our bodies. We live between what God has already done and what is still missing. Then Paul explains that the Spirit helps us in that weakness.

For today: when a prayer takes a long time or suffering continues, you do not have to pretend that everything is fine. You can wait calmly, pray honestly, and trust that God keeps what he promises, even when you do not yet see it.
exp.11:20:
It says that we should not let evil control us or change us. When someone harms us, the natural pull is to pay them back in kind, and in that way evil wins inside us. Instead, we are invited to overcome evil by doing good.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who lived surrounded by people who did not understand them and sometimes treated them badly. Earlier he asked them not to take revenge, but to leave justice to God. He gives the example of feeding a hungry enemy. The image of "burning coals of fire" is understood in several ways: shame that leads to repentance, or God's judgment. What is clear is that the response must be kindness.

Today, if someone offends you at work, in the family, or online, do not answer with insults or cold indifference. Pray for that person and make a concrete gesture of kindness, such as helping them or speaking to them with respect.
exp.1:21:
Paul asks the person who considers himself very religious: if you teach that no one should commit adultery, do you commit it yourself? If you say you hate idols, do you rob temples? The phrase "rob temples" means taking or defiling what belongs to God or to his temple. There are several ways to understand the exact detail of this accusation, but the central point is clear: the conduct does not match what is taught.

Paul is writing to the church in Rome. Here he speaks to a Jewish teacher who trusted that he knew the law. His aim is to show that knowing the law is not enough, because everyone needs the grace of God. As the next verse says, this inconsistency was causing others to speak badly of God.

Today: before correcting others, examine your own life. Ask God to make what you say you believe match what you do, because your example can draw others closer to him or push them away.
exp.7:32:
Paul says that no one can bring a valid charge against the people God has chosen, that is, his children. The reason is simple: God himself is the one who justifies them, meaning he declares them free from guilt and accepts them as righteous before him. The words for "accuse" and "chosen" are used the way they would be in a courtroom.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God gave his own Son for us. Confident of that, he asks questions as in a trial: if the Judge has already declared us righteous, who will be able to condemn us? He then goes on to speak of Christ, who died, rose again, and intercedes for us.

For today: when guilt or memories accuse you, do not give them the final word. Come before God trusting in what Christ has done for you, and rest in his forgiveness.
exp.5:15:
We all become slaves to whatever we offer ourselves to in order to obey. There are two paths: obeying sin, which ends in death, or obeying God, which leads to righteousness, that is, to a upright life before Him.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that they are under grace, not under the law, and he anticipates an objection: "Shall we sin, then?" He answers with a strong "Certainly not!" Grace is not permission to sin, because whoever gives themselves over to sin becomes a slave to it again. He then thanks God that they have already been set free.

For today: no one is completely neutral; what we repeat and obey shapes us. Today you can ask yourself which habit is mastering you, and hand it over to God, asking for His help to obey Him in one specific thing.
exp.13:17:
This verse says that whoever serves Christ in this way, that is, by living with righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit, is pleasing to God and approved by people.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were disagreements about which foods could be eaten. Some were judging others for it. Paul reminds them that the kingdom of God is not about food or drink, but about righteousness, peace, and joy. For that reason he asks them not to cause anyone to stumble.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are fighting over secondary things. Before arguing, let us seek peace and care for the weaker brothers and sisters in the faith. In this way we serve Christ with love and humility.
exp.2:28:
Paul asks a question and answers it himself: is God only the God of the Jews? No, he is also the God of the Gentiles, that is, of all the peoples who are not Jews. The word "yes" here means "without any doubt."

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, among whom there were believers who were Jews and believers who were not. He has just said that no one is saved by keeping the law, but by faith. If salvation came through works of the law, God would belong only to those who received it. But since it is by faith, the door is open to everyone. That is why he insists that God is one.

Today we can remember that God has no favorites by origin, country, culture or history. If God receives everyone through faith, then we too should welcome with respect and kindness anyone within the church who thinks or lives differently from us.
exp.9:3:
This verse says that Christ is the "end" of the law, meaning both its goal and its fulfillment. Through Him, righteousness, that is, being accepted by God, is brought to everyone who believes. The phrase "to bring righteousness" means that through Christ, righteousness is given. The word "end" can be understood as "termination" or as "purpose"; many believe Paul means both.

The apostle Paul speaks of his Jewish brothers. He acknowledges that they have great zeal for God, but they lack understanding that God himself gives righteousness. They tried to earn it by their own effort and did not submit to what God offered in Christ.

Today, you do not have to strive to deserve God's love. Trust in Christ, rest in what He has done, and let your obedience be born of gratitude, not of fear.
exp.7:0:
Those who are united with Christ Jesus no longer live under condemnation, that is, under a verdict of guilt. Being "in Christ" means belonging to him through faith and being joined to him.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Earlier, in chapter 7, he spoke of his struggle with sin. Now he answers with hope: sin and the law do not have the final word, because God acted in Christ. The following verses explain that God sent his Son to overcome sin.

Today, when you feel guilty over past failures, remember that if you trust in Christ, God does not condemn you. Come before him with sincerity and ask him for help to start again.
exp.7:2:
This verse says that the law of Moses could not save us, because our human nature, called here "the flesh," was weak and unable to keep it. So God sent his Son in a body like sinful human flesh, that is, with a real human body like ours, but without sin. The phrase "as an offering for sin" means that he came to deal with sin. Thus God condemned sin in the flesh: he pronounced judgment against sin in the person of Christ.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ. Now he explains why: what the law could not accomplish, God himself did through Jesus. Scholars understand the word "flesh" here in different ways, but in general it refers to human weakness apart from God.

For today: when you fail and feel guilty, do not try to earn forgiveness by your own efforts. Remember that Christ has already borne the condemnation, and ask him for his Spirit to live in a new way.
exp.10:4:
It says that, just as in the time of Elijah God kept a faithful group, so also now, in Paul's time, there is a remnant of Israelites who believe in Christ. The word "remnant" means a small leftover group. "Chosen by grace" means that God chose them out of his undeserved favor, not because of their merits.

In his letter to the Romans, Paul asks whether God has rejected his people Israel. He answers that he has not: he himself, an Israelite, is proof of this. He recalls Elijah, who felt alone, yet God had seven thousand faithful people. The following verses stress that this comes by grace and not by works.

For today: if you feel alone in your faith, remember that God knows who belongs to him and works more than you can see. And rest in the fact that your relationship with him is sustained by his grace, not by your performance.
exp.1:1:
He says that God judges based on truth, that is, with justice and without deception. "Such things" refers to the evil practices Paul described in chapter 1. "And we know" means this is something everyone recognizes: God's judgment is not based on appearances or opinions.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken about the sin of the pagans, and now he addresses the one who feels better than they are and points a finger at them. Paul reminds him that God also sees his own life, and that he does similar things.

Today, before criticizing others, it is wise to look honestly at my own heart. God is not fooled by appearances, but he is also patient and invites us to repentance. We can pray: "Lord, examine me, forgive me, and teach me to treat others with mercy."
exp.0:14:
Paul says he is eager to proclaim the gospel, that is, the good news about Jesus Christ, to the believers who live in Rome as well. "As far as it depends on me" captures the sense of his words, and "I am eager" shows how much he wants to do it.

Paul is writing this letter to believers in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. He explains that he had often wanted to visit them, but something kept him from doing so. He feels indebted to all kinds of people, whether educated or not, and for that reason he does not want to keep the message to himself. This eagerness leads him to say right away that he is not ashamed of the gospel.

For today: ask God who you can encourage or share the hope of Jesus with. Take on Paul's attitude: a simple and humble willingness, without waiting to feel perfect or fully prepared.
exp.2:15:
It says that wherever people who live apart from God go, they leave ruin and suffering behind. Ruin is the idea of damage or collapse, and suffering is the idea of distress and hardship. "Wake" refers to the trail a person leaves as they move through life. In other words, the way they act ends up hurting others and themselves too.

Here the apostle Paul is speaking. To show that everyone needs God, he joins several quotations from the Old Testament, mainly from the Psalms and from Isaiah (in this case, Isaiah 59:7). His purpose is to explain that both Jews and non-Jews are under sin, and that no one is saved by their own merits, but by the grace of God.

Today, this verse invites us to examine the effect of our words and decisions. We can ask ourselves: "Do I leave peace or harm around me?" With humility, let us ask God to transform us and teach us to be people who build up and do not destroy.
exp.6:20:
This verse says that, even when a person wants to do what is right, they discover a pattern that keeps repeating: evil is right there with them. The word "principle" here does not mean a commandment, but a constant rule or pattern. The word "discovered" means to find out or become aware of something.

The apostle Paul speaks here in his letter to the Christians in Rome. He describes the struggle between what his mind agrees with in God's law and the pull toward sin that remains within him. Scholars debate whether he is speaking of his life before he knew Christ or of his experience as a believer. What is clear is that it shows the law alone cannot give us the power to overcome sin.

Today, do not be surprised or sink into guilt when you notice that inner struggle. Acknowledge it honestly, ask God for help each day, and rely on his grace, not only on your own willpower.
exp.8:23:
He says that God called "vessels of mercy," and that this calling includes "us," that is, the believers. It comes not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, meaning the people of the other nations.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were both Jews and non-Jews. He is explaining that God's promise has not failed, even though many Israelites did not believe. God always acted out of his mercy and his call, not out of family origin. He then quotes Hosea to show that God had already announced he would call a new people. Christians have debated for centuries how God's choosing and human responsibility relate here.

Today, remember that your place before God does not depend on your background, your culture, or your merits. If God has called you, live grateful and welcome with kindness those who are different from you.
exp.2:22:
This verse says that all people have sinned, meaning they have fallen short before God. "Fall short of the glory of God" means that no one reaches the level of goodness and perfection that God is and expects. Something is lacking; we are far from that standard.

The apostle Paul is writing to Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God's righteousness comes through faith in Jesus Christ, because there is no difference: Jews and non-Jews are in the same need. For this reason, this verse explains why we all need to be justified freely, as the next verse says.

Today we can stop comparing ourselves with others to feel either better or worse. We all need the grace of God. That helps us to be humble, to treat others with mercy, and to trust in Christ, not in our own merits.
exp.7:19:
This verse says that all creation was subjected to "futility," that is, to emptiness, frailty and frustration. It did not do so by its own will, but because of the One who subjected it, and it was subjected in hope. Here "creation" refers to creation in general.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of the sufferings of the present and of the glory that is to come. Many understand that "the One who subjected it" is God, who allowed this condition after the fall of Adam (Genesis 3). Others think of Adam himself. Paul makes clear that this subjection has a purpose full of hope.

For today: if you suffer or see a broken world, remember that you are not the only one who groans. God has a plan of restoration. Wait with patience and care for his creation in the meantime.
exp.6:10:
Sin seized its opportunity. Using God's commandment, which is good, it deceived Paul and led him to spiritual death. The phrase "seizing its opportunity" means grabbing the moment or the open door. The problem was not with the commandment but with the sin that used it.

The apostle Paul is speaking here, explaining the relationship between God's law and sin. Some believe he draws on his own experience; others think he speaks in a more general way, and there are different opinions on this. What is clear is that he wants to defend the law: in the verses that follow, he says it is holy, just, and good. The fault lies with sin, not with the law.

For today: when a commandment of God shows us our weakness, let us not blame God or ignore it. Let us allow it to lead us to recognize our need of Christ, who does give us forgiveness and life.
exp.6:4:
He says that when we lived according to the flesh, that is, ruled by our old nature, sinful passions were stirred up by the law. Those passions were at work in our bodies, that is, in our conduct. The phrase "bearing fruit for death" means that what we produced ended in separation from God and destruction.

Paul is writing to believers in Rome. He has just used the example of marriage: death releases a person from the law, and so the believer, united to Christ, is free to bear fruit for God. Here he contrasts their past life with the new one.

For today: let us not trust in our own effort or in rules to make us good. Let us ask the Spirit to guide us, and remember that our life belongs to Christ.
exp.4:11:
Through one man, Adam, sin entered the world, and with sin came death, which reached all people, because all have sinned. The passage begins with "therefore," which links this verse to what came before, and Paul completes the comparison in the verses that follow. The phrase "death was passed on to all men" means death reached all people.

Paul, the apostle, is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God reconciled us to himself through the death of Jesus. Now he wants to show how far that gift reaches by comparing Adam, through whom ruin came, with Christ, through whom salvation comes. Christians understand in different ways how Adam's guilt is passed on, but all agree that death is shared by everyone.

Today we can humbly recognize that no one is saved alone, and rest thankfully in the work of Christ, not in our own merits.
exp.0:2:
This verse says that the gospel is about God's Son, Jesus Christ. In his human nature, he was born as a descendant of King David. The phrase "a descendant of David" means that he came into being, or was born, as a human being in that family line.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and introduces himself before he enters the subject. He says that the gospel had already been promised in the Scriptures. That is why he highlights that Jesus comes from the line of David, as the prophets announced about the Messiah. In this way he connects the Old Testament with the good news of Christ.

For today: Jesus is truly human, and so he understands our lives, our struggles, and our pain. You can approach him with confidence and speak to him honestly, knowing that he fulfills God's promises.
exp.4:7:
This verse says that God proves His love for us. The proof is that Christ died for us while we were still sinners.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has been explaining that God declares people righteous through faith. He makes a comparison: hardly anyone would die for a righteous man, though perhaps someone might dare to die for a very good person. God, on the other hand, acted on behalf of people who did not deserve it. Paul then concludes that, since we have already been reconciled, we can trust in our final salvation.

For today: you do not have to make yourself right first in order to draw near to God. His love came before your improvement. Come to Him honestly, and let that love give you peace and teach you to treat with grace those who fail.
exp.6:11:
This verse says that God's law, given through Moses, is holy, and that each commandment is also holy, righteous, and good. "Certainly" is the sense here. "Commandment" refers to what God orders in his law.

Here the apostle Paul is speaking. He has just said that sin used the law to deceive him and lead him to death. So that no one thinks the law is bad, he makes clear that the problem is not in the law but in sin. The law shows what God wants and exposes our need for help.

For today: when one of God's commands costs you something or makes you uncomfortable, do not see it as an enemy. Recognize that it is good and that the fault lies in our heart. Ask God for his grace and his Spirit so that you can obey it with confidence.
exp.4:1:
Through whom, the verse says, believers have gained access, that is, an open door, to enter by faith into the grace of God, which is his undeserved favor. In that grace we stand firm and secure. And the phrase "we rejoice" means that we are glad and boast with joy, not in ourselves, but in the hope of sharing the glory of God.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He had been explaining that God declares us righteous through faith, not through works. For that reason, in the previous verse he speaks of peace with God. Here he shows what follows from it: access, firmness, and hope. Later he will say that this hope sustains even in trials.

For today: when you feel unworthy or insecure, remember that your place before God does not depend on your performance, but on Christ. Pray with confidence and let that hope give you stability.
exp.13:19:
Paul asks that we not ruin what God is building in a person over a matter of food. He says that all food is clean, but that it is wrong to let your eating become a stumbling block to someone else. Here a stumbling block means something that causes another person to fall, not gossip.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome, where believers disagreed about what to eat. Some had a freer conscience and others a more sensitive one. He reminds them that what matters most is peace and building one another up, not winning the argument.

Today, if something you do freely confuses or wounds the conscience of a brother or sister who is weaker in the faith, it is worth giving it up out of love. Care for the person before you insist on your right.
exp.3:18:
Explanation:
It says that Abraham did not weaken in his trust in God. He looked honestly at his situation: his body was already decrepit, since he was about a hundred years old, and Sarah's womb was lifeless and unable to bear a child. Even so, his faith did not give way. The word for "weakening" means "becoming feeble."

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that God makes a person righteous through faith, not through works. He uses Abraham as an example: he believed God's promise to give him a son, even though it seemed humanly impossible (Genesis 15 and 17).

For today: faith does not mean denying problems, but looking at them honestly and trusting God's promise more than what seems impossible. Today you can bring your difficult situation to God and decide to believe that He is faithful.
exp.14:2:
He says that Christ did not seek to please himself or take the easy path. Instead, he bore the insults of those who insulted God. The word translated as "insults" refers to mocking or abuse, and "did not please himself" means he did not seek his own comfort. The quotation comes from Psalm 69:9.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were tensions between believers from a Jewish background and those from a non-Jewish background, especially over matters of conscience such as food and special days. Paul asks the strong to be patient with the weak, that is, those whose faith or conscience is more sensitive. He sets Christ before them as an example of love that gives itself up.

Today, when someone thinks differently or grows more slowly in faith, do not despise or pressure them. Help them with patience, and ask yourself: "What would help build them up?"
exp.15:20:
Paul sends greetings from his companions to the Christians in Rome. He mentions Timothy, whom he calls "my fellow worker," a word that means a colleague or helper in the work. He also names Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, whom he calls "my fellow countrymen," meaning people from the same nation, who were Jews.

Paul is ending his letter to the Romans, probably from Corinth. After his final instructions, he includes greetings from those who were with him. Although he did not know every member of the church in Rome in person, he wanted them to know that he was not working alone. About the exact identity of Lucius and Jason there is uncertainty.

For today: value those who walk alongside you in serving God. Give thanks for them, encourage them with your greeting, and remember that faith is best lived in community.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that God does not show favoritism. Showing favoritism means treating someone better or worse because of their background, their position, or their appearance, rather than because of who they really are. God judges with complete fairness.

The one speaking is Paul, in his letter to the Christians in Rome, where there were both Jews and non-Jews. Some Jews thought that, because they had the law of Moses, they were in a better position before God. Paul answers that God judges everyone by the same standard, both the Jew and the Greek (that is, the non-Jew). What counts is how each person lives before Him.

Today we can examine whether we treat others according to their nationality, their money, their church, or their culture. If God does not make distinctions like these, neither should we. Let us approach everyone with respect, with humility, and with the same love.
exp.7:36:
It says that, in the midst of all the difficulties Paul has just named, believers do not merely endure but come out more than conquerors. This does not happen through their own strength, but "through Him who loved us," that is, Christ. The word "No" here means "on the contrary." "More than conquerors" means that the victory is complete and certain.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just asked whether suffering (tribulation, hardship, famine, danger, the sword) could separate us from the love of Christ. He quotes a psalm that describes the faithful as "sheep to be slaughtered," and yet he affirms that God's love sustains the believer.

For today: when you face a trial, do not measure your victory by whether the problem disappears, but by who is with you. Repeat with confidence that Christ loves you and that no situation can separate you from that love. That assurance gives you strength to keep going.
exp.11:18:
Paul tells believers not to take justice into their own hands. The words "Beloved" show his affection for them. The phrase "leave room for God's wrath" means letting God's anger do its work, instead of wanting to get even ourselves. The statement "Vengeance is Mine" quotes the Old Testament (Deuteronomy 32:35): God keeps the judgment for himself.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where some were suffering rejection and mistreatment. Before and after this verse he teaches them to pursue peace and to respond with kindness. The passage about heaping burning coals on an enemy's head is debated, with some readers taking it as shame that may stir repentance and others as a reference to God's judgment. What is clear is that we should overcome evil with good.

Today, when someone offends you, do not pay them back with words or gossip. Pray for that person, do the good you can, and leave justice in God's hands.
exp.1:12:
It says that hearing what God commands is not enough to be right with Him. What counts is doing what it says. Those who only hear it are set against those who do it, and "declared righteous" means being approved by God.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. The Jews had the law and felt secure because they knew it. Paul reminds them that God judges fairly: whether a person had the law or did not have it, each one answers before Him. Later in this same letter, he explains that no one manages to keep it perfectly and that salvation comes through faith in Christ. Some scholars see here a hypothetical condition; others see a sign of true faith that shows itself in deeds.

For today: don't be satisfied with only listening to sermons or reading the Bible. Choose one thing God has shown you this week and put it into practice.
exp.7:31:
This verse says that God did not hold back his own Son, but gave him up to death for all of us. The phrase "did not spare" means that he did not rescue him from suffering. If God gave what was most precious to him, it makes sense that he will also give us all things along with Christ.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has been speaking about how God sustains his children in the middle of suffering and brings them to glory. With the question "if God is for us, who can be against us?" he affirms that no one can overcome the love of God. This verse is the proof of that love. Some understand "all things" to mean everything we need to reach final salvation.

When you doubt that God cares for you, look to the cross. If God gave up his Son, you can entrust your needs and your fears to him with confidence.
exp.7:15:
The Holy Spirit himself confirms deep within our being that we are God's children. The word "testifies" means giving assurance, like an inner voice that affirms something true.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that we no longer live in fear, like slaves, but as adopted children who cry out "Abba, Father," a tender word for calling on God. This verse adds that God himself gives us assurance of that relationship, and then Paul speaks of the inheritance and of present sufferings.

If you doubt your worth or whether God accepts you, pray calmly and trust his promise. Call him "Father" with simplicity, read his Word, and remember that your security rests on what God says, not on your feelings from day to day.
exp.2:30:
This verse raises a question: if we are made right with God through faith, do we then nullify the law? Paul answers emphatically: "Certainly not!" In other words, by no means. To "nullify" means to cancel out or make of no effect, and to "uphold" means to support and affirm. According to Paul, faith does not cancel the law's authority; rather, it supports it.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God declares people righteous, both Jews and non-Jews, through faith. He anticipates the objection that this would throw contempt on the law. Interpreters explain in several ways how faith upholds the law: some say that faith recognizes what the law teaches about sin, others that it fulfills the law's purpose. Paul will develop this later.

For today: trusting in Christ is no excuse for living as we please. We can be thankful for grace and, with that same faith, want to obey God out of love.
exp.15:3:
Paul says that Priscilla and Aquila "risked their lives" for him, meaning they took great dangers on themselves, perhaps even facing death, to protect him. Paul gives them thanks, and he makes clear that he is not the only one: all the churches of the Gentiles (the non-Jews) are also grateful to them.

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Rome and, at the end, greets several co-workers. It is not known exactly when or how they saved his life; some think of the uproar in Ephesus (Acts 19), but the text does not say so. What is clear is that their courage benefited many churches.

For today: Let us learn to thank out loud those who have cared for us at great cost, and to be willing to serve others even when it costs us.
exp.0:6:
Paul greets all the believers who live in Rome. He tells them that God loves them and that they are "called saints," that is, set apart for God. Then he wishes them "grace and peace": grace is the undeserved favor of God, and peace is the calm and reconciliation with Him. Both come from God our Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, who writes this letter to a church he had not yet met in person. Before this verse he presents himself as a messenger of Christ, and he says the Romans were also called by Jesus. After greeting them, he thanks God because their faith was known in many places.

For today: your worth does not depend on your achievements, but on God's love and His calling. Remember that He loves you, and live at peace in His grace and His peace. Encourage another believer with that same reminder.
exp.14:24:
Paul is about to travel to Jerusalem to serve the saints there, meaning the believers in Jesus. The word "however" at the start of the verse marks a change in his plans, and the city is Jerusalem. His plan to go on to Spain will have to wait for a little while.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He tells them about his plans to visit them on his way to Spain, but first he must deliver a gift. According to the verses that follow, the churches of Macedonia and Achaia collected money for the poorer believers in Jerusalem. Paul sees this as a debt of gratitude: the non-Jewish believers received spiritual blessings and now share material goods.

Today we can ask ourselves how we might concretely help others. Serving fellow believers with our time or resources is a real way to give thanks for what God has given us.
exp.10:31:
It says that God has left everyone, both Jews and non-Jews, locked in disobedience, as if in a prison, so that he might show his mercy to all. "Consigned" means that God handed everyone over to disobedience, and the verse places all people in that same condition. In this way, no one can boast of deserving his favor.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, both Jews and Gentiles. He explains to them that the rejection of the Messiah by many Jews did not close the door to anyone, and that God continues a plan full of mercy. The verses that follow end in praise of his wisdom. Some debate whether "everyone" means every person or all groups; the text stresses that mercy is for both.

Today, remember that no one is saved by their own merit. This takes away pride and the attitude of judging others. If God has had mercy on you, offer it with humility and hope.
exp.8:5:
This verse says that God's word has not failed, meaning that his promises have not come to nothing. The phrase "It is not as though" means "it is not that." The word "failed" means that something has fallen short or gone without being fulfilled. Paul explains that not everyone who descends from Israel (Jacob) forms the true Israel of God.

Paul speaks with sorrow for his people, since many Jews had not believed in Christ. In the verses before this one he mentions the great privileges Israel received. Someone might think that God had failed in his promises. Paul answers that God has always acted according to his promise and his calling, as the case of Isaac shows, and not only according to physical descent.

For today: do not rest on your origin, your church or your family to feel secure before God. Trust in his promise and respond to him with personal faith. You can also be confident that God keeps what he says, even when we cannot see everything at once.
exp.15:1:
What it says: Paul asks the Christians in Rome to welcome Phoebe in the Lord, meaning as a sister in the faith, in a way that is worthy of the saints (the believers). He also asks them to help her with anything she may need from them.

Context: Paul writes this letter from Corinth, and Cenchreae was a nearby port. Phoebe probably carried the letter to Rome, although the text does not say so outright. Paul recommends her because she had helped many people, including him. Some understand "deaconess" as a servant of the church, and others as a formal office; this is debated.

For today: When someone new comes to your church, welcome them warmly and ask how you can help. Serve generously too, as Phoebe did.
exp.10:15:
If the first part of the dough is holy, the whole batch is holy too; and if the root is holy, the branches are holy as well. The "first part" is the portion set apart for God, the first of the harvest. "Holy" means set apart for God.

Paul is writing to the believers in Rome, and he speaks of Israel, his own people. He uses these two images to show that God has not forgotten Israel because of their relationship to the patriarchs. Scholars debate whether the first part and the root are the patriarchs, the first Jewish believers, or both. Right after this, he warns the non-Jewish believers not to feel superior.

For today: remember that your faith rests on a root you did not plant, but on the grace of God. Treat with humility and respect those who think differently or do not yet believe, for God is still at work.
exp.14:26:
They were pleased to do it, and they indeed owe it to them. The Gentiles have shared in the spiritual blessings of the Jewish believers, so it is only right that they serve them with material blessings.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome before traveling to Jerusalem. He is carrying a collection for the poor believers there. He explains that the gift is given freely, yet it is also an act of thanks, because the good news of Christ reached the Gentiles through the Jewish people. He also wants the Romans to understand his mission before he visits them on his way to Spain.

For today: think about who has taught or strengthened you in the faith. Look for a concrete way to thank them, whether through practical help, a gift, or your time, giving with joy and not out of obligation.
exp.4:13:
Death ruled like a king from Adam until Moses. It reigned even over those who had not sinned by breaking a direct command, as Adam did. "He is a pattern of the One to come" means that Adam was a model that pointed forward to Christ.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that all of us need Christ. Death was already present before the law of Moses, which shows that sin affected everyone. He compares Adam with Christ: one brought death, the other brings grace. Interpreters debate how the effect of Adam's sin is passed on, but the central contrast is clear.

For today: do not carry your life as if it depended on your own record. If you are in Christ, your hope rests on his grace, which is greater than any failure. Today, thank him with a simple prayer.
exp.5:18:
Paul says he will speak "in human terms," using an everyday example, because believers find spiritual things hard to grasp. He reminds them that they once offered their bodies, their parts, in slavery to impurity and to ever-increasing wickedness. Now they must offer those same bodies, just as completely, in slavery to righteousness, so that they grow toward a life set apart for God, in holiness.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has already explained that, by grace, believers stopped being slaves to sin. He uses the image of slavery, something very familiar in that time, to encourage them to live in line with their new freedom.

For today: think about what you use your hands, your mouth, your time, and your eyes for. Choose one of those areas today and deliberately dedicate it to doing something good, such as helping, speaking with respect, or serving others.
exp.7:25:
What the passage says: Paul affirms that the Holy Spirit helps us in our weakness. "Weakness" here means the ways we fall short and our limitations, so the verse speaks to the everyday reality of being unable to do what we long to do. Sometimes we do not know how we ought to pray or what to ask God for. Then the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words, that is, sighs and longings that cannot be put into speech.

Context: Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he spoke of waiting patiently for what we do not yet see, and of how all creation waits for its freedom. In the middle of that waiting, our prayer can feel weak. He then says that God, who searches hearts, understands the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for believers according to the will of God.

For today: when you are so tired or confused that you do not know how to pray, do not stay silent out of shame. Speak to God honestly, even if your words are few or you offer only a sigh, and trust that the Spirit is with you.
exp.12:13:
We are told to clothe ourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, that is, to live as he lived, and to make no room for the desires of our human nature. The phrase "make no provision" means "do not give it attention" or "do not give it room." Here "the flesh" does not mean the body, but our tendency toward self-centeredness and sin.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Just before this, he speaks of the night being nearly over and the day arriving, and he urges them to put aside the works of darkness: drunkenness, debauchery, quarreling, and envy. This verse closes that appeal with an image: changing clothes, leaving the old behind and putting on Christ.

For today: when temptation comes, do not simply try to resist by your own strength. Ask yourself how Jesus would act in that situation, and decide to respond in that way. Begin the day by asking him to guide you, and avoid the places or habits that feed what you want to leave behind.
exp.1:13:
This verse says that people from other nations, the Gentiles, do not have the law that God gave to Moses. Even so, they sometimes do by nature what that law requires. "By nature" means they act from their own conscience, without anyone teaching them. So, although they do not have the law, they are a law to themselves.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome, who were both Jews and Gentiles. He shows them that no one can boast before God. The Jews had the law, but hearing it is not enough; it must be obeyed. And the Gentiles, without having the law, show that God placed in their conscience a sense of good and evil. Some understand this as a reference to Gentiles who do not believe, and others to believers; Paul does not clarify this here.

Today, do not compare yourself with others or boast that you know a great deal of the Bible. Ask God that your life shows what you say you believe.
exp.3:4:
This verse says that a person who does not work to earn God's approval, but trusts in God, who justifies the ungodly, has their faith credited to them as righteousness. An "ungodly" person is someone who lives without God. To be "credited" means to be placed into someone's account. "Righteousness" means being right before God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and uses Abraham as an example. Before the law of Moses, Abraham believed God, and God accepted him. Paul compares this to wages: the one who works receives what he has earned, but God's righteousness is a gift. Then he quotes David, who spoke of the happiness of being forgiven.

Today, you do not have to wait until you are "good enough" to come near to God. Trust in Jesus, thank him for his forgiveness, and let that gift move you to obey him out of love, not out of fear.
exp.2:10:
This verse says that no one, by themselves, has true spiritual understanding or seeks God from the heart. The phrase "no one who understands" refers to grasping who God is and what He wants.

Paul, the author of the letter, is speaking to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that Jews and non-Jews are equally under sin. To do this, he joins several quotations from the Old Testament, especially from Psalms 14 and 53. His aim is to prepare the way to explain that salvation is a gift of God through Jesus.

For today: if we depend on God to seek Him, we can live with humility and gratitude. If today you desire to know Him, it is a sign that He is already at work in you. Give thanks to Him and keep seeking Him with confidence.
exp.5:1:
Paul answers with strong feeling: "Certainly not!" He says that believers "died to sin," meaning that we are no longer under its control as we once were. So he asks: how can we keep living in something we have already died to?

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. In the earlier chapters he explained that God's grace is greater than sin. Now he corrects a wrong idea: that if grace forgives everything, then we could sin all the more. He shows that grace is not permission to sin, but a power that changes us. The verses that follow connect this with baptism and with Christ.

For today: when the thought tempts you that "God will forgive me anyway," remember who you are in Christ. Ask him for help, and take one concrete step today toward living in obedience, grateful for his grace.
exp.8:26:
This verse says that Isaiah speaks with force about Israel. Even though the people are as numerous as the sand of the sea, only the remnant, that is, the small part that is left, will be saved. The word "cries out" means that he says it loudly and with seriousness.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and quotes the prophet Isaiah (Isaiah 10:22). He wants to explain why many Israelites did not believe in Jesus, even though God had made promises to them. Paul shows that God has always worked through a faithful remnant, and that his salvation depends on his grace, not on the size or the origin of the people.

For today: salvation is not inherited or earned by belonging to a group. Ask God to give you a sincere faith in Christ, and trust that his mercy reaches even those who seem few or far away.
exp.2:6:
Here Paul repeats an objection that some people raised against him. He asks: "If my falsehood makes God's truthfulness stand out more and adds to his glory, why am I still condemned as a sinner?" The word "however" marks this as a challenge to what he has just said.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome and uses the style of a debate. Picture an opponent looking for excuses: if sin makes God's faithfulness look better, then God would not be right to punish. Paul answers firmly that this is absurd, because God does judge the world. Then he says that those who hold that idea deserve condemnation, since in the end everyone, Jews and Gentiles, is under sin.

For today: do not use God's grace as an excuse to justify your failings. That God can bring something good out of our mistakes does not make them good. Acknowledge your sin with humility and seek his forgiveness.
exp.13:5:
This verse says that the person who observes a special day does so with the aim of honoring the Lord, and the person who does not observe it also acts before Him. The same goes for food: the one who eats gives thanks to God, and the one who abstains also gives thanks to God. To "observe a special day" means to give a certain day special importance.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were believers who held different views about holy days and foods. Many interpret that the differences were between believers of Jewish background and those of non-Jewish background, although the text does not give all the details. Paul asks that they not judge one another in matters where each acts with sincerity before God.

For today: when faced with differences in customs between fellow believers, on matters the Bible does not clearly command, ask yourself whether the other person is seeking to honor God. If so, replace criticism with respect and gratitude.
exp.1:19:
He says that someone considers himself a teacher of those who do not understand, and of infants, that is, of people with little knowledge. Because you have in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth, he means that the law gives him a clear picture of what real knowledge and truth look like.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and speaks to a Jewish listener who feels secure because he has God's law. Some think he is a Jew in general, and others think he is a believing Jew who is presumptuous. Paul does not mock the law, but shows that knowing is not enough if one does not obey, as the verses that follow make clear.

For today: if you teach or advise others, first examine your own life. Before correcting, ask yourself with humility: "Am I practicing what I preach?"
exp.10:32:
Paul stands in wonder before God. He says that God's wisdom and knowledge are like a treasure so deep that its bottom cannot be seen. "Unsearchable" means that God's judgments cannot be fully explored or worked out, and "untraceable" means that his ways cannot be followed to their end. God's judgments are his decisions and his way of governing; his ways are the manner in which he acts.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that many of his people, Israel, have not believed, and that God, even so, has a plan of mercy for both Jews and non-Jews. Having reached that conclusion, Paul does not argue any further: he breaks out in praise. He will then go on with questions that show that no one advises God.

For today: when something in your life or in the world does not make sense, you do not have to understand everything in order to trust. Take a moment to thank God for his mercy and hand over that doubt to him, knowing that his wisdom surpasses yours.
exp.6:7:
Sin took advantage of God's commandment to stir up all kinds of wrong desires in Paul. "Covetous desire" here means disordered longing, such as greed. The phrase "seizing its opportunity" means that sin grabbed a chance to act. And the statement "apart from the law, sin is dead" means that without the commandment, sin lay quiet, not showing its strength.

The apostle Paul is the one speaking. He explains that God's law is good, but that it cannot save, because sin uses it to expose and provoke our rebellion. Scholars debate whether the "I" is Paul himself, Israel, or human experience in general; perhaps it includes all of these.

For today: God's law shows us our need, not our solution. When a command awakens in us the desire to do the opposite, let us remember that we need the grace of Christ and the help of the Spirit, not just more of our own effort.
exp.6:21:
It says that, in the deepest part of his being, Paul takes delight in God's law. The "inner being" is the most intimate part of a person, where desires and conscience dwell. To "delight" means he feels joy and pleasure, not just obligation.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and describes an inner struggle between what he desires to do and what he actually does. Scholars disagree about whether he is speaking of his life before he knew Christ or of his experience as a believer. In either case, he shows here that his heart loves God's law, even though sin still drags him down.

If you sometimes long to obey God and still fall short, do not lose heart. That desire to do good is a sign of a heart that is sensitive to God. Bring your struggle to him honestly, and ask for his help each day.
exp.8:1:
Paul says that he feels deep sorrow and an anguish that never lets up, and that this pain is in the deepest part of his being. The word "unceasing" means that it does not stop; it is constant. And "heart" refers to the innermost part of a person: their feelings and their will.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul. He has just affirmed that he is telling the truth, and that his conscience confirms it. He is speaking about his people, Israel, and about how many of them had not believed in Jesus. After the great verses of hope in chapter 8, Paul shows his personal burden for them. His words are neither cold nor critical, but full of love.

Today we can learn to feel sincere sorrow for those who do not yet know Christ, especially family members and friends. Instead of judging them, we can pray for them without ceasing and treat them with love.
exp.7:1:
This verse says that the Holy Spirit, who gives life to those united with Jesus, has set us free from another force that held us captive: sin, which ends in death. Here the word "law" is understood as a principle or an active force. "Set free" means liberated.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he spoke of his struggle against sin (Romans 7). Now he explains why there is no condemnation: what the law of Moses could not accomplish because of human weakness, God did by sending his Son.

For today: when guilt or a bad habit tells you that there is no remedy, remember that you are no longer a slave. Ask the Spirit for help each day, and walk trusting in what Christ has already done for you.
exp.15:11:
Paul sends greetings to three Christian women in Rome. He describes Tryphena and Tryphosa as women who have worked hard in the Lord, meaning they actively serve the work of God. He calls Persis his beloved and says she has worked very hard in the Lord. The word "greet" here means "give my warm regards."

Paul writes this letter to the church in Rome, and in the last chapter he names many people he knows or has heard about. We do not know with certainty what task each one carried out; the text only says that they worked hard in the Lord. Some think Tryphena and Tryphosa were sisters, but this is not certain.

God sees and values faithful service, even when it is quiet. Today we can imitate Paul by thanking out loud those who serve in our church: a message, a phone call, or a sincere word encourages people greatly.
exp.6:23:
Paul says he feels like a miserable man and asks who will rescue him from "this body of death." The word "wretched" means troubled and without strength. "Rescue" means to save or set free. The phrase "this body of death" is understood in several ways: our weak human nature, which is subject to sin, or the mortal body itself.

Paul writes in the first person and describes the struggle between wanting to obey God and feeling pulled toward sin. Scholars disagree about whether he is speaking of his life before he knew Christ or of his experience as a believer. What is clear is that his cry receives an answer right away: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord."

Today, when you are frustrated by your failures, do not hide or despair. Admit your weakness honestly and turn to Jesus, who is the one who rescues. He helps you day by day.
exp.0:15:
Here, Paul says he is not ashamed of the gospel, that is, the good news about Jesus. He calls it "the power of God," meaning God's power at work, for salvation, which here means being saved. That salvation is for everyone who believes, with no exceptions. The phrase "first to the Jew, then to the Greek" indicates that the message came first to the Jewish people, and then to the Greeks, who represent the other peoples.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, a powerful and cultured city, which he still wished to visit. He felt a debt to everyone, cultured or not, and that is why he wanted to proclaim the gospel to them. What follows explains why the gospel is the power of God: in it the righteousness of God is revealed, and it is received through faith.

For today: you do not need your faith to look impressive in order to share it. Trust that the power is in the message, not in your own skill. Share with simplicity and kindness what Christ has done for you.
exp.15:2:
Paul asks that they be greeted: Prisca and Aquila, a Christian married couple. He calls them "my fellow workers," a word meaning co-laborers who serve alongside him. He says they worked with him in the work of Christ Jesus. It is interesting that he names Prisca first, which was uncommon for that time.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, and at the end he greets many people by name. According to Acts, Prisca and Aquila were fellow tent-makers with Paul and hosted him in Corinth. The verses that follow say they risked their lives for him, although we do not know the details of when this happened. They also had a church that met in their home.

Today we can imitate this example: value and thank out loud those who serve alongside us. A message or a few words of gratitude can greatly encourage a brother or sister in the faith.
exp.13:3:
Paul asks, "Who are you to judge someone else's servant?" The servant belongs to a different master, that is, to another believer who belongs to Christ. The idea that he "stands or falls" means that his own Lord is the one who approves him or corrects him. And the promise that he will "stand" means that he will be upheld, because the Lord has the power to make him stand.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were disagreements about foods and special days. Some ate everything, while others ate only vegetables. He does not call them to fight over this, but to respect one another, since each one tries to honor the Lord according to his conscience. Scholars debate exactly who the two groups were, but the counsel is clear.

Today, when someone lives out his faith differently in secondary matters, do not despise or judge him. Instead, pray for him, trust that Christ sustains him, and seek peace.
exp.8:25:
It says that in the very place where God had said to them, "You are not My people," there they will be called "sons of the living God." It is a promise of change: those who were far from God become his children.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and quotes the prophet Hosea (Hosea 1:10). Hosea originally spoke to the northern kingdom of Israel, which had turned away from God. Paul uses that text to show that God calls his people both from among the Jews and from among the Gentiles. Some scholars think Paul applies Hosea's words to the Gentiles by analogy; others think the text also speaks of a restored Israel. Both ideas fit his argument.

For today: no one is so far away that God cannot call them his child. If you feel rejected or out of place, remember this promise. And treat others with that same grace.
exp.1:7:
Paragraph one describes people who are self-seeking: focused on their own interests, unwilling to yield, and quick to argue. They reject the truth and follow wickedness instead. The result is wrath and anger, which speaks of God's just judgment against evil.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that God judges with fairness and without favoritism, whether the person is Jew or Gentile. Each person is repaid according to their attitude and their actions. That is why this verse contrasts with the previous one, which speaks of those who keep on doing good.

For today: examine with humility whether there are areas where you resist what you know to be true out of pride or stubbornness. Ask God for a heart willing to listen and obey, and take one concrete step of obedience today.
exp.6:17:
Paul says that nothing good lives in him, that is, in his weak human nature (the flesh). He has the desire to do what is right, but he cannot carry it out.

Paul speaks in the first person as he explains the relationship between God's law and sin. He maintains that the law is good, but it has no power to change the heart. Scholars debate whether he describes his life before knowing Christ, his struggle as a believer, or an experience that represents everyone. What is clear is that he shows our need for divine help.

For today: when you fail even while wanting to do good, do not remain in discouragement or make excuses. Acknowledge your weakness with sincerity and ask God for his strength, for true change comes from his grace.
exp.2:1:
Paul says the Jews have an advantage "in every way," that is, in many respects. The first is that they have been entrusted with "the very words of God," his declarations or messages, which we today call the Scriptures of the Old Testament. Being given this trust means they were charged with guarding it with responsibility.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that being Jewish and being circumcised does not spare anyone from God's judgment if they do not live in obedience. Then he imagines an objection: is there no use at all in being Jewish? He answers that there is, because they received God's revelation. But receiving it is not the same as obeying it.

For today: if we have a Bible, we have a great privilege and also a responsibility. Having it at home is not enough; it is good to read it, believe it, and put it into practice with humility.
exp.3:6:
It says that the people whose lawless acts God forgives and whose sins he covers are happy, or blessed. "Blessed" here means deeply happy and favored. "Lawless acts" are deeds that break God's law, and "covered" means that God no longer holds them against those people.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. To show that God declares us righteous through faith and not through our works, he quotes King David in Psalm 32:1-2. David speaks of the joy of someone who has been forgiven without deserving it. Paul uses this as an example that forgiveness is a gift.

For today: if you trust in Christ, you do not have to live carrying old guilt. Bring your failure honestly to God, receive his forgiveness, and walk in joy and gratitude.
exp.7:26:
This verse says that God, who searches our hearts, knows what the Spirit has in mind when the Spirit prays for us. "Searches" means to examine carefully. "Mind" means thought or desire. The Spirit intercedes for believers, here called "the saints," and does so according to what God wills.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that we suffer and wait with patience, and that often we do not know how to pray. Then he encourages them: the Spirit helps us in our weakness. Some think the "groanings which cannot be uttered" are prayers without words; others think they are a deep cry of the Spirit within us.

When you are so tired or confused that you do not know what to ask for, do not be anxious. Pray sincerely, even with few words, and trust that God understands you and that the Spirit intercedes for you.
exp.10:24:
Paul says he does not want the brothers and sisters to be unaware of a "mystery," that is, something God has now revealed that was not understood before. A hardening has come to part of Israel, meaning they have closed themselves to believing in Jesus, but this is temporary: it will last until the full number of the Gentiles has come in, which means the complete number of people from the nations.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, many of whom were not Jewish. He has just used the image of the olive tree, in which they are grafted-in branches. He warns them not to be conceited and look down on Israel. How "and so all Israel will be saved" should be understood is debated among Christians, but Paul insists that God has not abandoned his promise.

Today: if you have received God's grace, do not think yourself better than others. Pray with hope for those who today seem far from God.
exp.0:22:
It says that people exchanged the glory of God, which is immortal and never ends, for images of things that do die and end: mortal humans, birds, animals, and reptiles. The word "exchanged" in this verse means giving one thing up in order to receive another. Being "immortal" means something that does not die or come to an end.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that all of us need the gospel. Before this verse, he says that people came to know God through what He made in creation, but they did not give Him thanks or honor Him. The verses that follow show that this rejection brought painful consequences.

For today: few of us make statues of animals now, but we can still exchange God for money, fame, or pleasure. Ask yourself what thing today receives your greatest attention and gratitude, and give God first place again.
exp.8:18:
Paul imagines someone raising an objection: "Then why does God still find fault? For who can resist His will?" The objection assumes that if God decides what happens, people cannot be blamed for what they do.

Paul is explaining that God is free and sovereign, using the example of Pharaoh. He anticipates the complaint of a reader who feels this is unjust. He does not answer with a theory; instead, in the following verse, he reminds the person who God is and who they are. Christians have understood in different ways how God's sovereignty and human responsibility relate, and the text does not fully resolve it.

For today: when you do not understand God's ways, do not silence your questions, but bring them to him with humility, trusting that his mercy is real and that he is just.
exp.2:7:
Paul repeats a false accusation that was made against him: that he taught, "Let us do evil that good may result." To "slander" someone is to falsely accuse or defame them. Paul answers that those who make such claims deserve their condemnation.

Paul is explaining that God's grace is no excuse for sin. His critics twisted his message: if sin makes God's faithfulness shine more brightly, then sinning would seem good. Paul firmly rejects that reasoning. He will soon show that both Jews and Gentiles equally need God's forgiveness.

For today: grace is not permission to do wrong, but an invitation to live differently. If you ever justify yourself by saying "the end justifies it," stop and ask whether you truly honor God. A good purpose never makes a wrong action good.
exp.10:26:
It says that God made a solemn promise, a covenant, with the people of Israel: that He Himself will take away their sins.
