The verse says "take away" in the present tense, so the sense is simply that God will remove their sins. Forgiveness does not depend on human effort, but on what God committed Himself to do.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, most of whom were not of Jewish origin. He quotes the prophet Isaiah (59:20-21; 27:9) to show that God has not abandoned Israel. Christians were not to feel superior. How and when "all Israel will be saved" is understood in various ways by believers, but Paul insists that God is faithful.

For today: trust that God's forgiveness rests on His faithfulness, not on your performance. Receive it with humility, and treat others with grace, without thinking you are better than anyone.
exp.0:20:
They knew God through creation, but they did not honor him as God or give him thanks. Instead, their thinking became futile, and their foolish hearts were darkened. "Glorify" means to acknowledge and honor God for who he is.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he explained that creation shows God's power and divinity, so no one has an excuse. Here he describes the source of the human problem: it is not a lack of information, but a heart that does not want to honor God or thank him. He then shows how this leads to idolatry.

For today: practice gratitude. Each day, thank God for something specific, and recognize that every good thing comes from him.
exp.15:25:
This verse says that the mystery of God, which had been hidden before, has now been revealed. It was made known through the writings of the prophets, by the command of the eternal God, and it is made known to all nations so that they may come to the obedience that comes from faith. The word "nations" in the verse refers to peoples or nations. The phrase "obedience that comes from faith" means responding to God by trusting in Christ.

Paul is closing his letter to the Romans. In this final sentence he sums up his message: the plan to save both Jews and non-Jews had already been announced in the Old Testament, but now it is understood clearly through Jesus Christ. Some scholars debate whether these final verses were part of the original letter, but they appear in most Bibles.

For today: if the gospel is for all peoples, we should not exclude anyone. This week, share a word of hope with someone outside your usual circle.
exp.7:13:
This verse says that all who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God. To be "led" means to be guided, like someone following a guide along the road. It does not describe a single special moment, but a life that lets itself be directed by God day by day.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the Christians in Rome. He had been explaining that a life lived according to the flesh leads to death, and that those who, by the Spirit, put aside evil deeds live. Then he adds that we have not received a spirit of slavery and fear, but a spirit of adoption, which lets us call out to God as Father, that is, as "Daddy."

Today, before deciding something important, pray and ask God what he wants. Check your Bible and look for wise counsel. Let the Spirit correct you without fear, because it is a Father who loves you who does it.
exp.3:21:
This verse says that, because of the faith Abraham had, God credited him as righteous. The word "credited" means that God put it to his account, that is, He recognized him as righteous.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has been explaining that no one becomes righteous before God by keeping the law, but by trusting in Him. He holds up Abraham as an example: Abraham believed that God would keep His promise to give him a son, even though it seemed humanly impossible. Paul adds that this was not written only for Abraham, but also for those who believe in God, who raised Jesus from the dead.

For today: you do not have to earn God's favor through perfect effort. Trust in His promises, even when you cannot see how they will be fulfilled, and rest in what Christ has already done for you.
exp.13:11:
This verse says that each person will have to answer personally before God for their own life. Where it says "give an account," the idea is to be accountable, to explain what one has done.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were differences among believers about food and special days. Some were judging others for thinking differently. Paul reminds them that all of us will stand before the judgment seat of Christ, and that the judge is God, not us. For that reason he asks them to stop judging one another and to avoid putting a stumbling block in the way of a brother or sister.

Today, before criticizing someone for the way they live their faith in matters that are not essential, remember that you too will give an account to God. Attend to your own obedience, and treat others with patience and respect.
exp.10:0:
Paul asks a question: Did God reject his people, Israel? He answers with a firm "Certainly not!" As proof, he points to himself: he is an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who were both Jews and non-Jews. In the earlier chapters he explained that many of Israel did not believe in Jesus. Now he makes clear that this does not mean God has abandoned his promise. Paul himself, once an opponent of the church, is a sign of God's faithfulness. He then mentions Elijah, who also thought he was alone.

For today: when you see someone far from God, or you feel far away yourself, remember that God is faithful and does not give up easily. Keep praying with hope.
exp.1:23:
This verse says that people who did not know God spoke disrespectfully about Him, and that the cause was the conduct of those who claimed to be His people. "Mocked" means treated with scorn or contempt. "Gentiles" are those who were not Jews. "As it is written" points to the Scriptures of the Old Testament, probably Isaiah 52:5 and Ezekiel 36:20-23.

Paul is speaking to Jews who took pride in knowing God's law. He shows them that teaching what is right does little good if one's life contradicts it. Their failures were causing others to think poorly of God. This prepares his argument that all of us need the grace of Christ.

For today: our way of living speaks of God to others. Ask Him that your actions, at work, at home and online, agree with what you say you believe.
exp.7:20:
This verse says that creation will one day be set free from its bondage to decay. That means it will be freed from breakdown, wearing out and death. This freedom will come together with the glorious freedom that the children of God will receive. "Creation" refers to the created world in general.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He explains that present suffering cannot be compared with the future glory. According to him, creation was made subject to frailty and emptiness and now waits in hope. Some think he refers to all of nature; others, to all of humanity that does not believe. The first reading is the most common.

For today: when you see pain, sickness or loss, remember that it is not the last word. God promises to restore all things. Care for creation with gratitude and wait with patience.
exp.10:34:
It says that no one has given something to God beforehand, so that God would be in debt and have to repay it. The verse uses the word "first," so the phrase "given to God first" is what the verse is pointing to. The question expects the answer "no one": there is no one who can make God a debtor.

The apostle Paul writes this as he closes his long explanation of God's mercy toward Jews and non-Jews (Romans 9–11). With wonder, he praises God's wisdom and quotes ideas from the Old Testament, probably from Job 41:11 and Isaiah 40:13. His point is that salvation springs from God's grace, not from human merit.

For today: serve God without feeling that in this way you are paying him back or that he owes you anything. Everything you have, including your ability to give, comes from him. That frees us from pride and fear, and leads us to gratitude.
exp.2:19:
This verse says that no one will be declared righteous before God by keeping the law's commands. "No one" in the verse refers to every human being. Being "justified" means being declared innocent and accepted by God. The law serves to make us aware of sin, not to remove it.

Paul is writing to believers in Rome. He has just quoted several passages from the Old Testament to show that both Jews and non-Jews are under sin. The law silences every mouth: no one can defend themselves or boast. With this, he prepares the next verse, where he presents the righteousness of God that comes through faith in Jesus Christ.

For today: stop trying to earn God's favor through your good behavior. Use the law as a mirror that shows you your need, and come to Christ with humility and confidence, resting in his grace.
exp.5:8:
He says that Christ was raised and cannot die again. Death no longer has power or authority over Him. The verse says that death no longer has dominion over Him, meaning it no longer rules over Him as a master would.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has been explaining that whoever believes in Jesus is united with Him in His death and in His resurrection. Paul uses Christ's final victory over death as the basis for encouraging believers not to keep living under the rule of sin. What follows shows that Christ died to sin once and now lives for God.

Today we can face our struggles with hope and not with defeat. If Christ overcame death, His power also sustains us in saying no to sin. When you feel that a bad habit dominates you, remember that you belong to Christ and ask Him for strength to live for God.
exp.15:18:
Paul says that everyone has heard about the obedience of the believers in Rome, and this gives him joy. But he wants them to be wise about what is good, that is, to understand and practice what is right, and innocent about what is evil, meaning untouched by it and not mixed up in it. Being innocent here means being free of any cunning or wrongdoing.

Paul writes this letter to the church in Rome. Just before, he warned about people who were causing divisions and deceiving the naive with smooth words. For that reason he commends their faithfulness, but encourages them to stay alert so that no one leads them astray. Right after, he promises that the God of peace will crush Satan.

For today: learn to know the Bible well so you can tell what is true from what is false, and guard your heart against harmful curiosities. Be mature in discernment, but sincere and pure in your conduct.
exp.5:16:
Paul thanks God that the believers in Rome, who had once been slaves to sin, now wholeheartedly obeyed the teaching of the gospel they had been committed to. The word "though" in the verse marks a contrast between their past and their present, and "the form of teaching" refers to the pattern or model of Christian instruction they received. "Committed" suggests that they were handed over to that teaching, like someone entrusted to the care of a new master.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just asked whether we may keep sinning because we are under grace, and he answers with a firm "God forbid." He explains that we all serve something: either sin or obedience. Here he celebrates that they have already changed masters.

For today: grace is not permission to sin, but power to live differently. Today you can thank God for your freedom and obey him wholeheartedly, not out of mere obligation. Ask yourself in which area you need to stop serving old habits.
exp.3:2:
Paul asks what the Scripture says and answers by quoting Genesis 15:6: Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness. "Credited" means put to his account, recognized. Abraham did not earn that standing through effort; God declared him righteous because he trusted God's promise.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, among both Jews and non-Jews. He is explaining that no one is saved by their works. He puts Abraham, highly respected by the Jews, forward as an example. If Abraham could have boasted in his works, he would have, but before God he had nothing to glory in. What counts is his faith.

For today: do not try to earn God's love or acceptance through good behavior. Trust in Him and in what He has done for you in Christ. From that trust, good works flow as gratitude, not as payment.
exp.14:23:
Paul tells the Christians in Rome that he hopes to see them on his way to Spain. He wants to enjoy their company for a while, and then he hopes they will help him prepare for the rest of his journey.

Paul writes this letter from the end of his work in the eastern part of the empire. He wants to preach where Christ is not yet known, and that is why he has Spain in mind. We do not know for certain whether he ever went there. He asks the Roman believers for support as partners in the mission, not as someone making demands.

For today: Paul joins large plans with friendship and cooperation. We can support those who serve God through prayer, practical help, or companionship, and we can let others help us too. No one serves alone.
exp.10:22:
It says that the Israelites who were "cut off" because of unbelief can be grafted back in, that is, put back into the olive tree, if they do not persist in their unbelief. The reason is that God has the power to do it. The verse uses the word "graft," which refers to joining a branch onto a tree.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, among them believers of non-Jewish origin. He uses the image of an olive tree with branches cut off and a wild olive branch grafted in. He wants the non-Jewish believers not to feel superior to Israel. How and when this restoration will happen is interpreted differently by Christians.

Today, do not look with pride or with contempt on someone who does not yet believe. God can change any heart, and our attitude should be one of humility, gratitude, and prayer for those who are far away.
exp.4:10:
Paul says that believers have not only been saved from punishment, but also rejoice in God. "We rejoice" here means we take real delight and find confidence in Him. This joy comes through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation, that is, the restored peace with God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and explains how God makes people right with Himself through faith. Earlier he said that we were enemies of God and that Christ died for us. Now he concludes that this work produces more than relief: it produces joy. What follows shows Christ as the one who repairs what Adam damaged.

Today, when you feel far from God because of your failures, remember that your relationship with Him rests on what Christ has done, not on your performance. Thank Him today for that peace.
exp.11:12:
Believers are called to share what they have with fellow Christians who are in need, and to actively practice welcoming others into their homes. To share means to take part in something with others or to give to them. The saints are the believers, the people of God. To practice hospitality means to pursue it actively rather than waiting for opportunities to come to you.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. After explaining what God has done for them in Christ, he shows them how to live a transformed life. These words describe a practical love within the church. In that time, traveling believers depended greatly on the hospitality of other brothers and sisters.

Today you might ask yourself who near you has a need: a meal, a place to stay for a while, companionship, or help with money. This week, take a concrete step: invite someone to your table or share something with a family that needs it.
exp.8:4:
This verse says that the Israelites have great ancestors, such as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and that from that people Christ was born in his human nature. It then affirms that this Christ is God over all things, forever worthy of praise. Here "worthy of praise" means that God is to be honored, and "Amen" means "so be it."

Paul speaks with deep sorrow for his people, who for the most part did not believe in Jesus. He lists the privileges of Israel and culminates with the greatest of them: that the Messiah came from them. Some scholars debate the original punctuation of the Greek text, but most translations and commentators understand that Paul calls Christ God.

Today we can honor Jesus as truly man and truly God, and at the same time love with compassion those who do not yet know him, praying for them as Paul did.
exp.13:9:
What the passage says: Paul asks two direct questions. "Judging" here means criticizing and condemning your brother, and "belittling" means treating him as if he were unimportant or beneath you. Then he gives the reason: we will all stand before God's judgment seat, that is, before his judgment.

Context: Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were disagreements about food and special days (Romans 14:1-9). Some criticized those who were more strict, and others looked down on those who had more scruples. Paul reminds them that all belong to the Lord, and that only he is the Judge. The next verse says that each one will give an account to God for himself.

For today: When you feel the urge to criticize or look down on another believer for how they live out their faith in secondary matters, stop. Pray for that person and remember that you too will give an account to God. Focus on living sincerely before the Lord yourself.
exp.12:8:
Paul cites several of the Ten Commandments: do not commit adultery, do not murder, do not steal, do not covet. He says that any other commandments are summed up in one decree: "Love your neighbor as yourself."

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he spoke about respecting the authorities and paying what is owed. Now he says that the debt that never ends is love. He quotes the law of Moses (Leviticus 19:18) to show that loving others is at the heart of what God asks.

Before you act, ask yourself: "Is this good for my neighbor, or only for me?" Love is not only avoiding harm; it is also seeking the good of the other person in everyday life, through words, time, and concrete help.
exp.2:11:
All people have turned away from God's path. The phrase "together" describes everyone as a group, without exception. "Worthless" speaks of something that has spoiled and no longer serves its purpose. Paul affirms that no one, on their own, truly does the good that God expects.

The speaker is the apostle Paul, writing to the Christians in Rome. Here he gathers several quotations from the Psalms (especially Psalm 14 and Psalm 53) to show that both Jews and non-Jews are under sin. His purpose is to prepare the way to explain that salvation comes through faith in Jesus Christ, not through one's own merits.

This verse invites us to humility. We do not have to pretend we are perfect or look down on others with pride. We can honestly acknowledge our failings and gratefully receive the grace that God offers freely in Christ.
exp.8:7:
Here Paul says that being a physical descendant of Abraham is not enough to make someone a child of God. Those born through ordinary family line are the "children of the flesh." Those who are born through God's promise are the "children of the promise." The words "regarded as offspring" mean that God counts them as true descendants.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who were both Jews and non-Jews. It grieved him that many of his own people did not accept Jesus, and some thought God had failed. Paul answers that God's word remains firm: from the beginning, God chose Isaac because of his promise, not because of ordinary family inheritance.

For today: do not rest on your family, your church, or your religious history. Trust God's promise and respond to it with sincere faith, for being part of his family is a gift of his grace.
exp.15:13:
Paul sends greetings to five men: Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, and Hermas. He also greets "the brothers with them," that is, other believers who probably met together with them.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. At the end he names many people, perhaps to show closeness and unity. Of these five we almost know nothing more; their names were common at that time. Some think they formed a group that met in a house, but the Bible does not make this clear.

God values every believer, even those whom almost no one remembers. Today we can imitate Paul: remember specific names, greet people, encourage them, and help those who go unnoticed feel part of the church.
exp.5:4:
Paul says that if we have been united with Christ in a death like his, we will certainly also be united with him in a resurrection. The image of being united with Christ speaks of being joined to him so closely that our lives are bound up with his. The phrase "in a way like" his death means that our union with him is real and shaped by what he went through. "We will certainly" points to the new life God gives, which begins now and is brought to completion in the final resurrection.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that grace abounds where sin is, and now he answers those who might think that one may therefore keep on sinning. He reminds them that baptism shows that whoever belongs to Christ has already died to the power of sin and received a new life.

For today: when you feel tied down by a bad habit, remember that you belong to Christ. Ask God for his strength, and take one concrete step today to live out that new life.
exp.11:1:
It says that we should not live according to the values and customs of this world, but be transformed from within, changing the way we think. The word "world" in this verse refers to the spirit and mindset of the present age. The phrase "be transformed" is a real change in the way we think and live. The verse goes on to say that this change lets us test and approve by experience what the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God is.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained God's mercy, and now he asks them to respond by giving their whole lives to him. This inner change prepares what follows: living with humility and serving in the church, as members of one body.

For today: before deciding something, ask yourself what the world thinks and what God's Word teaches. Spend a few minutes each day reading the Bible and praying, so that God renews your mind little by little.
exp.14:20:
Paul supports his goal with Scripture. His aim is to bring the good news to people who had never heard of Christ. He quotes Isaiah 52:15: "Those who were not told about Him will see, and those who have not heard will understand." The phrase "will see" means that these people will be given the news, and that is the whole point of the sentence.

Paul is writing to the believers in Rome. He tells them that he has preached the gospel from Jerusalem all the way to Illyricum, and that he made it his aim not to build on another person's foundation. He uses Isaiah to show that his mission fits with what God had already announced. He also explains why he had not been able to visit them before. Many read the Isaiah passage as speaking of the Servant of the Lord, and Paul applies it to his own labor.

For today, ask yourself who near you has not yet heard the gospel clearly. Pray for that person, and look for a simple and kind way to share what Christ has done for you.
exp.1:26:
It says that a person who is physically uncircumcised but keeps the law will condemn you, who have the written code and circumcision yet are a lawbreaker. Being a lawbreaker means you break the law. "The written code" refers to the law written down. "Physically uncircumcised" means not circumcised in the body.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He shows them that having religious signs or knowing the law is not enough if life does not go with it. Some understand the judging as a comparison that exposes the hypocrite, not as a final judgment.

Today we can ask ourselves: am I content with being in church, with knowing the Bible, or with doing religious things? God looks for a heart that truly obeys. Let us ask him that our faith show in what we do each day.
exp.8:17:
He says God is free to show mercy to whomever He decides, and that He also hardens whomever He decides. To harden means to make the heart stubborn. Salvation does not depend on what we deserve, but on the goodness of God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just recalled Pharaoh, who resisted God, and God used that hardness to show His power. Paul wants to stress that God is sovereign. Christians have debated for centuries how God's will and human responsibility relate here, and not everyone understands it the same way.

For today: instead of boasting of our merits, we can receive God's mercy with humility and give Him thanks. If today you sense His call, do not harden your heart; respond to Him with trust.
exp.8:8:
This verse recalls the promise God made to Abraham: "At the appointed time I will return, and Sarah will have a son." Paul is citing the story from Genesis 18:10, 14. "I will return" refers to God's visit, and "at the appointed time" means on the date God set. The important point is that Isaac was born through a promise, not through human strength.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He explains that being a descendant of Abraham by blood is not the same as being an heir of the promise. With the example of Isaac, he shows that God carries out his plans in the way he himself determines. Some interpreters discuss how this relates to election, but the central point here is the promise.

For today: trust that God does what he says, even when you cannot see how. Your faith rests not on your own abilities, but on his faithful word.
exp.0:21:
They claimed to be wise, but in reality they became foolish. Here "foolish" means empty of true understanding. Thinking oneself wise without acknowledging God ends in a deep foolishness.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that creation shows the power and greatness of God, so no one has an excuse. Here he describes those who, even knowing something about God, did not honor him or give him thanks. They relied on their own reasoning, and this led them to worship created things instead of the Creator.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, in some area of life, we trust our own intelligence more than God. A good practice is to begin the day by thanking him and asking him for wisdom with humility, accepting his guidance even when we do not understand everything.
exp.14:8:
This verse says that Christ also came so that the Gentiles, that is, people who are not Jews, would give glory to God for his mercy, meaning his compassion and kindness. "Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles" means that the psalmist promises to praise God openly among the nations, and "I will sing hymns to your name" means to sing to him with gratitude.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, where Jewish and Gentile believers sometimes clashed. He reminds them that Christ served the Jewish people to fulfill the promises made to their fathers, and that God always wanted the nations to praise him too. That is why he quotes the Old Testament (Psalm 18:49), where David promises to praise God among the nations.

For today: God received us through pure mercy, not because we earned it. That invites us to welcome with respect those who are different from us in the church and to praise God together.
exp.15:17:
Paul says that certain people are not truly serving Christ, but are serving their own appetites. Their own desires and comfort are what drive them. With smooth talk and flattery, they deceive the hearts of the naive, that is, those who do not suspect evil.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and, as he closes the letter, warns them about those who cause divisions and turn away from the teaching they have already received. He asks them to stay away from such people. Then he praises them for their obedience and asks them to be wise about what is good and to stay innocent when it comes to evil.

Today we might ask ourselves: does this message agree with what the Bible says, or does it only sound pleasant? A good habit is to compare what we hear with the Scriptures, without being carried away by the charm of the one speaking.
exp.2:0:
Paul asks a question: if God treats Jews and non-Jews alike, what advantage does the Jew have, then? What is the value of circumcision, the sign of the covenant that God gave to Israel? The words "what is the advantage" and "what is the value" ask the same thing.

Paul is the one speaking. He has just said in chapter 2 that having circumcision saves no one if the heart does not obey. He imagines a Jewish reader might object: "So is there no value in being part of Israel?" That is why he raises the question, and he immediately answers that there is great advantage: to them God entrusted his word.

For today: if we have received much, such as the Bible, a believing family, or a church, that is a gift to live out with humility, not a reason to feel superior. Let us be thankful for what God has entrusted to us and obey him from the heart.
exp.6:14:
Paul describes an inner struggle: he does things he does not understand, he fails to do the good he wants, and he ends up doing what he strongly rejects. "Hate" here means he is repulsed by what he does. "Does not understand" here means his own behavior baffles him.

Paul speaks of God's law, which is good, but which cannot give him the power to keep it. He presents sin as a force that uses the commandment to take control of a person. Christians have understood this struggle in different ways: some see Paul describing his life before Christ, others his life as a believer. Both views have serious defenders.

Today we can honestly admit our struggles, without hiding them or making excuses for ourselves. Recognizing that we cannot manage alone leads us to ask God for help, who in Christ offers forgiveness and strength to change little by little.
exp.6:6:
Paul asks whether God's law is itself sinful, and he answers firmly: "Certainly not!" He explains that he would not have been aware of sin if the law had not made it known to him. The law's command, "Do not covet," brought to light a desire in his heart that he had not recognized as wrong.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that we are no longer under the law as a way to become right with God, and someone might conclude that the law must therefore be at fault. Paul makes clear that the law is good; it simply exposes the problem. Interpreters debate whether the "I" refers to Paul's own past, to all of humanity, or to Israel, but they agree on the central teaching.

For today: when God's Word makes you uncomfortable, do not blame it. Use it as a mirror, confess what you see, and ask Christ for help to change.
exp.15:8:
Paul tells the believers in Rome to greet Urbanus, whom he calls "our fellow worker in Christ," and Stachys, whom he calls "my beloved." The phrase "fellow worker" means someone who labors alongside others in the work of the gospel, and the name Stachys is simply the name of this person, while "my beloved" expresses personal affection.

Paul writes this letter to the church in Rome and, at the end, sends greetings to many people by name. Beyond what this verse says, we know nothing more about Urbanus and Stachys. Urbanus seems to have worked with Paul and others, since Paul calls him "our." This list shows that Paul valued each person, not only the well-known leaders.

For today: notice those who serve without being seen and express your gratitude to them. A greeting, a message, or a word of affection can greatly encourage someone who faithfully helps in your church.
exp.14:5:
He says that God wants believers to live in harmony, so that together, with one mind and one voice, they glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. "One mind" means being united, in agreement. "One voice" means speaking together. "Glorify" means to honor and praise.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were Jews and non-Jews who had differences over customs and food. Before this, he asks that God give them patience and comfort so that they may be of one mind. Unity does not mean thinking identically about everything, but following the example of Christ. The final purpose is that God be praised.

For today: if there is tension with another believer over secondary matters, seek peace first. Pray for that person and, if you can, praise God together. Shared worship helps heal divisions.
exp.7:23:
This verse says that we were saved with our eyes fixed on the future. "In this hope we were saved" means that we have already received salvation, but we do not yet see its fullness. Hope, by its nature, concerns something that is not in plain sight. If we already see it, there is nothing left to hope for. "Who hopes for what he can already see?" is the point of the verse's question.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of creation groaning and of us, who also groan, waiting for the redemption of our bodies. He recognizes that present life carries pain, but he places it within a promise that has not yet been fulfilled.

For today: when you go through a difficult wait, do not lose heart because you cannot yet see the result. Entrust your patience to God and remember that waiting for what is not yet seen is a normal part of Christian faith.
exp.14:32:
This verse is a short blessing. Paul wishes that the God who gives peace will be with all the believers in Rome.

Paul writes at the end of his letter to the Romans. He has just asked them to pray for him: that he would be rescued from those who oppose him in Judea, that the help for the poor in Jerusalem would be well received, and that he could visit them with joy. After speaking of dangers and tensions, he closes with this wish of peace for the whole church.

For today: when you feel pressure or worry, pray for others and ask that God's peace be with them, and with you too. You can bless someone today with a simple prayer: "May the God of peace be with you."
exp.3:24:
This verse says that Jesus was handed over to death because of our sins, and that God raised him to life so that we would be declared righteous. "Trespasses" are the wrongs and faults we commit against God. "Justification" means being declared righteous before God, as if there were no guilt. "Handed over to death" is understood to refer to his death on the cross.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken about Abraham, whose faith God counted to him as righteousness. Now he says that this same principle applies to us, who believe in God, who raised Jesus from the dead. With this verse he closes the chapter and sums up the gospel: the cross and the resurrection go together.

For today: when you feel guilty for your failures, remember that Christ has already paid for them and that his resurrection confirms your forgiveness. Rest in that promise and respond with confidence and gratitude.
exp.0:18:
This verse says that what can be known about God is already plain to all people, because God himself has made it plain to them.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that the gospel shows God's righteousness and that his wrath is revealed against those who hold back the truth through wickedness. Here he explains why no one has an excuse: God has not hidden himself but has made himself known, above all through creation, as the next verse says.

For today: God is not a distant mystery. When you see a sunrise, or feel your conscience, you can stop and give thanks to him. And when you speak about God with others, do it with humility, remembering that he is already speaking to them in many ways.
exp.9:9:
It says that faith begins in the deepest part of a person, in the heart, and that God declares us right with him when we truly believe. But that faith does not stay hidden: it is expressed with the mouth, by confessing Jesus. "Justified" means being declared righteous before God. "Saved" here means saved, not just the healing of the body.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that salvation is not earned by keeping the law, but is received through faith in Christ. He quotes Deuteronomy to show that the message is near to everyone and that it is for Jews and Greeks alike. The verses that follow stress that God is generous with everyone who calls on him.

For today: do not keep your faith only in your mind. This week, tell someone simply and without pressure what Jesus has done in your life.
exp.5:11:
This verse says that sin should not rule over our lives. "Reign" is like a king who gives orders. "Mortal body" is our present life, weak and temporary. "Desires" are the urges that push us toward wrong. "Obey" reminds us that we can choose whom we follow.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that, because the believer is joined to Christ in his death and resurrection, the believer no longer belongs to the realm of sin. That is why he tells them to consider themselves dead to sin and alive to God. His aim is to encourage, not to condemn: they live under grace.

For today: when temptation comes, remember who you are in Christ. Before you react, pray briefly and ask God for strength. Then choose one concrete action that honors God.
exp.9:16:
Romans 10:17 says that faith comes from hearing, and that hearing comes through the word of Christ. The message is the gospel. "Consequently" means "as a result," and "hearing" means more than catching sounds: it means taking in with attention what is announced. The verse speaks of the word of Christ, which is the message of the gospel.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He explains that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, needs to hear the gospel in order to believe. For this reason he speaks of messengers who are sent and of Israel's response, which not everyone accepted. Then he insists that they have indeed heard.

For today: make room each day to listen to the Bible, whether by reading it or hearing it with others. And if you want others to believe, share the word of Christ simply, trusting that He makes faith grow.
exp.13:18:
This verse says that Christians should make an effort to pursue what brings peace and what helps others grow in faith. "Let us pursue" means to go after something with determination. "Mutual edification" means building up and strengthening one another, the way a house is built. The word "mutual" shows that this is meant to go in both directions.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there was tension among believers about what to eat and which days to observe. Some were stricter and others were freer. Paul reminds them that the kingdom of God is not about food, but about righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. For that reason he asks them not to cause a fellow believer to stumble over secondary matters.

Today, before arguing over an opinion or a custom, ask yourself: "Does this bring peace and help my brother or sister grow?" Sometimes it is good to give way, in love, to take care of someone who is weaker in faith.
exp.15:6:
Paul sends greetings to Andronicus and Junia. He calls them "fellow countrymen," which probably means they were Jews like him, and "fellow prisoners," meaning that at some point they were imprisoned with him. He says they are "outstanding among the apostles," and that they were in Christ before he was. Some understand that the apostles held them in high regard; others take it that they themselves were apostles in the sense of messengers sent out. This is a debated point.

Paul closes his letter to the Romans with a long list of personal greetings. He does not know everyone, but he wants to honor those who have served the gospel faithfully and at great cost.

Today, we can imitate Paul by openly recognizing those who have served faithfully, especially those who suffered or worked without anyone noticing. Thanking someone today for their service to Christ can encourage them greatly.
exp.5:14:
Paul asks a question: if we are not under law but under grace, can we go on sinning? His answer is firm: "Certainly not!" That is, by no means. To be under the law means to depend on keeping rules in order to be accepted; to be under grace means to live by God's undeserved favor.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome. He has already explained that God's grace is abundant, and now he anticipates a misunderstanding: thinking that grace is permission to sin. He uses the image of serving a master. Whoever gives himself over to sin serves sin, but whoever obeys God lives in righteousness.

For today: grace is not an excuse but a new freedom. When you feel the temptation to justify something wrong by saying that God will forgive you, remember that his grace was given to you so that you might live for him.
exp.14:15:
Paul says that God gave him the task of serving Christ Jesus as a minister to the Gentiles, the non-Jewish peoples. His work is to carry out the gospel of God in a sacred service, like a priest at the altar. His goal is that the Gentiles become an offering acceptable to God, made holy by the Holy Spirit.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, whom he praises for their goodness and knowledge. He explains that it was a bold thing for him to write to them because God gave him that responsibility. He uses temple language, like a priest presenting an offering, but the offering is the people who believe in Christ.

God does not only save us; he also sets us apart for himself through his Spirit. If you share the gospel, remember that your service is valuable to God, and that the change in people is his work.
exp.10:20:
This verse says that if God did not spare the natural branches, that is, the people of Israel who did not believe, then he will certainly not spare the non-Jewish believers either if they become proud. "Spare" here means he did not hold back from judgment or free them from punishment. "Grafted in" means joined on by grafting.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He uses the image of an olive tree: Israel is the original branches, and the non-Jews are branches grafted in. He warns them not to think themselves superior to Israel, since all of them stand only by faith. How this warning applies to the security of salvation, Christians have understood in different ways.

For today: when you feel firm in your faith, do not become proud or judge others. Live with humility and gratitude, trusting each day in the goodness of God.
exp.7:16:
It says that if we are children of God, then we are also heirs: we will receive what God has prepared, together with Christ. The condition is that we suffer with Him, so that we may also be glorified with Him.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that the Spirit makes us adopted children and allows us to call God "Abba, Father." Now he explains that being a child brings an inheritance, but also the path of Christ, who went through suffering before glory. Later he will say that this suffering is not worth comparing with the glory to come.

For today: when you suffer for following Jesus, or for doing what is right, remember that you are not alone or forsaken. You are a beloved child, and your pain is not the end of the story.
exp.2:3:
It says that the unbelief of some does not cancel out the faithfulness of God. "Certainly not!" is a firm refusal: never! Even if every human being turned out to be a liar, God would still be true. "So that You may be proved right when You speak" means that God is shown to be right and faithful in what he says. "And victorious when You judge" means that God comes out the winner when someone tries to bring a charge against him.

In this letter Paul writes to believers in Rome, and he answers possible objections from a Jew. If some of Israel did not believe, did God fail in his promises? Paul says no. He quotes Psalm 51:4, where David acknowledges his sin and declares that God is just. Many scholars see the same turn there: human sin brings out the righteousness of God.

For today: when you doubt God or his Word because others fail, or even because you yourself fail, rest in the fact that he remains faithful. Trust what God says more than the changing opinions of people.
exp.10:35:
Everything that exists comes from God, is held together by his power, and exists for him. Nothing falls outside his work. For that reason, the right response is to give him glory forever. Those words of "forever" are the only part that needs no further comment here.

The apostle Paul is speaking in his letter to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of God's plan for Israel and for the nations, and he is left in awe of his wisdom. The earlier questions, which recall the prophet Isaiah and Job, show that no one advises God or can put him in debt. This verse closes that praise.

Today, when something is hard for you to understand, remember that God owes you no explanations, but he does deserve your trust. Thank him for what you have, since all of it comes from him, and offer him your work and your plans as a way of giving him glory.

sum.5: Paul teaches that whoever is united with Christ in his death and resurrection has already died to sin and now lives for God. Because of this, we should not keep sinning or let sin rule us. Instead, we should give ourselves to God to do what is right. Sin pays with death, but God gives the gift of eternal life in Christ.
sum.9: Paul longs with all his heart for Israel to be saved, but he says they have zeal for God without understanding that righteousness comes through faith in Christ, not through their own effort. He teaches that whoever confesses Jesus as Lord and believes that God raised him from the dead will be saved, whether Jew or Greek. For this reason, it is necessary that the gospel be preached and heard.
sum.10: Paul teaches that God has not rejected Israel, since there has always remained a chosen remnant by grace. Their stumbling opened the way of salvation to the Gentiles, who must be humble, like branches grafted into an olive tree. God is faithful and merciful to all, and for this reason Paul concludes by praising his wisdom.
sum.13: Paul teaches that believers should not judge or look down on one another over differences such as food or special days, because each person lives and answers to the Lord, and all of us will stand before Christ. He asks people to love their brother, not to cause him to stumble, and to pursue peace, since the kingdom of God is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.
sum.15: Paul commends Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchreae, and warmly greets many believers in Rome who worked for the Lord, including Priscilla and Aquila. He asks the believers to keep away from those who cause divisions and deceive people with smooth talk, and to be wise about what is good. He ends with greetings from his companions and with praise to the one wise God.
sum.0: Paul introduces himself to the Christians in Rome, thanks God for their faith, and says he wants to visit them. He affirms that the gospel is the power of God to save everyone who believes, and that the righteous will live by faith. He then explains that people rejected God, even though God could be known through creation, and so they fell into idolatry and wickedness.
sum.7: Paul teaches that those who are in Christ no longer face condemnation, because the Spirit gives them life, makes them children of God, and supports them in their weakness. Although there is suffering today, and all creation is waiting to be set free, God works all things together for good. Nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
sum.4: Through believing in Christ, we are justified and have peace with God, hope, and the love of God in our hearts, even in trials. Christ died for us while we were still sinners and enemies, and in this way he reconciled us to God. Through Adam's disobedience, sin and death entered, but through Jesus's obedience, grace overflowed into eternal life.
sum.6: Paul uses the example of marriage to explain that, just as death frees a person from the husband's law, believers have died to the law through Christ so that they can serve God in a new spirit. The law is holy and good, but it reveals sin and does not give the power to overcome it. Paul describes his inner struggle and thanks God through Jesus Christ.
sum.3: Paul explains that Abraham was declared righteous because he believed God, not because of his works or because of circumcision, since the promise came before he was circumcised. In this way, Abraham is the father of all who believe, whether Jewish or not. That same faith, trusting in the God who raised Jesus from the dead, is also counted to us as righteousness.
sum.14: Paul urges those who are strong in faith to help the weak and to live in unity, following the example of Christ, who welcomed both Jews and non-Jews. He then describes how he has preached the gospel to the Gentiles and his plan to visit Rome on his way to Spain, after first taking a collection to the poor in Jerusalem. He asks for prayers.
sum.1: Paul shows that God judges with truth and without partiality, and that no one can condemn others while doing the same things themselves. God is patient, leading us toward repentance, and he will repay each person according to their deeds. Both Jews and Gentiles will be judged, because what matters is obeying from the heart, not merely knowing the law or having circumcision.
sum.2: Paul explains that God is faithful even when people fail, and that both Jews and non-Jews are under sin, so no one is saved by keeping the law. God's righteousness comes as a free gift through faith in Jesus Christ, through his redemption, for everyone who believes.
sum.8: Paul feels deep sorrow for his people, Israel, who received so many promises and who gave rise to Christ. He explains that God acts according to his promise and his mercy, not because of human merit, and that he calls both Jews and Gentiles. Israel stumbled because they sought righteousness through works rather than through faith.
sum.12: Paul teaches that people should submit to governing authorities, since God has established them to reward good and punish wrongdoing, and that everyone should pay what they owe. All of this comes down to loving your neighbor, because love fulfills the law. Since the day of salvation is near, believers should put aside the deeds of darkness and clothe themselves with Jesus Christ.
sum.11: Paul asks believers, in light of God's mercy, to offer themselves fully to Him and to renew their minds instead of following the patterns of the world. He teaches them to live with humility, to use their gifts in service to everyone as one body, and to love sincerely. He also calls them to live at peace, not to take revenge, and to overcome evil with good.
